abstract: Inverse matrix calculation can be considered as an optimization. We have demonstrated that this problem can be rapidly solved by highly interconnected simple neuron-like analog processors. A network for matrix inversion based on the concept of Hopfield's neural network was designed, and implemented with electronic hardware. With slight modifications, the network is readily applicable to solving a linear simultaneous equation efficiently. Notable features of this circuit are potential speed due to parallel processing, and robustness against variations of device parameters.

paragraphs: This paper treats matrix inversion as an optimization problem and builds an electronic neural network to perform the calculation. Matrix inversion is an algebraic task, so the network serves as a numerical computing device. The authors report that highly interconnected, simple analog processors can solve the problem rapidly.

The design draws on Hopfield's neural network concept. Instead of organizing the calculation only as a sequence of separate arithmetic instructions, the circuit uses interactions among many processors. The optimization formulation connects the desired matrix calculation to the collective behavior of the network, and the authors implement that design in electronic hardware.

Two practical features motivate the approach: the potential speed of parallel processing and robustness to differences in device parameters. The latter matters because the computational elements of a physical circuit need not behave identically. The authors also state that small modifications make the network applicable to simultaneous linear equations. Together, these features position the circuit as a reusable approach to related numerical problems.
summary.tldr: The authors implement a Hopfield-inspired analog circuit that computes matrix inverses through optimization and can be adapted to solve linear equations.

title: An Optimization Network for Matrix Inversion

abstract: We present a novel, modular, recurrent connectionist network architec(cid:173) ture which learns to robustly perform incremental parsing of complex sentences. From sequential input, one word at a time, our networks learn to do semantic role assignment, noun phrase attachment, and clause structure recognition for sentences with passive constructions and center embedded clauses. The networks make syntactic and semantic predictions at every point in time, and previous predictions are revised as expectations are affirmed or violated with the arrival of new informa(cid:173) tion. Our networks induce their own "grammar rules" for dynamically transforming an input sequence of words into a syntactic/semantic in(cid:173) terpretation. These networks generalize and display tolerance to input which has been corrupted in ways common in spoken language.

paragraphs: The paper presents a modular recurrent neural architecture that learns to interpret complex sentences one word at a time. Its tasks include assigning semantic roles, determining noun phrase attachment, and recognizing clause structure. The sentences include passive constructions and clauses embedded within other clauses, requiring interpretation to account for relationships across the sequence.

At each point, the networks make predictions about syntax and meaning. As another word arrives, earlier predictions can be revised according to whether the new information supports or contradicts expectations. Parsing is therefore an evolving interpretation: the system continually updates its understanding while the sentence is still being presented.

The networks learn their own rules for transforming word sequences into syntactic and semantic interpretations. The authors report generalization and tolerance of input corrupted in ways common in spoken language. These findings matter because incremental understanding requires both learned structural relationships and the ability to adjust to imperfect evidence. The architecture brings those requirements together within a recurrent, modular learning system.
summary.tldr: Modular recurrent networks learn to parse complex sentences incrementally, revising structural and semantic predictions as words arrive.

title: Incremental Parsing by Modular Recurrent Connectionist Networks

abstract: In this paper, we prove that the vectors in the LVQ learning algorithm converge. We do this by showing that the learning algorithm performs stochastic approximation. Convergence is then obtained by identifying the appropriate conditions on the learning rate and on the underlying statistics of the classification problem. We also present a modification to the learning algorithm which we argue results in convergence of the LVQ error to the Bayesian optimal error as the appropriate parameters become large.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we prove that the vectors in the LVQ learning algorithm converge. We do this by showing that the learning algorithm performs stochastic approximation. Convergence is then obtained by identifying the appropriate conditions on the learning rate and on the underlying statistics of the classification problem. We also present a modification to the learning algorithm which we argue results in convergence of the LVQ error to the Bayesian optimal error as the appropriate parameters become large.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the vectors adjusted by the LVQ classification algorithm settle down as learning proceeds. Convergence matters because repeated updates alone do not establish that a learning process approaches a stable result. The authors provide a proof of vector convergence by connecting the algorithm to a mathematical framework for learning from noisy observations.

That framework is stochastic approximation. Viewing LVQ through it allows the authors to identify conditions involving the learning rate and the statistical properties of the classification problem. The guarantee is therefore conditional: stability follows when the update schedule and the underlying data statistics satisfy the appropriate requirements.

The paper also proposes a modification aimed at a stronger objective than stable vectors. The authors argue that its classification error approaches the Bayesian optimal error as suitable parameters become large. This is the best error achievable given the classification problem's underlying probabilities. The distinction matters: the first result establishes convergence of the representation, while the second addresses how accurate the resulting classifier can ultimately become.
summary.tldr: The paper proves conditional convergence of LVQ vectors and argues that a modified algorithm can approach Bayesian optimal classification error.

title: Convergence of a Neural Network Classifier

abstract: We present a Mean Field Theory method for locating two(cid:173) dimensional objects that have undergone rigid transformations. The resulting algorithm is a form of coarse-to-fine correlation matching. We first consider problems of matching synthetic point data, and derive a point matching objective function. A tractable line segment matching objective function is derived by considering each line segment as a dense collection of points, and approximat(cid:173) ing it by a sum of Gaussians. The algorithm is tested on real images from which line segments are extracted and matched.
originalAbstract: We present a Mean Field Theory method for locating two(cid:173) dimensional objects that have undergone rigid transformations. The resulting algorithm is a form of coarse-to-fine correlation matching. We first consider problems of matching synthetic point data, and derive a point matching objective function. A tractable line segment matching objective function is derived by considering each line segment as a dense collection of points, and approximat(cid:173) ing it by a sum of Gaussians. The algorithm is tested on real images from which line segments are extracted and matched.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for locating two-dimensional objects after rigid transformations, which change placement or orientation while preserving shape. The approach uses mean field theory and produces a coarse-to-fine correlation-matching algorithm. Its purpose is to find an alignment between object descriptions by refining the matching process across levels of detail.

The authors begin with synthetic point data and derive an objective function for matching points. They then extend the construction to line segments by treating each segment as a dense collection of points. Approximating that collection with a sum of Gaussians makes the resulting line-segment matching objective tractable.

The algorithm is tested on real images by extracting line segments and matching them. This links the mathematical point-matching formulation to an image representation used in the reported tests. The contribution is the chain from a mean-field formulation to a manageable segment objective and then to object localization in images, within the stated setting of rigidly transformed two-dimensional objects.
summary.tldr: A mean-field matching method locates rigidly transformed two-dimensional objects through coarse-to-fine alignment of points and line segments.

title: Two-Dimensional Object Localization by Coarse-to-Fine Correlation Matching

abstract: We provide a computational description of the function of the Mau(cid:173) thner system. This is the brainstem circuit which initiates fast(cid:173) start escapes in teleost fish in response to sounds. Our simula(cid:173) tions, using back propagation in a realistically constrained feedfor(cid:173) ward network, have generated hypotheses which are directly inter(cid:173) pretable in terms of the activity of the auditory nerve fibers, the principle cells of the system and their associated inhibitory neu(cid:173) rons.

This is the brainstem circuit which initiates fast(cid:173) start escapes in teleost fish in response to sounds. Our simula(cid:173) tions, using back propagation in a realistically constrained feedfor(cid:173) ward network, have generated hypotheses which are directly inter(cid:173) pretable in terms of the activity of the auditory nerve fibers, the principle cells of the system and their associated inhibitory neu(cid:173) rons.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of the Mauthner system, a brainstem circuit that triggers rapid escape responses to sounds in teleost fish. Its focus is the circuit's function in directional hearing. The modeling task connects a sensory signal to a fast behavioral response through a network constrained by the biological system.

The authors use backpropagation to train a feedforward neural network with realistic constraints. Those constraints are important to the purpose of the simulations: the resulting network behavior should be interpretable in terms of the circuit being studied. Learning provides a way to generate candidate explanations for how activity within that circuit supports its function.

The simulations produce hypotheses that can be expressed directly in terms of auditory nerve fibers, the system's principal cells, and associated inhibitory neurons. This is the central reported outcome. The network serves as a source of biologically interpretable hypotheses, connecting a computational description of directional hearing to activity in identifiable parts of the escape circuit.
summary.tldr: A biologically constrained neural simulation generates interpretable hypotheses about the fish brainstem circuit responsible for sound-triggered escapes.

title: Directional Hearing by the Mauthner System

paragraphs: This paper introduces a way for nonlinear regression models to predict error bars that change with the input. A prediction of the target's mean does not describe how uncertain that prediction is at a particular location. The method learns additional distributional information so confidence can vary across the input space.

The approach assumes a parameterized error distribution and estimates its parameters by maximum likelihood. For a Gaussian distribution, the learned width supplies the local error bar, and the paper derives the corresponding update rules. The authors state that the framework can also use other parameterized unimodal distributions, making the chosen distribution an explicit modeling assumption.

The method is demonstrated on generated data with locally varying Gaussian noise and on laser data from the Santa Fe Time Series Competition. In the laser case, known quantization noise allows the error bars to provide local estimates of model misspecification. In both applications, training also induces a weighted-regression effect that improves generalization. The contribution therefore links input-dependent uncertainty estimates with improvements in the fitted predictor.
summary.tldr: Maximum-likelihood learning produces input-dependent regression error bars and a weighting effect that improves generalization.

title: Learning Local Error Bars for Nonlinear Regression

abstract: A novel two-terminal device, consisting of a thin 1000Å layer of p+ a-Si:H sandwiched between Vanadium and Chromium electrodes, exhibits a non-volatile, analogue memory action. This device stores synaptic weights in an ANN chip, replacing the capacitor previously used for dynamic weight storage. Two different synapse designs are discussed and results are presented.
originalAbstract: A novel two-terminal device, consisting of a thin 1000Å layer of p+ a-Si:H sandwiched between Vanadium and Chromium electrodes, exhibits a non-volatile, analogue memory action. This device stores synaptic weights in an ANN chip, replacing the capacitor previously used for dynamic weight storage. Two different synapse designs are discussed and results are presented.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a physical memory device for storing synaptic weights in an artificial neural-network chip. Its defining property is non-volatile analog storage: it retains an adjustable value rather than relying on the dynamic storage previously provided by a capacitor. The stored value serves as the strength of a hardware synapse.

The device has two terminals and contains a thin, 1000-angstrom layer of p+ hydrogenated amorphous silicon between vanadium and chromium electrodes. This material arrangement exhibits the memory behavior used by the circuit. The contribution therefore connects a specific device structure with a neural-hardware requirement, rather than treating weight storage as an abstract numerical operation.

The authors discuss two synapse designs and present results for the proposed approach. The architectural significance is the replacement of a dynamic weight-storage component with a non-volatile analog memory element. A neural chip needs both computation and a physical way to retain its connection strengths; this work addresses that storage function directly within pulsestream synapses.
summary.tldr: A two-terminal amorphous-silicon analog memory replaces dynamic capacitor storage for synaptic weights in neural hardware.

title: Pulsestream Synapses with Non-Volatile Analogue Amorphous-Silicon Memories

abstract: Deformable models are an attractive approach to recognizing nonrigid objects which have considerable within class variability. However, there are severe search problems associated with fitting the models to data. We show that by using neural networks to provide better starting points, the search time can be significantly reduced. The method is demonstrated on a character recognition task.
originalAbstract: Deformable models are an attractive approach to recognizing nonrigid objects which have considerable within class variability. However, there are severe search problems associated with fitting the models to data. We show that by using neural networks to provide better starting points, the search time can be significantly reduced. The method is demonstrated on a character recognition task.

paragraphs: Objects in the same category can have substantially different shapes. A deformable model handles this variability by allowing its shape to change as it is fitted to an observation. This makes the approach attractive for recognizing nonrigid objects, but fitting introduces a difficult search problem: the system must find a configuration that matches the data.

The paper uses a neural network to supply a better initial configuration for that search. The network therefore contributes an informed starting point, after which the deformable model can be fitted. This division of work connects a learned prediction with a representation designed to accommodate differences in shape.

The method is demonstrated on character recognition, and the authors report a significant reduction in search time. The finding highlights the importance of initialization: improving where fitting begins can make a flexible recognition model more practical to use. The central contribution is a way to reduce the computational burden associated with fitting deformable models to variable examples.
summary.tldr: A neural network supplies better starting configurations for deformable models, significantly reducing fitting time in character recognition.

title: Using a neural net to instantiate a deformable model

abstract: We propose local error estimates together with algorithms for adap(cid:173) tive a-posteriori grid and time refinement in reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing. We consider a deterministic system with continuous state and time with infinite horizon discounted cost functional. For grid re(cid:173) finement we follow the procedure of numerical methods for the Bellman-equation. For time refinement we propose a new criterion, based on consistency estimates of discrete solutions of the Bellman(cid:173) equation. We demonstrate, that an optimal ratio of time to space discretization is crucial for optimal learning rates and accuracy of the approximate optimal value function.
originalAbstract: We propose local error estimates together with algorithms for adap(cid:173) tive a-posteriori grid and time refinement in reinforcement learn(cid:173) ing. We consider a deterministic system with continuous state and time with infinite horizon discounted cost functional. For grid re(cid:173) finement we follow the procedure of numerical methods for the Bellman-equation. For time refinement we propose a new criterion, based on consistency estimates of discrete solutions of the Bellman(cid:173) equation. We demonstrate, that an optimal ratio of time to space discretization is crucial for optimal learning rates and accuracy of the approximate optimal value function.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose the spatial grid and time resolution used in reinforcement learning for a continuous control problem. Its setting is deterministic, with continuous states and time, and an objective that discounts costs over an infinite future. Computation requires discrete approximations, making the choice of resolution part of the learning problem.

The authors propose local error estimates and algorithms that refine the grid and time discretization after examining an approximate solution. Spatial refinement follows numerical methods for the Bellman equation, which characterizes optimal value. For time refinement, they introduce a criterion based on consistency estimates, assessing how the discrete solution agrees with that equation.

The central finding is that the balance between temporal and spatial resolution is crucial for both learning rate and value-function accuracy. Refinement therefore requires coordinating two choices rather than treating each independently. The approach makes numerical approximation error an explicit guide for adapting the representation used during reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Adaptive error estimates coordinate spatial and temporal refinement to improve reinforcement learning for continuous deterministic control.

title: Adaptive Choice of Grid and Time in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A robust, integrative algorithm is presented for computing the position of the focus of expansion or axis of rotation (the singular point) in optical flow fields such as those generated by self-motion. Measurements are shown of a fully parallel CMOS analog VLSI motion sensor array which computes the direction of local motion (sign of optical flow) at each pixel and can directly implement this algorithm. The flow field singular point is computed in real time with a power consumption of less than 2 m W. Computation of the singular point for more general flow fields requires measures of field expansion and rotation, which it is shown can also be computed in real-time hardware, again using only the sign of the optical flow field. These measures, along with the location of the singular point, provide robust real-time self-motion information for the visual guidance of a moving platform such as a robot.
originalAbstract: A robust, integrative algorithm is presented for computing the position of the focus of expansion or axis of rotation (the singular point) in optical flow fields such as those generated by self-motion. Measurements are shown of a fully parallel CMOS analog VLSI motion sensor array which computes the direction of local motion (sign of optical flow) at each pixel and can directly implement this algorithm. The flow field singular point is computed in real time with a power consumption of less than 2 m W. Computation of the singular point for more general flow fields requires measures of field expansion and rotation, which it is shown can also be computed in real-time hardware, again using only the sign of the optical flow field. These measures, along with the location of the singular point, provide robust real-time self-motion information for the visual guidance of a moving platform such as a robot.

paragraphs: The paper develops an algorithm and integrated vision sensor for extracting self-motion information from optical flow, the pattern of apparent motion across an image. It targets a singular point associated with expansion or rotation. Locating this point provides a compact description of motion that can support visual guidance for a moving platform.

The sensor is a fully parallel analog CMOS VLSI array. Each pixel determines the sign of local optical flow, supplying directional information without requiring the full flow magnitude. The array can directly implement the authors' integrative algorithm. Measurements show real-time computation of the singular point with power consumption below 2 milliwatts, linking the method to a concrete low-power hardware implementation.

More general flow fields require additional information about expansion and rotation. The authors show that these quantities can also be computed in real-time hardware using flow signs alone. Together with the singular point's location, these measurements provide the robust self-motion information described in the paper. The contribution combines a compact motion representation with hardware suited to computing it continuously.
summary.tldr: A parallel analog vision sensor extracts optical-flow singular points in real time using motion signs and less than 2 milliwatts.

title: An Integrated Vision Sensor for the Computation of Optical Flow Singular Points

abstract: We analyze the conditions under which synaptic learning rules based on action potential timing can be approximated by learning rules based on firing rates. In particular, we consider a form of plasticity in which synapses depress when a presynaptic spike is followed by a postsynaptic spike, and potentiate with the opposite temporal ordering. Such differen(cid:173) tial anti-Hebbian plasticity can be approximated under certain conditions by a learning rule that depends on the time derivative of the postsynaptic firing rate. Such a learning rule acts to stabilize persistent neural activity patterns in recurrent neural networks.
originalAbstract: We analyze the conditions under which synaptic learning rules based on action potential timing can be approximated by learning rules based on firing rates. In particular, we consider a form of plasticity in which synapses depress when a presynaptic spike is followed by a postsynaptic spike, and potentiate with the opposite temporal ordering. Such differen(cid:173) tial anti-Hebbian plasticity can be approximated under certain conditions by a learning rule that depends on the time derivative of the postsynaptic firing rate. Such a learning rule acts to stabilize persistent neural activity patterns in recurrent neural networks.

paragraphs: The paper examines when a learning rule defined by individual spike times can be approximated using firing rates. These descriptions operate at different levels: one depends on the ordering of discrete neural events, while the other summarizes activity through rates. Connecting them helps explain how a spike-level mechanism can influence network dynamics.

The authors consider differential anti-Hebbian plasticity. In this rule, a synapse weakens when a presynaptic spike precedes a postsynaptic spike and strengthens when that order is reversed. Under certain conditions, the timing-based rule can be approximated by a rule depending on the time derivative of the postsynaptic firing rate, meaning how quickly that rate changes.

The resulting rate-based rule acts to stabilize persistent activity patterns in recurrent neural networks. This links sensitivity to temporal ordering at individual synapses with stability at the network level. The approximation is explicitly conditional, so the connection depends on the circumstances under which spike timing can be represented by the stated rate-change rule.
summary.tldr: Under certain conditions, anti-Hebbian spike-timing plasticity becomes a firing-rate-change rule that stabilizes persistent network activity.

title: Spike-based Learning Rules and Stabilization of Persistent Neural Activity

abstract: Many processes in biology, from the regulation of gene expression in bacteria to memory in the brain, involve switches constructed from networks of biochemical reactions. Crucial molecules are present in small numbers, raising questions about noise and stability. Analysis of noise in simple reaction schemes indicates that switches stable for years and switchable in milliseconds can be built from fewer than one hundred molecules. Prospects for direct tests of this prediction, as well as implications, are discussed.
originalAbstract: Many processes in biology, from the regulation of gene expression in bacteria to memory in the brain, involve switches constructed from networks of biochemical reactions. Crucial molecules are present in small numbers, raising questions about noise and stability. Analysis of noise in simple reaction schemes indicates that switches stable for years and switchable in milliseconds can be built from fewer than one hundred molecules. Prospects for direct tests of this prediction, as well as implications, are discussed.

paragraphs: Biological switches can be built from networks of chemical reactions, with roles ranging from gene regulation to memory in the brain. When only small numbers of important molecules are present, fluctuations raise a basic question: can such a switch reliably retain its state? This paper studies that question through noise analysis in simple reaction schemes.

The analysis indicates that fewer than one hundred molecules can support switches stable for years yet capable of switching within milliseconds. These are two different properties: resistance to unwanted state changes and the ability to change state quickly. The finding suggests that a small molecular system can combine both, despite the importance of noise at that scale.

The result is presented as a prediction from the analyzed reaction schemes. The paper discusses prospects for direct experimental tests and considers its implications. Its significance is that long-lasting stability and rapid switching need not require a large population of molecules in those schemes, making small biochemical networks plausible candidates for reliable switch-like behavior.
summary.tldr: Noise analysis predicts that biochemical switches with fewer than one hundred molecules can remain stable for years while switching in milliseconds.

title: Stability and Noise in Biochemical Switches

abstract: We present a new approach to bounding the true error rate of a continuous valued classiﬁer based upon PAC-Bayes bounds. The method ﬁrst con- structs a distribution over classiﬁers by determining how sensitive each parameter in the model is to noise. The true error rate of the stochastic classiﬁer found with the sensitivity analysis can then be tightly bounded using a PAC-Bayes bound. In this paper we demonstrate the method on artiﬁcial neural networks with results of a  order of magnitude im- provement vs. the best deterministic neural net bounds.
originalAbstract: We present a new approach to bounding the true error rate of a continuous valued classiﬁer based upon PAC-Bayes bounds. The method ﬁrst con- structs a distribution over classiﬁers by determining how sensitive each parameter in the model is to noise. The true error rate of the stochastic classiﬁer found with the sensitivity analysis can then be tightly bounded using a PAC-Bayes bound. In this paper we demonstrate the method on artiﬁcial neural networks with results of a  order of magnitude im- provement vs. the best deterministic neural net bounds.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to bound a classifier’s true error rate using PAC-Bayes theory. Its starting point is sensitivity: how much does the model’s behavior change when noise is added to each parameter? This information is used to construct a distribution over classifiers from a continuous-valued model.

The resulting object is a stochastic classifier defined through that distribution. A PAC-Bayes bound is then applied to its true error rate. The sensitivity analysis and the bound serve complementary roles: the analysis determines the classifier distribution, and the bound provides an error guarantee for the stochastic classifier that results.

The authors demonstrate the method on artificial neural networks and report substantially tighter bounds than the best deterministic neural-network bounds used in their comparison. The supplied text does not preserve the numerical improvement clearly. The essential distinction is that the reported guarantee concerns the stochastic classifier constructed by the method. The contribution is a route from parameter sensitivity to informative error bounds through a distribution over models.
summary.tldr: Parameter-noise sensitivity guides a stochastic classifier construction whose PAC-Bayes error bounds substantially improve on compared deterministic neural-network bounds.

title: (Not) Bounding the True Error

abstract: We show the existence of critical points as lines for the likelihood func- tion of mixture-type models. They are given by embedding of a critical point for models with less components. A sufﬁcient condition that the critical line gives local maxima or saddle points is also derived. Based on this fact, a component-split method is proposed for a mixture of Gaus- sian components, and its effectiveness is veriﬁed through experiments.
originalAbstract: We show the existence of critical points as lines for the likelihood func- tion of mixture-type models. They are given by embedding of a critical point for models with less components. A sufﬁcient condition that the critical line gives local maxima or saddle points is also derived. Based on this fact, a component-split method is proposed for a mixture of Gaus- sian components, and its effectiveness is veriﬁed through experiments.

paragraphs: Fitting a mixture model involves searching a likelihood surface whose shape can affect how learning proceeds. This paper shows that critical points in mixture-type models can form entire lines. These lines arise by embedding a critical point from a model with fewer components into a model with more components.

The result connects the optimization geometry of models of different sizes. A solution in the smaller model can correspond to a family of critical configurations in the larger one. The authors also derive a sufficient condition for identifying when such a critical line consists of local maxima or saddle points. A sufficient condition establishes a case where the conclusion holds without claiming to cover every case.

Using this analysis, the paper proposes a component-splitting method for Gaussian mixture models. The method turns the structural result about critical lines into a practical approach to modifying mixture components. Experiments verify its effectiveness, connecting the theoretical account of the likelihood surface with an evaluated learning procedure.
summary.tldr: An analysis of critical lines in mixture-model likelihoods motivates a Gaussian component-splitting method whose effectiveness is verified experimentally.

title: Critical Lines in Symmetry of Mixture Models and its Application to Component Splitting

abstract: Optimal solutions to Markov Decision Problems (MDPs) are very sen- sitive with respect to the state transition probabilities. In many practi- cal problems, the estimation of those probabilities is far from accurate. Hence, estimation errors are limiting factors in applying MDPs to real- world problems. We propose an algorithm for solving ﬁnite-state and ﬁnite-action MDPs, where the solution is guaranteed to be robust with respect to estimation errors on the state transition probabilities. Our al- gorithm involves a statistically accurate yet numerically efﬁcient repre- sentation of uncertainty, via Kullback-Leibler divergence bounds. The worst-case complexity of the robust algorithm is the same as the origi- nal Bellman recursion. Hence, robustness can be added at practically no extra computing cost.
originalAbstract: Optimal solutions to Markov Decision Problems (MDPs) are very sen- sitive with respect to the state transition probabilities. In many practi- cal problems, the estimation of those probabilities is far from accurate. Hence, estimation errors are limiting factors in applying MDPs to real- world problems. We propose an algorithm for solving ﬁnite-state and ﬁnite-action MDPs, where the solution is guaranteed to be robust with respect to estimation errors on the state transition probabilities. Our al- gorithm involves a statistically accurate yet numerically efﬁcient repre- sentation of uncertainty, via Kullback-Leibler divergence bounds. paragraphs: A Markov decision problem requires probabilities describing how actions move the system between states. The paper addresses the sensitivity of optimal solutions to errors in those probabilities. Since transition estimates can be inaccurate in practical applications, a policy optimized for the estimated model may depend heavily on uncertain information.

The authors propose an algorithm for problems with finite state and action sets that explicitly represents transition uncertainty. They use bounds based on Kullback–Leibler divergence, describing the representation as statistically accurate and numerically efficient. The resulting solution has a robustness guarantee with respect to transition-estimation errors covered by this uncertainty representation.

The algorithm’s worst-case complexity matches that of the original Bellman recursion. The authors consequently argue that robustness can be introduced at practically no extra computational cost. This combines two aims that matter together: accounting for uncertain dynamics and preserving computational tractability. The guarantee concerns the modeled transition uncertainty in the stated finite setting, while the complexity result explains why incorporating that uncertainty need not change the worst-case computational order.
summary.tldr: An algorithm uses KL-divergence bounds to make finite MDP solutions robust to transition uncertainty while matching Bellman recursion’s worst-case complexity.

title: Robustness in Markov Decision Problems with Uncertain Transition Matrices

abstract: A recent area of signiﬁcant progress in speaker recognition is the use of high level features—idiolect, phonetic relations, prosody, discourse structure, etc. A speaker not only has a distinctive acoustic sound but uses language in a characteristic manner. Large corpora of speech data available in recent years allow experimentation with long term statistics of phone patterns, word patterns, etc. of an individual. We propose the use of support vector machines and term frequency analysis of phone se- quences to model a given speaker. To this end, we explore techniques for text categorization applied to the problem. We derive a new kernel based upon a linearization of likelihood ratio scoring. We introduce a new phone-based SVM speaker recognition approach that halves the er- ror rate of conventional phone-based approaches.

Large speech corpora make it possible to study these patterns statistically and use them to model individual speakers.

The approach combines support vector machines with term-frequency analysis of phone sequences, borrowing techniques from text categorization. Instead of treating the recording only as an acoustic signal, it uses counts of phonetic patterns as evidence about the speaker. The authors also derive a new kernel by linearizing likelihood-ratio scoring, connecting the classifier to a scoring approach used for recognition.

The resulting phone-based SVM approach halves the error rate of conventional phone-based approaches in the reported comparison. This is a substantial stated improvement within that category of speaker-recognition methods. The result supports the usefulness of characteristic phonetic sequence usage and shows how methods for classifying text can be adapted to identity information contained in speech patterns.
summary.tldr: Support vector machines using phone-sequence frequencies halve the reported error rate of conventional phone-based speaker recognition.

title: Phonetic Speaker Recognition with Support Vector Machines

abstract: Planning in partially observable domains is a notoriously difﬁcult problem. How- ever, in many real-world scenarios, planning can be simpliﬁed by decomposing the task into a hierarchy of smaller planning problems. Several approaches have been proposed to optimize a policy that decomposes according to a hierarchy speciﬁed a priori. In this paper, we investigate the problem of automatically discovering the hierarchy. More precisely, we frame the optimization of a hierarchical policy as a non-convex optimization problem that can be solved with general non-linear solvers, a mixed-integer non-linear approximation or a form of bounded hierar- chical policy iteration. By encoding the hierarchical structure as variables of the optimization problem, we can automatically discover a hierarchy. Our method is ﬂexible enough to allow any parts of the hierarchy to be speciﬁed based on prior knowledge while letting the optimization discover the unknown parts. It can also discover hierarchical policies, including recursive policies, that are more compact (potentially inﬁnitely fewer parameters) and often easier to understand given the decomposition induced by the hierarchy.

paragraphs: Planning becomes difficult when an agent cannot fully observe its environment. Breaking a task into smaller planning problems can help, but many approaches require someone to supply that hierarchy in advance. This paper investigates how to discover the hierarchy automatically while optimizing the policy that uses it.

The authors formulate hierarchical policy optimization as a non-convex optimization problem. The hierarchy itself is represented by variables, allowing its structure to be chosen during optimization. They describe approaches using general nonlinear solvers, a mixed-integer nonlinear approximation, and bounded hierarchical policy iteration. Known pieces of the hierarchy can be fixed from prior knowledge while the remaining pieces are learned.

The framework can discover hierarchical policies that include recursion. The authors state that such policies can be more compact, potentially requiring infinitely fewer parameters, and are often easier to understand through their decomposition. The significance is that task organization becomes part of the planning problem rather than a prerequisite supplied entirely by a designer. Compactness and interpretability are possible benefits of the discovered structure.
summary.tldr: Encoding policy hierarchy as optimization variables lets a planner discover task decompositions, including recursive structures, in partially observable environments.

title: Automated Hierarchy Discovery for Planning in Partially Observable Environments

abstract: The time-histogram method is a handy tool for capturing the instantaneous rate of spike occurrence. In most of the neurophysiological literature, the bin size that critically determines the goodness of the fit of the time-histogram to the underlying rate has been selected by individual researchers in an unsystematic manner. We propose an objective method for selecting the bin size of a time-histogram from the spike data, so that the time-histogram best approximates the unknown underlying rate. The resolution of the histogram increases, or the optimal bin size decreases, with the number of spike sequences sampled. It is notable that the optimal bin size diverges if only a small number of experimental trials are available from a moderately fluctuating rate process. In this case, any attempt to characterize the underlying spike rate will lead to spurious results. Given a paucity of data, our method can also suggest how many more trials are needed until the set of data can be analyzed with the required resolution.

paragraphs: A time histogram estimates how a neuron's spike rate changes by collecting spikes into time bins. The width of those bins determines the time resolution and strongly affects how faithfully the histogram represents the underlying rate. This paper replaces an informal researcher choice with an objective selection method based on the recorded spikes.

The method selects a bin size intended to best approximate the unknown rate. Its analysis connects achievable resolution to the amount of data: more sampled spike sequences permit smaller optimal bins. This makes the time scale visible in a histogram a question of what the observations support, rather than simply how finely someone chooses to plot them.

A particularly consequential result concerns too few trials from a moderately fluctuating rate process. In that case, the optimal bin size can diverge, signaling that attempts to characterize the changing rate would produce spurious results. The method can also suggest how many additional trials are needed to reach a requested resolution, connecting analysis choices directly to experimental planning.
summary.tldr: An objective histogram rule selects time-bin widths from spike data and can indicate when more trials are needed.

title: A recipe for optimizing a time-histogram

abstract: We introduce a new Bayesian model for hierarchical clustering based on a prior over trees called Kingman’s coalescent. We develop novel greedy and sequential Monte Carlo inferences which operate in a bottom-up agglomerative fashion. We show experimentally the superiority of our algorithms over the state-of-the-art, and demonstrate our approach in document clustering and phylolinguistics.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new Bayesian model for hierarchical clustering based on a prior over trees called Kingman’s coalescent. We develop novel greedy and sequential Monte Carlo inferences which operate in a bottom-up agglomerative fashion. We show experimentally the superiority of our algorithms over the state-of-the-art, and demonstrate our approach in document clustering and phylolinguistics.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering describes data through nested groups, represented as a tree. This paper gives that tree a Bayesian treatment by using Kingman’s coalescent as a prior. The prior provides a probabilistic starting point for possible hierarchies, so the clustering problem becomes inference about a tree rather than simply a sequence of grouping decisions.

The authors develop two inference approaches that construct the hierarchy from the bottom upward by merging groups. One is greedy, committing to choices as construction proceeds. The other uses sequential Monte Carlo, a sampling approach to inference. Both retain the agglomerative structure of repeatedly combining smaller groups into larger ones within the proposed probabilistic model.

The paper reports experimental superiority over the state of the art and demonstrates applications to document clustering and phylolinguistics. These examples show the model being used to organize both documents and language relationships. The central contribution is the combination of a tree prior with workable bottom-up inference methods; the reported performance advantage is an experimental finding.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian hierarchy model based on Kingman’s coalescent supports bottom-up clustering algorithms with reported experimental advantages.

title: Bayesian Agglomerative Clustering with Coalescents

abstract: The learning of probabilistic models with many hidden variables and non- decomposable dependencies is an important and challenging problem. In contrast to traditional approaches based on approximate inference in a single intractable model, our approach is to train a set of tractable submodels by encouraging them to agree on the hidden variables. This allows us to capture non-decomposable aspects of the data while still maintaining tractability. We propose an objective function for our approach, derive EM-style algorithms for parameter estimation, and demonstrate their effectiveness on three challenging real-world learning tasks.

This allows us to capture non-decomposable aspects of the data while still maintaining tractability. We propose an objective function for our approach, derive EM-style algorithms for parameter estimation, and demonstrate their effectiveness on three challenging real-world learning tasks.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models become difficult to train when they contain many unobserved variables and dependencies that do not break into convenient pieces. Those dependencies may be important for describing the data, yet inference in the resulting model can become computationally intractable. The paper addresses how to retain useful dependencies while keeping learning manageable.

Its central idea is to train several tractable submodels and encourage them to agree about the hidden variables. Each submodel supports manageable inference, while agreement connects the explanations they learn. The authors introduce an objective function for this approach and derive parameter-estimation algorithms in the style of expectation maximization.

The approach therefore places coordination among simpler models at the center of learning, allowing the collection to capture aspects of the data that do not decompose easily. Experiments on three challenging real-world learning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. The stated contribution combines a learning objective, a practical estimation procedure, and empirical support for using agreement to connect tractable models.
summary.tldr: Training tractable submodels to agree on hidden variables offers a manageable way to learn complex probabilistic dependencies.

title: Agreement-Based Learning

abstract: Clustering is often formulated as a discrete optimization problem. The objective is to ﬁnd, among all partitions of the data set, the best one according to some quality measure. However, in the statistical setting where we assume that the ﬁnite data set has been sampled from some underlying space, the goal is not to ﬁnd the best partition of the given sample, but to approximate the true partition of the under- lying space. We argue that the discrete optimization approach usually does not achieve this goal. As an alternative, we suggest the paradigm of “nearest neighbor clustering”. Instead of selecting the best out of all partitions of the sample, it only considers partitions in some restricted function class. Using tools from statistical learning theory we prove that nearest neighbor clustering is statistically consis- tent. Moreover, its worst case complexity is polynomial by construction, and it can be implemented with small average case complexity using branch and bound.

Moreover, its worst case complexity is polynomial by construction, and it can be implemented with small average case complexity using branch and bound.

paragraphs: A clustering method can find the best partition of a dataset without recovering the structure that generated those observations. This paper makes that distinction central. When the observed data are a sample from a larger space, the statistical goal is to approximate a partition of that space. The authors argue that unrestricted optimization over sample partitions usually does not accomplish this.

Their alternative, nearest neighbor clustering, restricts the partitions considered to a particular class of functions. This changes the search problem: success is no longer defined solely by choosing the highest-scoring partition among every possible arrangement of the observed points. The restriction becomes part of how the method connects finite observations to an underlying population.

Using statistical learning theory, the authors prove statistical consistency for this approach. They also establish polynomial worst-case computational complexity by construction and describe a branch-and-bound implementation with low average-case complexity. The contribution therefore connects a statistical objective with computational design: restricting the search can support both meaningful recovery and manageable computation.
summary.tldr: Restricting the clustering search yields a statistically consistent method with polynomial worst-case complexity.

title: Consistent Minimization of Clustering Objective Functions

abstract: Sparse coding, a method of explaining sensory data with as few dictionary bases as possible, has attracted much attention in computer vision. For visual object category recognition, L1 regularized sparse coding is combined with spatial pyramid representation to obtain state-of-the-art performance. However, because of its iterative optimization, applying sparse coding onto every local feature descriptor extracted from an image database can become a major bottleneck. To overcome this computational challenge, this paper presents "Generalized Lasso based Approximation of Sparse coding" (GLAS). By representing the distribution of sparse coefficients with slice transform, we fit a piece-wise linear mapping function with generalized lasso. We also propose an efficient post-refinement procedure to perform mutual inhibition between bases which is essential for an overcomplete setting. The experiments show that GLAS obtains comparable performance to L1 regularized sparse coding, yet achieves significant speed up demonstrating its effectiveness for large-scale visual recognition problems.

paragraphs: Sparse coding represents an image descriptor using relatively few elements from a dictionary. Combined with spatial pyramid representations, it had achieved strong visual recognition performance. Its computational difficulty is repeated iterative optimization: applying that process to every local descriptor in a large image collection can become a major bottleneck.

The paper proposes GLAS, an approximation that learns a piecewise linear mapping using generalized Lasso. A slice transform represents the distribution of sparse coefficients used in fitting this mapping. The method also includes an efficient refinement step that introduces mutual inhibition between dictionary elements, addressing competition between bases in an overcomplete representation.

Experiments report recognition performance comparable to L1-regularized sparse coding alongside a significant speed improvement. The result suggests that approximating the coefficient computation can preserve useful recognition behavior while reducing its expense. The refinement step is part of that approach: the method includes interactions between bases as well as the fitted mapping.
summary.tldr: GLAS approximates sparse coding with a learned piecewise linear mapping and refinement, achieving comparable recognition performance with significant speedup.

title: Generalized Lasso based Approximation of Sparse Coding for Visual Recognition

abstract: We are motivated by an application to extract a representative subset of machine learning training data and by the poor empirical performance we observe of the popular minimum norm algorithm. In fact, for our application, minimum norm can have a running time of about O(n^7 ) (O(n^5 ) oracle calls). We therefore propose a fast approximate method to minimize arbitrary submodular functions. For a large sub-class of submodular functions, the algorithm is exact. Other submodular functions are iteratively approximated by tight submodular upper bounds, and then repeatedly optimized. We show theoretical properties, and empirical results suggest significant speedups over minimum norm while retaining higher accuracies.

paragraphs: The paper is motivated by selecting a representative subset of training data and by the poor practical performance of the minimum norm algorithm in that application. The authors report running time around O(n^7), including O(n^5) oracle calls. This motivates a faster approach to minimizing submodular functions, with approximation available when exact optimization is not supplied by their method.

The proposed algorithm can be applied to arbitrary submodular functions and is exact for a large subclass. For other functions, it repeatedly constructs tight submodular upper bounds and optimizes them. The process replaces the original objective with successive bounding objectives, providing an iterative route to an approximate solution.

The authors establish theoretical properties and report empirical results suggesting substantial speedups over minimum norm while retaining higher accuracies. The exactness claim remains specific to the stated subclass; the broader method is approximate. Its contribution is a practical alternative motivated by a concrete data-selection bottleneck, with both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence supporting the proposed optimization strategy.
summary.tldr: An iterative upper-bound method offers fast approximate submodular minimization and is exact for a large subclass of objectives.

title: On fast approximate submodular minimization

abstract: In this paper we apply boosting to learn complex non-linear local visual feature representations, drawing inspiration from its successful application to visual object detection. The main goal of local feature descriptors is to distinctively represent a salient image region while remaining invariant to viewpoint and illumination changes. This representation can be improved using machine learning, however, past approaches have been mostly limited to learning linear feature mappings in either the original input or a kernelized input feature space. While kernelized methods have proven somewhat effective for learning non-linear local feature descriptors, they rely heavily on the choice of an appropriate kernel function whose selection is often difficult and non-intuitive. We propose to use the boosting-trick to obtain a non-linear mapping of the input to a high-dimensional feature space. The non-linear feature mapping obtained with the boosting-trick is highly intuitive. We employ gradient-based weak learners resulting in a learned descriptor that closely resembles the well-known SIFT. As demonstrated in our experiments, the resulting descriptor can be learned directly from intensity patches achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Local image descriptors aim to identify an image region distinctively while remaining stable under changes in viewpoint and illumination. The paper learns these representations using boosting. Its motivation is that earlier learned descriptors largely relied on linear mappings, while kernel-based nonlinear methods depended heavily on choosing an appropriate kernel.

The authors use gradient-based weak learners, producing a learned descriptor that closely resembles SIFT. This gives the representation an intuitive connection to image gradients while allowing the mapping to be learned directly from intensity patches.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance with the resulting descriptor. The finding supports boosting as a useful route to nonlinear local representations, alongside its established use in object detection that inspired the work. The methodological contribution is the way the feature mapping is constructed and learned; the performance claim refers to the experiments reported in the paper.
summary.tldr: Boosting learns nonlinear local image descriptors directly from intensity patches, producing a SIFT-like representation with reported state-of-the-art performance.

title: Learning Image Descriptors with the Boosting-Trick

abstract: We estimate the sample complexity of a recent robust estimator for a generalized version of the inverse covariance matrix. This estimator is used in a convex algorithm for robust subspace recovery (i.e., robust PCA). Our model assumes a sub-Gaussian underlying distribution and an i.i.d.~sample from it. Our main result shows with high probability that the norm of the difference between the generalized inverse covariance of the underlying distribution and its estimator from an i.i.d.~sample of size $N$ is of order $O(N^{-0.5+\eps})$ for arbitrarily small $\eps>0$ (affecting the probabilistic estimate); this rate of convergence is close to one of direct covariance and inverse covariance estimation, i.e., $O(N^{-0.5})$. Our precise probabilistic estimate implies for some natural settings that the sample complexity of the generalized inverse covariance estimation when using the Frobenius norm is $O(D^{2+\delta})$ for arbitrarily small $\delta>0$ (whereas the sample complexity of direct covariance estimation with Frobenius norm is $O(D^{2})$). These results provide similar rates of convergence and sample complexity for the corresponding robust subspace recovery algorithm, which are close to those of PCA. To the best of our knowledge, this is the only work analyzing the sample complexity of any robust PCA algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper asks how many observations a particular robust subspace recovery method needs to estimate its target accurately. The analysis focuses on a robust estimator of a generalized inverse covariance matrix, used within a convex robust PCA algorithm. Its assumptions include independent, identically distributed observations from an underlying sub-Gaussian distribution.

The main result bounds the estimation error with high probability at order N^(-0.5 + epsilon), for arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The choice of epsilon affects the probability estimate. This convergence rate approaches the N^(-0.5) rate associated with direct covariance and inverse covariance estimation, giving a quantitative comparison between this robust estimator and familiar matrix estimators.

Similar convergence and sample-complexity results follow for the corresponding robust subspace recovery algorithm. The findings show rates close to those of PCA under the stated assumptions, rather than establishing identical requirements for every robust PCA method.
summary.tldr: Under i.i.d. sub-Gaussian sampling, a particular robust PCA method has convergence and sample-complexity rates close to those of ordinary PCA.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Robust PCA

abstract: Structured output learning has been successfully applied to object localization, where the mapping between an image and an object bounding box can be well captured. Its extension to action localization in videos, however, is much more challenging, because one needs to predict the locations of the action patterns both spatially and temporally, i.e., identifying a sequence of bounding boxes that track the action in video. The problem becomes intractable due to the exponentially large size of the structured video space where actions could occur. We propose a novel structured learning approach for spatio-temporal action localization. The mapping between a video and a spatio-temporal action trajectory is learned. The intractable inference and learning problems are addressed by leveraging an efficient Max-Path search method, thus makes it feasible to optimize the model over the whole structured space. Experiments on two challenging benchmark datasets show that our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

Its extension to action localization in videos, however, is much more challenging, because one needs to predict the locations of the action patterns both spatially and temporally, i.e., identifying a sequence of bounding boxes that track the action in video. The problem becomes intractable due to the exponentially large size of the structured video space where actions could occur. We propose a novel structured learning approach for spatio-temporal action localization. The mapping between a video and a spatio-temporal action trajectory is learned. The intractable inference and learning problems are addressed by leveraging an efficient Max-Path search method, thus makes it feasible to optimize the model over the whole structured space. Experiments on two challenging benchmark datasets show that our proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Localizing an action in video requires predicting both where it occurs and how its location changes over time. The output is a sequence of bounding boxes tracking the action. This is considerably more complex than locating an object in one image because the space of possible video trajectories grows exponentially.

The paper learns a mapping from a video to a complete spatio-temporal action trajectory using structured output learning. Its central computational component is an efficient Max-Path search method. This search addresses the otherwise intractable inference and learning steps, making optimization over the full structured output space feasible.

Treating the trajectory as the prediction object allows the learning problem to reflect the spatial and temporal extent of an action together. The search procedure is essential because that richer output would otherwise be too expensive to handle. Experiments on two challenging benchmark datasets show better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The reported result supports pairing trajectory-level structured learning with an inference method designed for the large video search space.
summary.tldr: Structured trajectory prediction and efficient Max-Path search make joint spatial and temporal action localization feasible.

title: Max-Margin Structured Output Regression for Spatio-Temporal Action Localization

abstract: In this work we consider a setting where we have a very large number of related tasks with few examples from each individual task. Rather than either learning each task individually (and having a large generalization error) or learning all the tasks together using a single hypothesis (and suffering a potentially large inherent error), we consider learning a small pool of {\em shared hypotheses}. Each task is then mapped to a single hypothesis in the pool (hard association). We derive VC dimension generalization bounds for our model, based on the number of tasks, shared hypothesis and the VC dimension of the hypotheses class. We conducted experiments with both synthetic problems and sentiment of reviews, which strongly support our approach.

Rather than either learning each task individually (and having a large generalization error) or learning all the tasks together using a single hypothesis (and suffering a potentially large inherent error), we consider learning a small pool of {\em shared hypotheses}. Each task is then mapped to a single hypothesis in the pool (hard association). We derive VC dimension generalization bounds for our model, based on the number of tasks, shared hypothesis and the VC dimension of the hypotheses class. We conducted experiments with both synthetic problems and sentiment of reviews, which strongly support our approach.

paragraphs: The paper considers many related learning tasks, each with only a few examples. Training a separate predictor for every task can produce large generalization error, while forcing all tasks to share one predictor can introduce substantial inherent error. The proposed solution is a small collection of predictors shared across tasks.

Each task is assigned to exactly one hypothesis in that collection, a choice called hard association. This lets multiple tasks use the same predictor without requiring every task to behave alike. The model therefore makes the size of the shared pool an explicit part of how it represents commonality and differences across tasks.

The authors derive VC-dimension generalization bounds involving the number of tasks, the number of shared hypotheses, and the complexity of the hypothesis class. Experiments on synthetic problems and review sentiment strongly support the approach. Together, the analysis and experiments support sharing at the level of a small predictor pool in the stated setting of many related tasks with scarce individual data.
summary.tldr: Assigning many data-scarce tasks to a small pool of shared predictors balances sharing with differences among tasks.

title: Learning Multiple Tasks using Shared Hypotheses

abstract: This paper proposes a way of improving classification performance for classes which have very few training examples. The key idea is to discover classes which are similar and transfer knowledge among them. Our method organizes the classes into a tree hierarchy. The tree structure can be used to impose a generative prior over classification parameters. We show that these priors can be combined with discriminative models such as deep neural networks. Our method benefits from the power of discriminative training of deep neural networks, at the same time using tree-based generative priors over classification parameters. We also propose an algorithm for learning the underlying tree structure. This gives the model some flexibility to tune the tree so that the tree is pertinent to task being solved. We show that the model can transfer knowledge across related classes using fixed semantic trees. Moreover, it can learn new meaningful trees usually leading to improved performance. Our method achieves state-of-the-art classification results on the CIFAR-100 image data set and the MIR Flickr multimodal data set.

title: Discriminative Transfer Learning with Tree-based Priors

abstract: The chief difficulty in object recognition is that objects' classes are obscured by a large number of extraneous sources of variability, such as pose and part deformation. These sources of variation can be represented by symmetry groups, sets of composable transformations that preserve object identity. Convolutional neural networks (convnets) achieve a degree of translational invariance by computing feature maps over the translation group, but cannot handle other groups. As a result, these groups' effects have to be approximated by small translations, which often requires augmenting datasets and leads to high sample complexity. In this paper, we introduce deep symmetry networks (symnets), a generalization of convnets that forms feature maps over arbitrary symmetry groups. Symnets use kernel-based interpolation to tractably tie parameters and pool over symmetry spaces of any dimension. Like convnets, they are trained with backpropagation. The composition of feature transformations through the layers of a symnet provides a new approach to deep learning. Experiments on NORB and MNIST-rot show that symnets over the affine group greatly reduce sample complexity relative to convnets by better capturing the symmetries in the data.

paragraphs: An object's appearance can vary with pose or deformation while its identity stays the same. This paper represents such identity-preserving changes through symmetry groups: collections of transformations that can be composed. It extends the idea behind convolutional feature maps, which organize responses over translations, to feature maps defined over arbitrary symmetry groups.

The resulting deep symmetry networks use kernel-based interpolation to share parameters and pool responses across symmetry spaces of any dimension in a tractable way. They are trained with backpropagation. Across layers, the composition of feature transformations provides a way to build deep representations that explicitly reflect the chosen symmetries.

Experiments on NORB and MNIST-rot use symmetry networks over the affine group. The reported results show substantially lower sample complexity than convolutional networks, attributed to better capture of the data's symmetries. This supports the idea that representing relevant transformations directly can reduce the amount of training data required in these settings. The experimental finding concerns the tested affine-group networks, while the proposed architecture has a broader formulation.
summary.tldr: Deep symmetry networks extend convolutional feature maps to symmetry groups and reduce sample complexity in the reported affine-group experiments.

title: Deep Symmetry Networks

abstract: We consider online learning problems under a a partial observability model capturing situations where the information conveyed to the learner is between full information and bandit feedback. In the simplest variant, we assume that in addition to its own loss, the learner also gets to observe losses of some other actions. The revealed losses depend on the learner's action and a directed observation system chosen by the environment. For this setting, we propose the first algorithm that enjoys near-optimal regret guarantees without having to know the observation system before selecting its actions. Along similar lines, we also define a new partial information setting that models online combinatorial optimization problems where the feedback received by the learner is between semi-bandit and full feedback. As the predictions of our first algorithm cannot be always computed efficiently in this setting, we propose another algorithm with similar properties and with the benefit of always being computationally efficient, at the price of a slightly more complicated tuning mechanism. Both algorithms rely on a novel exploration strategy called implicit exploration, which is shown to be more efficient both computationally and information-theoretically than previously studied exploration strategies for the problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies online learning when choosing an action reveals its loss and possibly the losses of other actions. Which additional losses become visible depends on the chosen action and a directed observation system selected by the environment. This creates a feedback setting between ordinary bandit feedback and observing every action's loss.

The first algorithm achieves near-optimal regret guarantees without knowing the observation system before choosing an action. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison choice. The result therefore provides a strong learning guarantee despite uncertainty about which side observations the current decision will reveal.

The authors also introduce a combinatorial setting with feedback between semi-bandit and full information. Because the first algorithm's predictions are not always efficiently computable there, they develop a second algorithm with similar properties and guaranteed computational efficiency, at the cost of more complicated tuning. Both use implicit exploration, a new strategy shown to improve computational and information-theoretic efficiency over previously studied exploration strategies for the problem.
summary.tldr: Implicit exploration gives efficient learning with strong regret guarantees when actions reveal extra losses through an initially unknown observation system.

title: Efficient learning by implicit exploration in bandit problems with side observations

abstract: We study the estimation of low rank matrices via nonconvex optimization. Compared with convex relaxation, nonconvex optimization exhibits superior empirical performance for large scale instances of low rank matrix estimation. However, the understanding of its theoretical guarantees are limited. In this paper, we define the notion of projected oracle divergence based on which we establish sufficient conditions for the success of nonconvex optimization. We illustrate the consequences of this general framework for matrix sensing and completion. In particular, we prove that a broad class of nonconvex optimization algorithms, including alternating minimization and gradient-type methods, geometrically converge to the global optimum and exactly recover the true low rank matrices under standard conditions.

We illustrate the consequences of this general framework for matrix sensing and completion. In particular, we prove that a broad class of nonconvex optimization algorithms, including alternating minimization and gradient-type methods, geometrically converge to the global optimum and exactly recover the true low rank matrices under standard conditions.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix can be approached through convex relaxation or by directly optimizing a nonconvex formulation. The paper starts from an empirical motivation: nonconvex methods have performed better on large instances, while theoretical explanations for their success have been limited. It develops a framework for identifying when that success can be guaranteed.

The framework introduces a quantity called projected oracle divergence and uses it to establish sufficient conditions for successful nonconvex optimization. These conditions provide a way to organize the analysis across algorithms. Their role is to identify settings where success follows; they are not presented as necessary conditions that every successful method must satisfy.

The authors apply the framework to matrix sensing and matrix completion. Under standard conditions, they prove geometric convergence to a global optimum and exact recovery of the underlying low-rank matrix for a broad class of algorithms, including alternating minimization and gradient-type methods. This connects several practical optimization approaches through a common conditional recovery theory.
summary.tldr: A common theoretical framework gives sufficient conditions for several nonconvex algorithms to converge geometrically and exactly recover low-rank matrices.

title: A Nonconvex Optimization Framework for Low Rank Matrix Estimation

abstract: In a traditional convolutional layer, the learned filters stay fixed after training. In contrast, we introduce a new framework, the Dynamic Filter Network, where filters are generated dynamically conditioned on an input. We show that this architecture is a powerful one, with increased flexibility thanks to its adaptive nature, yet without an excessive increase in the number of model parameters. A wide variety of filtering operation can be learned this way, including local spatial transformations, but also others like selective (de)blurring or adaptive feature extraction. Moreover, multiple such layers can be combined, e.g. in a recurrent architecture. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the dynamic filter network on the tasks of video and stereo prediction, and reach state-of-the-art performance on the moving MNIST dataset with a much smaller model. By visualizing the learned filters, we illustrate that the network has picked up flow information by only looking at unlabelled training data. This suggests that the network can be used to pretrain networks for various supervised tasks in an unsupervised way, like optical flow and depth estimation.

paragraphs: Dynamic Filter Networks make a convolutional network's filtering operations depend on the input. Ordinary convolutional filters remain fixed after training; here, the network generates filters dynamically for the data it receives. The paper argues that this adaptability expands what the architecture can do without requiring an excessive increase in model parameters.

The framework can learn operations including local spatial transformations, selective blurring or deblurring, and adaptive feature extraction. Several dynamic filtering layers can also be combined, including within recurrent architectures. This allows the filtering operation itself to change with the input rather than relying only on the responses of a fixed collection of filters.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness for video and stereo prediction, including state-of-the-art moving MNIST performance with a much smaller model. Visualizations indicate that filters learned from unlabeled data capture flow information. The authors suggest that this could make the framework useful for unsupervised pretraining for optical flow or depth estimation; that proposed use is distinct from the prediction results demonstrated.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Filter Networks generate input-dependent filters and demonstrate effective, compact models for video and stereo prediction.

title: Dynamic Filter Networks

abstract: Kernel embeddings of distributions and the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), the resulting distance between distributions, are useful tools for fully nonparametric two-sample testing and learning on distributions. However, it is rarely that all possible differences between samples are of interest -- discovered differences can be due to different types of measurement noise, data collection artefacts or other irrelevant sources of variability. We propose distances between distributions which encode invariance to additive symmetric noise, aimed at testing whether the assumed true underlying processes differ. Moreover, we construct invariant features of distributions, leading to learning algorithms robust to the impairment of the input distributions with symmetric additive noise.
