However, it is rarely that all possible differences between samples are of interest -- discovered differences can be due to different types of measurement noise, data collection artefacts or other irrelevant sources of variability. We propose distances between distributions which encode invariance to additive symmetric noise, aimed at testing whether the assumed true underlying processes differ. Moreover, we construct invariant features of distributions, leading to learning algorithms robust to the impairment of the input distributions with symmetric additive noise.

paragraphs: Comparing observed distributions can reveal differences that come from measurement noise or collection artifacts rather than the underlying processes of interest. Kernel embeddings and Maximum Mean Discrepancy provide general tools for distribution comparison, but detecting every observed difference may answer the wrong question. This paper builds a specific kind of noise invariance into that comparison.

The authors propose distances between distributions that are invariant to additive symmetric noise. The intended target is whether the assumed underlying processes differ after accounting for this source of variability. The noise condition is central: the method encodes invariance to a specified class of perturbations, giving a precise meaning to which observed differences should be disregarded.

The paper also constructs invariant features of distributions, extending the idea from two-sample testing to learning with distribution-valued inputs. These features yield learning algorithms robust to symmetric additive noise affecting those inputs. The contribution connects the comparison criterion and the learned representation to the same goal: retaining distinctions relevant to underlying processes while accounting for the stipulated noise.
summary.tldr: Noise-invariant distribution distances and features support testing and learning that account for additive symmetric noise.

title: Testing and Learning on Distributions with Symmetric Noise Invariance

abstract: Stimulus-driven brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), such as the P300 speller, rely on using a sequence of sensory stimuli to elicit specific neural responses as control signals, while a user attends to relevant target stimuli that occur within the sequence. In current BCIs, the stimulus presentation schedule is typically generated in a pseudo-random fashion. Given the non-stationarity of brain electrical signals, a better strategy could be to adapt the stimulus presentation schedule in real-time by selecting the optimal stimuli that will maximize the signal-to-noise ratios of the elicited neural responses and provide the most information about the user's intent based on the uncertainties of the data being measured. However, the high-dimensional stimulus space limits the development of algorithms with tractable solutions for optimized stimulus selection to allow for real-time decision-making within the stringent time requirements of BCI processing. We derive a simple analytical solution of an information-based objective function for BCI stimulus selection by transforming the high-dimensional stimulus space into a one-dimensional space that parameterizes the objective function - the prior probability mass of the stimulus under consideration, irrespective of its contents. We demonstrate the utility of our adaptive stimulus selection algorithm in improving BCI performance with results from simulation and real-time human experiments.

paragraphs: Stimulus-driven brain-computer interfaces infer a user's intent from neural responses to a sequence of sensory events. The user attends to relevant targets within that sequence. Presentation schedules are typically pseudo-random, even though changing brain signals and current uncertainty suggest that some stimuli could be more informative than others at a particular moment.

This paper develops an information-based method for selecting stimuli adaptively. The computational obstacle is the large space of possible stimuli, which must be searched within strict real-time processing requirements. The authors reduce the objective to a single quantity: the prior probability mass associated with the stimulus under consideration, irrespective of its particular contents.

That reduction yields a simple analytical solution for the selection objective, making an otherwise high-dimensional decision more tractable. Simulations and real-time experiments with human participants demonstrate improvements in BCI performance. The contribution links uncertainty about user intent to stimulus scheduling, while providing a computational simplification that allows adaptive selection to operate within the interface's timing constraints.
summary.tldr: Reducing stimulus selection to a one-dimensional information objective enables adaptive BCI scheduling that improves performance in simulations and human experiments.

title: Information-based Adaptive Stimulus Selection to Optimize Communication Efficiency in Brain-Computer Interfaces

abstract: Evolution strategies (ES) are a family of black-box optimization algorithms able to train deep neural networks roughly as well as Q-learning and policy gradient methods on challenging deep reinforcement learning (RL) problems, but are much faster (e.g. hours vs. days) because they parallelize better. However, many RL problems require directed exploration because they have reward functions that are sparse or deceptive (i.e. contain local optima), and it is unknown how to encourage such exploration with ES. Here we show that algorithms that have been invented to promote directed exploration in small-scale evolved neural networks via populations of exploring agents, specifically novelty search (NS) and quality diversity (QD) algorithms, can be hybridized with ES to improve its performance on sparse or deceptive deep RL tasks, while retaining scalability. Our experiments confirm that the resultant new algorithms, NS-ES and two QD algorithms, NSR-ES and NSRA-ES, avoid local optima encountered by ES to achieve higher performance on Atari and simulated robots learning to walk around a deceptive trap. This paper thus introduces a family of fast, scalable algorithms for reinforcement learning that are capable of directed exploration. It also adds this new family of exploration algorithms to the RL toolbox and raises the interesting possibility that analogous algorithms with multiple simultaneous paths of exploration might also combine well with existing RL algorithms outside ES.

paragraphs: Evolution strategies can train deep reinforcement-learning agents efficiently because their computations parallelize well. However, efficient optimization alone does not solve exploration. When rewards are scarce or misleading, an agent can settle on locally attractive behavior and fail to discover more successful alternatives.

The paper combines evolution strategies with novelty search and quality-diversity methods, which encourage populations of agents to pursue different behaviors. The resulting algorithms are NS-ES, NSR-ES, and NSRA-ES. Their purpose is to make exploration directed while preserving the scalability that makes evolution strategies attractive for training large neural networks.

Experiments on Atari and simulated walking robots facing a deceptive trap show that these algorithms avoid local optima encountered by ordinary evolution strategies and achieve higher performance. The findings support maintaining multiple exploration paths for the sparse or deceptive tasks examined. The authors also suggest that analogous population-based exploration could work with reinforcement-learning methods outside evolution strategies, presenting that broader connection as a possibility rather than an established result.
summary.tldr: Combining evolution strategies with novelty-seeking populations improves exploration and performance on tested sparse or deceptive reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: Improving Exploration in Evolution Strategies for Deep Reinforcement Learning via a Population of Novelty-Seeking Agents

abstract: In dictionary selection, several atoms are selected from finite candidates that successfully approximate given data points in the sparse representation. We propose a novel efficient greedy algorithm for dictionary selection. Not only does our algorithm work much faster than the known methods, but it can also handle more complex sparsity constraints, such as average sparsity. Using numerical experiments, we show that our algorithm outperforms the known methods for dictionary selection, achieving competitive performances with dictionary learning algorithms in a smaller running time.

We propose a novel efficient greedy algorithm for dictionary selection. Not only does our algorithm work much faster than the known methods, but it can also handle more complex sparsity constraints, such as average sparsity. Using numerical experiments, we show that our algorithm outperforms the known methods for dictionary selection, achieving competitive performances with dictionary learning algorithms in a smaller running time.

paragraphs: Dictionary selection chooses a collection of building blocks, called atoms, from a finite set of candidates. The selected atoms should approximate the given data using sparse representations, so individual reconstructions use relatively few building blocks. The computational problem is to find a useful shared dictionary while respecting restrictions on how those atoms can be used.

The paper proposes an efficient greedy algorithm for this selection process. Beyond speed, it supports more complex sparsity constraints, including average sparsity. Such a constraint concerns sparsity across the collection of representations, making the allowable representation structure more flexible. The contribution therefore addresses both the cost of choosing a dictionary and the range of constraints that selection can accommodate.

Numerical experiments show that the algorithm outperforms existing dictionary-selection methods. The authors also report performance competitive with dictionary-learning algorithms while requiring less running time. These findings suggest that selecting from available candidates can offer an effective computational option in the evaluated settings, with generalized sparsity constraints incorporated into the selection procedure.
summary.tldr: A fast greedy dictionary-selection algorithm supports generalized sparsity constraints and achieves competitive representation performance with shorter running times.

title: Fast greedy algorithms for dictionary selection with generalized sparsity constraints

abstract: We introduce Generative Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a latent variable architecture which is designed to model the semantics of the source and target sentences. We modify an encoder-decoder translation model by adding a latent variable as a language agnostic representation which is encouraged to learn the meaning of the sentence. GNMT achieves competitive BLEU scores on pure translation tasks, and is superior when there are missing words in the source sentence. We augment the model to facilitate multilingual translation and semi-supervised learning without adding parameters. This framework significantly reduces overfitting when there is limited paired data available, and is effective for translating between pairs of languages not seen during training.

We modify an encoder-decoder translation model by adding a latent variable as a language agnostic representation which is encouraged to learn the meaning of the sentence. GNMT achieves competitive BLEU scores on pure translation tasks, and is superior when there are missing words in the source sentence. We augment the model to facilitate multilingual translation and semi-supervised learning without adding parameters. This framework significantly reduces overfitting when there is limited paired data available, and is effective for translating between pairs of languages not seen during training.

paragraphs: Translation requires preserving meaning across different linguistic forms. This paper introduces Generative Neural Machine Translation, a latent-variable architecture designed to model the semantics shared by source and target sentences. It extends an encoder-decoder model with a hidden representation encouraged to capture sentence meaning independently of the language used.

That representation gives the model a way to account for shared meaning within its translation architecture. On ordinary translation tasks, the authors report competitive BLEU scores. When words are missing from the source sentence, they report superior performance. The latter finding supports the usefulness of the proposed semantic representation when the input provides incomplete information.

The framework is also extended to multilingual translation and semi-supervised learning without adding parameters. With limited paired training data, the authors report a substantial reduction in overfitting. They also find it effective for translating between language pairs absent from training. Together, these findings suggest that modeling a shared latent representation can help the evaluated system use limited, incomplete, or differently paired language evidence.
summary.tldr: A language-agnostic latent representation supports competitive translation, improved handling of missing source words, and learning with limited or unseen language pairings.

title: Generative Neural Machine Translation

abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative models has the potential of discovering rich representations of 3D scenes. While geometric deep learning has explored 3D-structure-aware representations of scene geometry, these models typically require explicit 3D supervision. Emerging neural scene representations can be trained only with posed 2D images, but existing methods ignore the three-dimensional structure of scenes. We propose Scene Representation Networks (SRNs), a continuous, 3D-structure-aware scene representation that encodes both geometry and appearance. SRNs represent scenes as continuous functions that map world coordinates to a feature representation of local scene properties. By formulating the image formation as a differentiable ray-marching algorithm, SRNs can be trained end-to-end from only 2D images and their camera poses, without access to depth or shape. This formulation naturally generalizes across scenes, learning powerful geometry and appearance priors in the process. We demonstrate the potential of SRNs by evaluating them for novel view synthesis, few-shot reconstruction, joint shape and appearance interpolation, and unsupervised discovery of a non-rigid face model.

paragraphs: Scene Representation Networks learn a representation of a scene's geometry and appearance from 2D images with known camera poses. The paper addresses a gap between methods that explicitly respect 3D structure but require 3D supervision and image-trained neural representations that ignore that structure. Its representation builds three-dimensional organization into the model without requiring depth or shape data.

An SRN represents a scene as a continuous function from world coordinates to features describing local scene properties. Images are formed through a differentiable ray-marching procedure, allowing image observations to train the representation end to end. Camera poses connect each observed image to the scene's coordinates and are part of the required training information.

The formulation generalizes across scenes and learns priors over geometry and appearance. The authors evaluate its potential through novel-view synthesis, reconstruction from few observations, joint interpolation of shape and appearance, and unsupervised discovery of a non-rigid face model. These demonstrations explore how a shared continuous representation can support multiple tasks involving scene structure and image formation.
summary.tldr: Scene Representation Networks learn continuous geometry-and-appearance representations from posed 2D images through differentiable ray marching.

title: Scene Representation Networks: Continuous 3D-Structure-Aware Neural Scene Representations

abstract: Recent theoretical work has shown that massively overparameterized neural networks are equivalent to kernel regressors that use Neural Tangent Kernels (NTKs). Experiments show that these kernel methods perform similarly to real neural networks. Here we show that NTK for fully connected networks with ReLU activation is closely related to the standard Laplace kernel. We show theoretically that for normalized data on the hypersphere both kernels have the same eigenfunctions and their eigenvalues decay polynomially at the same rate, implying that their Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS) include the same sets of functions. This means that both kernels give rise to classes of functions with the same smoothness properties. The two kernels differ for data off the hypersphere, but experiments indicate that when data is properly normalized these differences are not significant. Finally, we provide experiments on real data comparing NTK and the Laplace kernel, along with a larger class of $\gamma$-exponential kernels. We show that these perform almost identically. Our results suggest that much insight about neural networks can be obtained from analysis of the well-known Laplace kernel, which has a simple closed form.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernels provide a way to study massively overparameterized neural networks through kernel regression. This paper investigates how the neural tangent kernel of a fully connected ReLU network relates to the familiar Laplace kernel. The comparison asks whether a simpler mathematical object can capture important properties of the network-associated kernel.

Consequently, their reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces contain the same sets of functions. In plain terms, they support function classes with the same smoothness properties under this normalization condition.

The kernels differ away from the hypersphere, but experiments indicate that these differences have little significance when data is properly normalized. Real-data comparisons also find nearly identical performance for the neural tangent kernel, the Laplace kernel, and a broader family of gamma-exponential kernels. The results suggest that analyzing the Laplace kernel’s simple closed form can provide insight into neural networks through this established kernel connection.
summary.tldr: For data on a hypersphere, the ReLU neural tangent kernel and Laplace kernel support the same function sets and show similar empirical performance.

title: On the Similarity between the Laplace and Neural Tangent Kernels

abstract: We find separation rates for testing multinomial or more general discrete distributions under the constraint of alpha-local differential privacy. We construct efficient randomized algorithms and test procedures, in both the case where only non-interactive privacy mechanisms are allowed and also in the case where all sequentially interactive privacy mechanisms are allowed. The separation rates are faster in the latter case. We prove general information theoretical bounds that allow us to establish the optimality of our algorithms among all pairs of privacy mechanisms and test procedures, in most usual cases. Considered examples include testing uniform, polynomially and exponentially decreasing distributions.

paragraphs: This paper studies testing discrete distributions when observations must satisfy alpha-local differential privacy. Its main quantity is the separation rate: how far distributions must differ for the testing procedure to distinguish them under the privacy constraint. The analysis covers multinomial distributions and more general discrete distributions, comparing different ways to obtain privatized information.

The authors construct efficient randomized mechanisms and testing procedures for two settings. In the non-interactive setting, the privacy mechanism does not adapt sequentially to earlier responses. In the sequentially interactive setting, that adaptation is permitted. They find faster separation rates with interaction, showing that the ability to adapt the information-gathering process can improve statistical distinguishability under local privacy.

General information-theoretic bounds establish the optimality of their algorithms among combinations of privacy mechanisms and tests in most usual cases. Examples include uniform distributions and distributions with polynomially or exponentially decreasing probabilities. The resulting comparison concerns statistical testing rates, explaining a benefit of interaction beyond simply designing an efficient implementation of a fixed private test.
summary.tldr: Sequential interaction improves separation rates for testing discrete distributions under local differential privacy, with optimality established in most usual cases.

title: Locally private non-asymptotic testing of discrete distributions is faster using interactive mechanisms

abstract: Many real-world sequential decision-making problems involve critical systems with financial risks and human-life risks. While several works in the past have proposed methods that are safe for deployment, they assume that the underlying problem is stationary. However, many real-world problems of interest exhibit non-stationarity, and when stakes are high, the cost associated with a false stationarity assumption may be unacceptable. We take the first steps towards ensuring safety, with high confidence, for smoothly-varying non-stationary decision problems. Our proposed method extends a type of safe algorithm, called a Seldonian algorithm, through a synthesis of model-free reinforcement learning with time-series analysis. Safety is ensured using sequential hypothesis testing of a policy’s forecasted performance, and confidence intervals are obtained using wild bootstrap.

paragraphs: Safety methods for sequential decision-making often assume that the environment stays unchanged. In critical applications, that assumption can be costly when conditions evolve. This paper takes initial steps toward high-confidence safety for decision problems that change smoothly over time, making non-stationarity part of the evaluation of a proposed policy.

The method extends a Seldonian algorithm by combining model-free reinforcement learning with time-series analysis. It forecasts a policy's performance and applies sequential hypothesis testing to that forecast. Confidence intervals are constructed using the wild bootstrap. These components connect the assessment of future policy behavior with statistical uncertainty about that assessment.

The central contribution is a safety framework that explicitly addresses smooth environmental change. Forecasted performance becomes the object of testing, so the deployment decision accounts for the evolving problem rather than assuming past conditions persist. The stated safety objective is high confidence under the smoothly varying setting, preserving both the probabilistic nature of the assurance and the scope of non-stationarity considered.
summary.tldr: A Seldonian approach combines performance forecasting and sequential testing to pursue high-confidence policy safety in smoothly changing environments.

title: Towards Safe Policy Improvement for Non-Stationary MDPs

abstract: We consider a commonly studied supervised classification of a synthetic dataset whose labels are generated by feeding a one-layer non-linear neural network with random iid inputs. We study the generalization performances of standard classifiers in the high-dimensional regime where $\alpha=\frac{n}{d}$ is kept finite in the limit of a high dimension $d$ and number of samples $n$. Our contribution is three-fold: First, we prove a formula for the generalization error achieved by $\ell_2$ regularized classifiers that minimize a convex loss. This formula was first obtained by the heuristic replica method of statistical physics. Secondly, focussing on commonly used loss functions and optimizing the $\ell_2$ regularization strength, we observe that while ridge regression performance is poor, logistic and hinge regression are surprisingly able to approach the Bayes-optimal generalization error extremely closely. As $\alpha \to \infty$ they lead to Bayes-optimal rates, a fact that does not follow from predictions of margin-based generalization error bounds. Third, we design an optimal loss and regularizer that provably leads to Bayes-optimal generalization error.

paragraphs: This paper studies classification on synthetic data whose labels come from a one-layer nonlinear neural network receiving independent, identically distributed random inputs. It considers a high-dimensional limit in which both sample count and input dimension grow while their ratio remains finite. Within this setting, it asks how closely standard convex learning methods can approach Bayes-optimal generalization error.

The authors first prove an error formula for classifiers trained with a convex loss and L2 regularization. The formula had previously been obtained through a heuristic statistical-physics technique. They then examine familiar losses with optimized regularization strength. Ridge regression performs poorly in their analysis, whereas logistic and hinge regression approach the Bayes-optimal error extremely closely.

As the sample-to-dimension ratio grows without bound, logistic and hinge regression attain Bayes-optimal rates, a conclusion not supplied by the margin-based bounds discussed in the abstract. Finally, the authors construct a loss and regularizer that provably attain Bayes-optimal generalization error. These results establish what convex optimization can achieve under the paper's specified data model and asymptotic regime.
summary.tldr: For a specified high-dimensional synthetic classification model, carefully regularized convex methods can closely approach or provably attain Bayes-optimal generalization.

title: Generalization error in high-dimensional perceptrons: Approaching Bayes error with convex optimization

abstract: A differentially private algorithm guarantees that the input of a single user won’t significantly change the output distribution of the algorithm. When a user contributes more data points, more information can be collected to improve the algorithm’s performance. But at the same time, more noise might need to be added to the algorithm in order to keep the algorithm differentially private and this might hurt the algorithm’s performance. Amin et al. (2019) initiates the study on bounding user contributions and proposes a very natural algorithm which limits the number of samples each user can contribute by a threshold. For a better trade-off between utility and privacy guarantee, we propose a method which smoothly bounds user contributions by setting appropriate weights on data points and apply it to estimating the mean/quantiles, linear regression, and empirical risk minimization. We show that our algorithm provably outperforms the sample limiting algorithm. We conclude with experimental evaluations which validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy limits how much one person's data can change an algorithm's output distribution. When a person supplies many observations, those observations can improve estimation, but their larger influence may require more privacy noise. Choosing how much each person contributes is therefore part of the accuracy problem.

A simple approach caps the number of samples allowed from each user. This paper instead assigns weights to data points to bound contributions smoothly. Weighting provides a more gradual way to manage influence than a sample-count threshold. The authors apply the method to mean and quantile estimation, linear regression, and empirical risk minimization.

The paper proves that its algorithm outperforms the sample-limiting approach and reports experiments validating the theoretical results. The contribution is a different way to balance information use against the noise needed for privacy. By controlling contributions through appropriate weights, the method improves the stated utility trade-off across the estimation and learning problems considered, while continuing to treat the user as the unit whose influence must be protected.
summary.tldr: Smoothly weighting users' data improves the privacy–utility trade-off over limiting each user to a fixed number of samples.

title: Smoothly Bounding User Contributions in Differential Privacy

abstract: We present the Supermasks in Superposition (SupSup) model, capable of sequentially learning thousands of tasks without catastrophic forgetting. Our approach uses a randomly initialized, fixed base network and for each task finds a subnetwork (supermask) that achieves good performance. If task identity is given at test time, the correct subnetwork can be retrieved with minimal memory usage. If not provided, SupSup can infer the task using gradient-based optimization to find a linear superposition of learned supermasks which minimizes the output entropy. In practice we find that a single gradient step is often sufficient to identify the correct mask, even among 2500 tasks. We also showcase two promising extensions. First, SupSup models can be trained entirely without task identity information, as they may detect when they are uncertain about new data and allocate an additional supermask for the new training distribution. Finally the entire, growing set of supermasks can be stored in a constant-sized reservoir by implicitly storing them as attractors in a fixed-sized Hopfield network.

paragraphs: Supermasks in Superposition addresses sequential learning across thousands of tasks without catastrophic forgetting. It starts with a randomly initialized network whose weights remain fixed. For each task, the method finds a subnetwork, represented by a supermask, that performs well. Learning therefore selects task-specific portions of a shared fixed network.

When task identity is available at test time, the corresponding mask can be retrieved with minimal memory usage. Without that identity, the method searches for a linear combination of learned masks that minimizes output entropy. In practice, the authors find that one gradient step is often enough to identify the appropriate mask, even among 2,500 tasks.

The paper also demonstrates two promising extensions. Uncertainty can signal a new training distribution and prompt allocation of another mask, allowing training without task identities. Separately, a fixed-size Hopfield network can implicitly store the growing mask collection as attractors in a constant-sized reservoir. These extensions broaden the approach beyond explicit task lookup while retaining masks as the central representation of task-specific knowledge.
summary.tldr: SupSup learns task-specific subnetworks inside a fixed random network and can often infer the needed mask with a single gradient step.

title: Supermasks in Superposition

abstract: We present a novel nonparametric algorithm for symmetry-based disentangling of data manifolds, the Geometric Manifold Component Estimator (GEOMANCER). GEOMANCER provides a partial answer to the question posed by Higgins et al.(2018): is it possible to learn how to factorize a Lie group solely from observations of the orbit of an object it acts on? We show that fully unsupervised factorization of a data manifold is possible *if* the true metric of the manifold is known and each factor manifold has nontrivial holonomy – for example, rotation in 3D. Our algorithm works by estimating the subspaces that are invariant under random walk diffusion, giving an approximation to the de Rham decomposition from differential geometry. We demonstrate the efficacy of GEOMANCER on several complex synthetic manifolds. Our work reduces the question of whether unsupervised disentangling is possible to the question of whether unsupervised metric learning is possible, providing a unifying insight into the geometric nature of representation learning.

paragraphs: Disentangling seeks to separate the underlying factors of variation in observations. This paper approaches that goal geometrically, asking whether observations of an object under transformations can reveal a factorization of the associated structure. Its nonparametric algorithm, GEOMANCER, provides a conditional answer based on properties of the data manifold.

GEOMANCER estimates subspaces that remain invariant under random-walk diffusion. These subspaces approximate the de Rham decomposition from differential geometry. The paper shows that fully unsupervised factorization is possible when the manifold's true metric is known and every factor has nontrivial holonomy, a geometric property exemplified by three-dimensional rotation. Both conditions are part of the result.

Experiments demonstrate the method on several complex synthetic manifolds. The broader insight is that the geometry used to measure the data plays a central role in separating its factors. Within the stated conditions, the work shifts attention toward whether the necessary metric can itself be learned without supervision. It therefore offers a partial resolution of unsupervised disentangling, with metric learning remaining central to the question.
summary.tldr: GEOMANCER enables unsupervised geometric factorization when the true manifold metric is known and each factor has nontrivial holonomy.

title: Disentangling by Subspace Diffusion

abstract: We consider Bayesian optimization of objective functions of the form $\rho[ F(x, W) ]$, where $F$ is a black-box expensive-to-evaluate function and $\rho$ denotes either the VaR or CVaR risk measure, computed with respect to the randomness induced by the environmental random variable $W$. Such problems arise in decision making under uncertainty, such as in portfolio optimization and robust systems design. We propose a family of novel Bayesian optimization algorithms that exploit the structure of the objective function to substantially improve sampling efficiency. Instead of modeling the objective function directly as is typical in Bayesian optimization, these algorithms model $F$ as a Gaussian process, and use the implied posterior on the objective function to decide which points to evaluate. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of numerical experiments.

Such problems arise in decision making under uncertainty, such as in portfolio optimization and robust systems design. We propose a family of novel Bayesian optimization algorithms that exploit the structure of the objective function to substantially improve sampling efficiency. Instead of modeling the objective function directly as is typical in Bayesian optimization, these algorithms model $F$ as a Gaussian process, and use the implied posterior on the objective function to decide which points to evaluate. paragraphs: Some optimization problems evaluate a decision by its risk under uncertain environmental conditions. This paper considers objectives defined by either value at risk or conditional value at risk, calculated from an expensive black-box function. A decision and a random environmental variable jointly determine the function’s outcome, so the quantity being optimized depends on a distribution of possible outcomes.

The proposed algorithms exploit this structure rather than modeling the final risk objective directly. They place a Gaussian-process model on the underlying function of the decision and environment. That model induces uncertainty about the risk measure, and the algorithms use this implied posterior to choose which function evaluations to perform next.

This distinction matters when evaluations are costly: the sampling strategy uses information about the process producing the risk, not just isolated values of the resulting objective. The authors introduce a family of Bayesian optimization algorithms and report substantial improvements in sampling efficiency. Numerical experiments demonstrate their effectiveness across multiple problems. The framework is motivated by decisions under uncertainty, including portfolio optimization and robust systems design.
summary.tldr: Modeling the underlying uncertain function with a Gaussian process improves the sampling efficiency of Bayesian optimization for VaR and CVaR objectives.

title: Bayesian Optimization of Risk Measures

abstract: Finding approximate Nash equilibria in zero-sum imperfect-information games is challenging when the number of information states is large. Policy Space Response Oracles (PSRO) is a deep reinforcement learning algorithm grounded in game theory that is guaranteed to converge to an approximate Nash equilibrium. However, PSRO requires training a reinforcement learning policy at each iteration, making it too slow for large games. We show through counterexamples and experiments that DCH and Rectified PSRO, two existing approaches to scaling up PSRO, fail to converge even in small games. We introduce Pipeline PSRO (P2SRO), the first scalable PSRO-based method for finding approximate Nash equilibria in large zero-sum imperfect-information games. P2SRO is able to parallelize PSRO with convergence guarantees by maintaining a hierarchical pipeline of reinforcement learning workers, each training against the policies generated by lower levels in the hierarchy. We show that unlike existing methods, P2SRO converges to an approximate Nash equilibrium, and does so faster as the number of parallel workers increases, across a variety of imperfect information games. We also introduce an open-source environment for Barrage Stratego, a variant of Stratego with an approximate game tree complexity of 10^50. P2SRO is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on Barrage Stratego and beats all existing bots. Experiment code is available at https://github.com/JBLanier/pipeline-psro.

Policy Space Response Oracles, or PSRO, has a convergence guarantee, but training a reinforcement-learning policy at every iteration makes it slow. The authors also show through counterexamples and experiments that two scaling approaches, DCH and Rectified PSRO, can fail to converge even in small games.

Pipeline PSRO organizes reinforcement-learning workers into a hierarchy. Each worker trains against policies generated at lower levels, allowing training to proceed in parallel while retaining convergence guarantees. This pipeline is the mechanism used to connect increased computational parallelism with equilibrium finding.

Across several imperfect-information games, the authors show convergence to an approximate Nash equilibrium and faster convergence with more parallel workers. They also introduce an open-source Barrage Stratego environment, whose approximate game-tree complexity is 10^50. P2SRO achieves state-of-the-art performance there and beats all existing bots in the reported results, demonstrating the method on a particularly large game.
summary.tldr: Pipeline PSRO parallelizes policy training through a hierarchy while preserving approximate-equilibrium convergence and improving speed in evaluated games.

title: Pipeline PSRO: A Scalable Approach for Finding Approximate Nash Equilibria in Large Games

abstract: Learning to control the structure of sentences is a challenging problem in text generation. Existing work either relies on simple deterministic approaches or RL-based hard structures. We explore the use of structured variational autoencoders to infer latent templates for sentence generation using a soft, continuous relaxation in order to utilize reparameterization for training. Specifically, we propose a Gumbel-CRF, a continuous relaxation of the CRF sampling algorithm using a relaxed Forward-Filtering Backward-Sampling (FFBS) approach. As a reparameterized gradient estimator, the Gumbel-CRF gives more stable gradients than score-function based estimators. As a structured inference network, we show that it learns interpretable templates during training, which allows us to control the decoder during testing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods with experiments on data-to-text generation and unsupervised paraphrase generation.

paragraphs: Controlling sentence structure requires a text generator to represent more than the words it produces. This paper explores learning hidden templates inside a structured variational autoencoder, so the model can infer sentence organization during training and use it to guide generation. The training challenge is how to learn through the structured choices that define those templates.

The proposed Gumbel-CRF replaces discrete CRF sampling with a soft, continuous relaxation. It does this through a relaxed version of Forward-Filtering Backward-Sampling. This allows reparameterized gradient estimation, giving the training process a way to adjust the model through relaxed structured samples.

The authors report more stable gradients than score-function estimators and show that the inference network learns interpretable templates. Those templates allow control of the decoder at test time. Experiments on data-to-text generation and unsupervised paraphrase generation demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution combines a training mechanism for structured latent variables with a practical use for those variables: controlling how generated sentences are organized.
summary.tldr: Gumbel-CRFs enable stable training of structured latent sentence templates that can control text generation.

title: Latent Template Induction with Gumbel-CRFs

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection has received much attention lately due to its practical importance in enhancing the safe deployment of neural networks. One of the primary challenges is that models often produce highly confident predictions on OOD data, which undermines the driving principle in OOD detection that the model should only be confident about in-distribution samples. In this work, we propose ReAct—a simple and effective technique for reducing model overconfidence on OOD data. Our method is motivated by novel analysis on internal activations of neural networks, which displays highly distinctive signature patterns for OOD distributions. Our method can generalize effectively to different network architectures and different OOD detection scores. We empirically demonstrate that ReAct achieves competitive detection performance on a comprehensive suite of benchmark datasets, and give theoretical explication for our method’s efficacy. On the ImageNet benchmark, ReAct reduces the false positive rate (FPR95) by 25.05% compared to the previous best method.

paragraphs: Neural networks can make highly confident predictions on inputs from outside their training distribution. That behavior undermines detection methods that expect confidence to distinguish familiar inputs from unfamiliar ones. ReAct addresses this problem with a simple technique based on rectifying internal network activations to reduce overconfidence on out-of-distribution data.

The method is motivated by an analysis showing distinctive patterns in internal activations for out-of-distribution inputs. These patterns provide a basis for intervening inside the network to improve detection. The authors also give a theoretical explanation of the method’s effectiveness and report that it works across different network architectures and different detection scores.

Across a comprehensive benchmark suite, ReAct achieves competitive detection performance. On ImageNet, the abstract reports a 25.05% reduction in the false positive rate measured by FPR95 relative to the previous best method. The results support internal activation behavior as a useful target for improving unfamiliar-input detection, with applicability across more than one architecture or scoring choice in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: ReAct uses distinctive internal activation behavior to reduce overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs and improve detection across tested architectures and scores.

title: ReAct: Out-of-distribution Detection With Rectified Activations

abstract: Deep models trained through maximum likelihood have achieved state-of-the-art results for survival analysis. Despite this training scheme, practitioners evaluate models under other criteria, such as binary classification losses at a chosen set of time horizons, e.g. Brier score (BS) and Bernoulli log likelihood (BLL). Models trained with maximum likelihood may have poor BS or BLL since maximum likelihood does not directly optimize these criteria. Directly optimizing criteria like BS requires inverse-weighting by the censoring distribution. However, estimating the censoring model under these metrics requires inverse-weighting by the failure distribution. The objective for each model requires the other, but neither are known. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Inverse-Weighted Survival Games. In these games, objectives for each model are built from re-weighted estimates featuring the other model, where the latter is held fixed during training. When the loss is proper, we show that the games always have the true failure and censoring distributions as a stationary point. This means models in the game do not leave the correct distributions once reached. We construct one case where this stationary point is unique. We show that these games optimize BS on simulations and then apply these principles on real world cancer and critically-ill patient data.

Models trained with maximum likelihood may have poor BS or BLL since maximum likelihood does not directly optimize these criteria. Directly optimizing criteria like BS requires inverse-weighting by the censoring distribution. However, estimating the censoring model under these metrics requires inverse-weighting by the failure distribution. The objective for each model requires the other, but neither are known. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Inverse-Weighted Survival Games. In these games, objectives for each model are built from re-weighted estimates featuring the other model, where the latter is held fixed during training. When the loss is proper, we show that the games always have the true failure and censoring distributions as a stationary point. This means models in the game do not leave the correct distributions once reached. We construct one case where this stationary point is unique. paragraphs: Survival models predict the timing of events when some outcomes are censored, meaning their event time is not fully observed. Models trained by maximum likelihood may perform poorly on evaluation criteria such as Brier score or Bernoulli log likelihood at selected time horizons, because training does not directly optimize those criteria.

Direct optimization creates a circular dependency. Correcting a failure-model objective for censoring requires a censoring distribution, while estimating the censoring model under these criteria requires the failure distribution. Inverse-Weighted Survival Games couples the two models: each objective uses reweighted estimates based on the other model, which is held fixed while that objective is trained.

For proper losses, the authors prove that the true failure and censoring distributions form a stationary point: once there, the game does not move away. They establish uniqueness in one constructed case, without claiming universal convergence to that point. Simulations show Brier-score optimization, and applications to cancer and critically ill patient data demonstrate the approach in real-world survival settings.
summary.tldr: Coupled survival and censoring models enable direct training for evaluation losses, with the true distributions forming a stationary point under proper losses.

title: Inverse-Weighted Survival Games

abstract: We provide theoretical guarantees for label consistency in generalized $k$-means problems, with an emphasis on the overfitted case where the number of clusters used by the algorithm is more than the ground truth. We provide conditions under which the estimated labels are close to a refinement of the true cluster labels. We consider both exact and approximate recovery of the labels. Our results hold for any constant-factor approximation to the $k$-means problem. The results are also model-free and only based on bounds on the maximum or average distance of the data points to the true cluster centers. These centers themselves are loosely defined and can be taken to be any set of points for which the aforementioned distances can be controlled. We show the usefulness of the results with applications to some manifold clustering problems.
originalAbstract: We provide theoretical guarantees for label consistency in generalized $k$-means problems, with an emphasis on the overfitted case where the number of clusters used by the algorithm is more than the ground truth. We provide conditions under which the estimated labels are close to a refinement of the true cluster labels. We consider both exact and approximate recovery of the labels. Our results hold for any constant-factor approximation to the $k$-means problem. The results are also model-free and only based on bounds on the maximum or average distance of the data points to the true cluster centers. These centers themselves are loosely defined and can be taken to be any set of points for which the aforementioned distances can be controlled. We show the usefulness of the results with applications to some manifold clustering problems.

The relevant question is whether the extra clusters mostly subdivide genuine groups or mix together points from different groups. This paper formalizes that question for generalized k-means by studying closeness to a refinement of the true cluster labels.

The authors provide conditions for both exact and approximate label recovery in this overfitted setting. Their guarantees apply to any constant-factor approximation to the k-means problem, so they do not depend on finding an exact optimum. The assumptions involve bounds on the maximum or average distance from data points to designated true centers.

The results are model-free: they do not require a particular probabilistic model for how the clusters were generated. Even the centers are flexible, provided the required distance bounds can be controlled. Applications to manifold clustering demonstrate the usefulness of this formulation. The main message is conditional but practical: overfitting the number of clusters can preserve meaningful label structure when the geometric conditions support a refinement.
summary.tldr: The paper gives geometric conditions under which overfitted generalized k-means preserves true groups through label refinements.

title: Label consistency in overfitted generalized $k$-means

abstract: Progress in machine learning (ML) stems from a combination of data availability, computational resources, and an appropriate encoding of inductive biases. Useful biases often exploit symmetries in the prediction problem, such as convolutional networks relying on translation equivariance. Automatically discovering these useful symmetries holds the potential to greatly improve the performance of ML systems, but still remains a challenge. In this work, we focus on sequential prediction problems and take inspiration from Noether's theorem to reduce the problem of finding inductive biases to meta-learning useful conserved quantities. We propose Noether Networks: a new type of architecture where a meta-learned conservation loss is optimized inside the prediction function. We show, theoretically and experimentally, that Noether Networks improve prediction quality, providing a general framework for discovering inductive biases in sequential problems.

This paper focuses on sequential prediction and asks whether a model can learn quantities whose conservation helps it predict.

Their Noether Network architecture includes a learned conservation loss that is optimized inside the prediction function. Consequently, conservation is an active part of producing a prediction, rather than merely an observation made after training.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental evidence that this architecture improves prediction quality. The significance is the route to finding structure: the system learns which conservation-based constraint is useful instead of relying entirely on a manually selected symmetry. The paper presents this as a general framework for discovering inductive biases in sequential problems. Its findings support the usefulness of learned conservation objectives without implying that every sequence must follow a particular predefined physical conservation law.
summary.tldr: Noether Networks meta-learn conservation objectives and optimize them during prediction to discover useful structure in sequential tasks.

title: Noether Networks: meta-learning useful conserved quantities

abstract: Piano transcription systems are typically optimized to estimate pitch activity at each frame of audio. They are often followed by carefully designed heuristics and post-processing algorithms to estimate note events from the frame-level predictions. Recent methods have also framed piano transcription as a multi-task learning problem, where the activation of different stages of a note event are estimated independently. These practices are not well aligned with the desired outcome of the task, which is the specification of note intervals as holistic events, rather than the aggregation of disjoint observations. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of piano transcription, which is optimized to directly predict note events. Our method is based on Semi-Markov Conditional Random Fields (semi-CRF), which produce scores for intervals rather than individual frames. When formulating piano transcription in this way, we eliminate the need to rely on disjoint frame-level estimates for different stages of a note event. We conduct experiments on the MAESTRO dataset and demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses the current state-of-the-art for piano transcription. Our results suggest that the semi-CRF output layer, while still quadratic in complexity, is a simple, fast and well-performing solution for event-based prediction, and may lead to similar success in other areas which currently rely on frame-level estimates.

title: Skipping the Frame-Level: Event-Based Piano Transcription With Neural Semi-CRFs

abstract: Most existing geometry processing algorithms use meshes as the default shape representation. Manipulating meshes, however, requires one to maintain high quality in the surface discretization. For example, changing the topology of a mesh usually requires additional procedures such as remeshing. This paper instead proposes the use of neural fields for geometry processing. Neural fields can compactly store complicated shapes without spatial discretization. Moreover, neural fields are infinitely differentiable, which allows them to be optimized for objectives that involve higher-order derivatives. This raises the question: can geometry processing be done entirely using neural fields? We introduce loss functions and architectures to show that some of the most challenging geometry processing tasks, such as deformation and filtering, can be done with neural fields. Experimental results show that our methods are on par with the well-established mesh-based methods without committing to a particular surface discretization. Code is available at https://github.com/stevenygd/NFGP.

Manipulating that shape also means maintaining the quality of its surface discretization, and changing its topology can require additional procedures such as remeshing. This paper investigates whether challenging geometry operations can instead be performed using neural fields as the underlying shape representation.

Neural fields offer a compact way to represent complicated shapes without committing to a spatial discretization. The paper also highlights their differentiability, which enables optimization objectives involving higher-order derivatives. The authors introduce architectures and loss functions that use these properties for tasks including shape deformation and filtering, moving the processing itself into the neural-field representation.

Experiments show performance on par with established mesh-based approaches for the studied tasks. The result supports neural fields as a workable basis for geometry processing, with the benefit of avoiding commitment to a particular surface discretization. The paper demonstrates this possibility through concrete operations rather than establishing that neural fields replace every mesh-based geometry algorithm.
summary.tldr: Neural-field architectures and losses perform deformation and filtering competitively with mesh-based methods without fixing a surface discretization.

title: Geometry Processing with Neural Fields

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a flexible and powerful approach for learning over graphs. Despite this success, existing GNNs are constrained by their local message-passing architecture and are provably limited in their expressive power. In this work, we propose a new GNN architecture – the Neural Tree. The neural tree architecture does not perform message passing on the input graph, but on a tree-structured graph, called the H-tree, that is constructed from the input graph. Nodes in the H-tree correspond to subgraphs in the input graph, and they are reorganized in a hierarchical manner such that the parent of a node in the H-tree always corresponds to a larger subgraph in the input graph. We show that the neural tree architecture can approximate any smooth probability distribution function over an undirected graph. We also prove that the number of parameters needed to achieve an $\epsilon$-approximation of the distribution function is exponential in the treewidth of the input graph, but linear in its size. We prove that any continuous G-invariant/equivariant function can be approximated by a nonlinear combination of such probability distribution functions over G. We apply the neural tree to semi-supervised node classification in 3D scene graphs, and show that these theoretical properties translate into significant gains in prediction accuracy, over the more traditional GNN architectures. We also show the applicability of the neural tree architecture to citation networks with large treewidth, by using a graph sub-sampling technique.

title: Neural Trees for Learning on Graphs

abstract: We develop two new algorithms, called, FedDR and asyncFedDR, for solving a fundamental nonconvex composite optimization problem in federated learning. Our algorithms rely on a novel combination between a nonconvex Douglas-Rachford splitting method, randomized block-coordinate strategies, and asynchronous im- plementation. They can also handle convex regularizers. Unlike recent methods in the literature, e.g., FedSplit and FedPD, our algorithms update only a subset of users at each communication round, and possibly in an asynchronous manner, making them more practical. These new algorithms can handle statistical and sys- tem heterogeneity, which are the two main challenges in federated learning, while achieving the best known communication complexity. In fact, our new algorithms match the communication complexity lower bound up to a constant factor under standard assumptions. Our numerical experiments illustrate the advantages of our methods over existing algorithms on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Federated optimization must coordinate users whose data and computing conditions differ. This paper develops FedDR and asyncFedDR for nonconvex composite optimization, including objectives with convex regularizers. The aim is to make distributed training practical when participation and execution conditions vary across users.

The algorithms combine nonconvex Douglas-Rachford splitting with randomized block-coordinate updates and asynchronous implementation. In practical terms, they update only a subset of users during a communication round, and updates can also occur asynchronously. Partial participation is central to the approach: the algorithms do not require every user to update in every round. The authors state that the methods handle both statistical and system heterogeneity.

Under standard assumptions, the communication complexity matches a lower bound up to a constant factor. This establishes a strong efficiency result for the analyzed problem class, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every federated system. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate advantages over existing algorithms, complementing the theoretical result with evidence of practical benefits.
summary.tldr: FedDR and asyncFedDR support partial and asynchronous participation while attaining communication complexity optimal up to constants under standard assumptions.

title: FedDR – Randomized Douglas-Rachford Splitting Algorithms for Nonconvex Federated Composite Optimization

abstract: Scene understanding is an active research area. Commercial depth sensors, such as Kinect, have enabled the release of several RGB-D datasets over the past few years which spawned novel methods in 3D scene understanding. More recently with the launch of the LiDAR sensor in Apple’s iPads and iPhones, high qual- ity RGB-D data is accessible to millions of people on a device they commonly use. This opens a whole new era in scene understanding for the Computer Vision community as well as app developers. The fundamental research in scene understanding together with the advances in machine learning can now impact people’s everyday experiences. However, transforming these scene un- derstanding methods to real-world experiences requires additional innovation and development. In this paper we introduce ARKitScenes. It is not only the first RGB-D dataset that is captured with a now widely available depth sensor, but to our best knowledge, it also is the largest indoor scene understanding data released. In addition to the raw and processed data from the mobile device, ARKitScenes includes high resolution depth maps captured using a stationary laser scanner, as well as manually labeled 3D oriented bounding boxes for a large taxonomy of furniture. We further analyze the usefulness of the data for two downstream tasks: 3D object detection and color-guided depth upsam- pling. We demonstrate that our dataset can help push the boundaries of existing state-of-the-art methods and it introduces new challenges that better represent real-world scenarios.

title: ARKitScenes: A Diverse Real-World Dataset For 3D Indoor Scene Understanding Using Mobile RGB-D Data

abstract: Ranking from noisy comparisons is of great practical interest in machine learning. In this paper, we consider the problem of recovering the exact full ranking for a list of items under ranking models that do *not* assume the Strong Stochastic Transitivity property. We propose a $$\delta$$-correct algorithm, Probe-Rank, that actively learns the ranking of the items from noisy pairwise comparisons. We prove a sample complexity upper bound for Probe-Rank, which only depends on the preference probabilities between items that are adjacent in the true ranking. This improves upon existing sample complexity results that depend on the preference probabilities for all pairs of items. Probe-Rank thus outperforms existing methods over a large collection of instances that do not satisfy Strong Stochastic Transitivity. Thorough numerical experiments in various settings are conducted, demonstrating that Probe-Rank is significantly more sample-efficient than the state-of-the-art active ranking method.

paragraphs: Recovering a complete ranking becomes difficult when pairwise comparisons are noisy: an item can lose a comparison even when it belongs higher in the ordering. This paper studies exact ranking without assuming Strong Stochastic Transitivity, a structural property that restricts how comparison probabilities relate across items.

The proposed algorithm, Probe-Rank, actively chooses comparisons to learn the ordering. It is delta-correct, meaning its probability of returning an incorrect ranking is controlled by the chosen error tolerance delta. The main theoretical result bounds the number of comparisons using only preference probabilities between items that are neighbors in the true ranking.

This dependence matters because earlier bounds involve probabilities for every pair, allowing comparisons between distant items to affect the stated difficulty. The new bound improves those results and supports advantages over a large collection of instances that violate Strong Stochastic Transitivity. Numerical experiments across several settings also find substantially greater sample efficiency than the state-of-the-art active ranking method used for comparison.
summary.tldr: Probe-Rank learns exact rankings from noisy comparisons with guarantees depending only on neighboring items, without requiring Strong Stochastic Transitivity.

title: Active Ranking without Strong Stochastic Transitivity

abstract: The practical success of overparameterized neural networks has motivated the recent scientific study of \emph{interpolating methods}-- learning methods which are able fit their training data perfectly. Empirically, certain interpolating methods can fit noisy training data without catastrophically bad test performance, which defies standard intuitions from statistical learning theory. Aiming to explain this, a large body of recent work has studied \emph{benign overfitting}, a behavior seen in certain asymptotic settings under which interpolating methods approach Bayes-optimality, even in the presence of noise. In this work, we argue that, while benign overfitting has been instructive to study, real interpolating methods like deep networks do not fit benignly. That is, noise in the train set leads to suboptimal generalization, suggesting that these methods fall in an intermediate regime between benign and catastrophic overfitting, in which asymptotic risk is neither is neither Bayes-optimal nor unbounded, with the confounding effect of the noise being ``tempered" but non-negligible. We call this behavior \textit{tempered overfitting}. We first provide broad empirical evidence for our three-part taxonomy, demonstrating that deep neural networks and kernel machines fit to noisy data can be reasonably well classified as benign, tempered, or catastrophic. We then specialize to kernel (ridge) regression (KR), obtaining conditions on the ridge parameter and kernel eigenspectrum under which KR exhibits each of the three behaviors, demonstrating the consequences for KR with common kernels and trained neural networks of infinite width using experiments on natural and synthetic datasets.

paragraphs: Models that fit their training data perfectly can still perform reasonably well on new data, even when training labels contain noise. This paper argues that explaining this behavior requires more than a distinction between harmless and disastrous overfitting. It introduces an intermediate category called tempered overfitting.

The three categories describe different limiting behaviors of prediction risk. In benign overfitting, performance approaches the Bayes-optimal level despite noise. In catastrophic overfitting, risk becomes unbounded. Tempered overfitting lies between them: the influence of noise remains bounded but still causes a persistent performance penalty. The authors argue that this middle category better captures the noisy-data behavior of practical interpolating models such as deep networks.

The paper supplies broad empirical evidence for this taxonomy across neural networks and kernel methods. It then derives conditions involving regularization and the kernel eigenspectrum that produce each behavior in kernel ridge regression. Experiments with natural and synthetic data illustrate consequences for common kernels and infinite-width trained neural networks. The resulting framework distinguishes tolerable noise sensitivity from genuinely optimal generalization.
summary.tldr: Tempered overfitting describes models whose fitting of noisy data causes bounded but persistent generalization error.

title: Benign, Tempered, or Catastrophic: Toward a Refined Taxonomy of Overfitting

abstract: Recent progress in vision Transformers exhibits great success in various tasks driven by the new spatial modeling mechanism based on dot-product self-attention. In this paper, we show that the key ingredients behind the vision Transformers, namely input-adaptive, long-range and high-order spatial interactions, can also be efficiently implemented with a convolution-based framework. We present the Recursive Gated Convolution ($\textit{g}^\textit{n}$Conv) that performs high-order spatial interactions with gated convolutions and recursive designs. The new operation is highly flexible and customizable, which is compatible with various variants of convolution and extends the two-order interactions in self-attention to arbitrary orders without introducing significant extra computation. $\textit{g}^\textit{n}$Conv can serve as a plug-and-play module to improve various vision Transformers and convolution-based models. Based on the operation, we construct a new family of generic vision backbones named HorNet. Extensive experiments on ImageNet classification, COCO object detection and ADE20K semantic segmentation show HorNet outperform Swin Transformers and ConvNeXt by a significant margin with similar overall architecture and training configurations. HorNet also shows favorable scalability to more training data and larger model sizes. Apart from the effectiveness in visual encoders, we also show $\textit{g}^\textit{n}$Conv can be applied to task-specific decoders and consistently improve dense prediction performance with less computation. Our results demonstrate that $\textit{g}^\textit{n}$Conv can be a new basic module for visual modeling that effectively combines the merits of both vision Transformers and CNNs. Code is available at https://github.com/raoyongming/HorNet.

This paper asks whether convolution-based models can efficiently provide key properties associated with that mechanism: interactions that adapt to the input, span long distances, and operate at higher orders. Its answer is a new operation called Recursive Gated Convolution.

The operation combines gated convolutions with a recursive design. It extends the second-order interactions described for self-attention to arbitrary orders without significant extra computation, and supports different convolution variants. The authors also report favorable scaling with more data and larger models. Applying the operation to task-specific decoders improves dense prediction with less computation, suggesting that its benefits extend beyond the main visual encoder.
summary.tldr: HorNet uses recursive gated convolutions to efficiently model adaptive, long-range, higher-order visual interactions.

title: HorNet: Efficient High-Order Spatial Interactions with Recursive Gated Convolutions

abstract: Machine learning models trained on private datasets have been shown to leak their private data. Recent work has found that the average data point is rarely leaked---it is often the outlier samples that are subject to memorization and, consequently, leakage. We demonstrate and analyze an Onion Effect of memorization: removing the "layer" of outlier points that are most vulnerable to a privacy attack exposes a new layer of previously-safe points to the same attack. We perform several experiments that are consistent with this hypothesis. For example, we show that for membership inference attacks, when the layer of easiest-to-attack examples is removed, another layer below becomes easy-to-attack. The existence of this effect has various consequences. For example, it suggests that proposals to defend against memorization without training with rigorous privacy guarantees are unlikely to be effective. Further, it suggests that privacy-enhancing technologies such as machine unlearning could actually harm the privacy of other users.

For example, we show that for membership inference attacks, when the layer of easiest-to-attack examples is removed, another layer below becomes easy-to-attack. The existence of this effect has various consequences. For example, it suggests that proposals to defend against memorization without training with rigorous privacy guarantees are unlikely to be effective. Further, it suggests that privacy-enhancing technologies such as machine unlearning could actually harm the privacy of other users.

paragraphs: Privacy leakage from a trained model is often concentrated among unusual training examples rather than the average example. This can suggest removing the most vulnerable records as a defense. The paper investigates why that strategy may be insufficient: vulnerability can depend on which other examples remain in the training dataset.

The authors describe an onion effect in which removing the most exposed layer makes previously safer examples vulnerable to the same attack. Several experiments are consistent with this hypothesis. In the membership-inference setting, removing the examples whose training membership is easiest to detect exposes another set that then becomes easy to attack. The identity of the most vulnerable records therefore changes as the dataset changes.

The findings suggest that defenses against memorization without rigorous privacy guarantees are unlikely to be effective. They also raise the possibility that machine unlearning could harm other users' privacy. These are implications of relative memorization: reducing exposure for selected records may alter, rather than simply reduce, the privacy risks faced by those remaining.
summary.tldr: Removing the records most vulnerable to privacy attacks can expose a new layer of previously safer records.

title: The Privacy Onion Effect: Memorization is Relative

abstract: Formulating and answering logical queries is a standard communication interface for knowledge graphs (KGs). Alleviating the notorious incompleteness of real-world KGs, neural methods achieved impressive results in link prediction and complex query answering tasks by learning representations of entities, relations, and queries. Still, most existing query answering methods rely on transductive entity embeddings and cannot generalize to KGs containing new entities without retraining entity embeddings. In this work, we study the inductive query answering task where inference is performed on a graph containing new entities with queries over both seen and unseen entities. To this end, we devise two mechanisms leveraging inductive node and relational structure representations powered by graph neural networks (GNNs).Experimentally, we show that inductive models are able to perform logical reasoning at inference time over unseen nodes generalizing to graphs up to 500% larger than training ones. Exploring the efficiency--effectiveness trade-off, we find the inductive relational structure representation method generally achieves higher performance, while the inductive node representation method is able to answer complex queries in the inference-only regime without any training on queries and scale to graphs of millions of nodes. Code is available at https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/InductiveQE

paragraphs: Neural query answering can help reason over incomplete knowledge graphs, but many methods attach learned representations to the particular entities present during training. When new entities appear, those representations need retraining. This paper studies inductive query answering, where queries can involve both familiar and previously unseen entities at inference time.

The authors develop two mechanisms powered by graph neural networks. One uses inductive node representations, while the other represents relational structure. Both approaches aim to make reasoning depend on transferable graph information rather than solely on a fixed inventory of entity embeddings. This changes how a query-answering system can accommodate a growing graph.

Experiments show reasoning over unseen nodes and generalization to graphs reported as up to 500% larger than the training graphs. The two mechanisms offer different efficiency and effectiveness tradeoffs. Relational structure representations generally perform better, while the node-based method can answer complex queries without training on queries and scale to graphs containing millions of nodes. The findings distinguish these capabilities rather than identifying one approach as best in every respect.
summary.tldr: Two graph-based representation methods enable logical query answering over new entities, with different accuracy and scalability tradeoffs.

title: Inductive Logical Query Answering in Knowledge Graphs

abstract: We introduce the Multi-Agent Tracking Environment (MATE), a novel multi-agent environment simulates the target coverage control problems in the real world. MATE hosts an asymmetric cooperative-competitive game consisting of two groups of learning agents--"cameras" and "targets"--with opposing interests. Specifically, "cameras", a group of directional sensors, are mandated to actively control the directional perception area to maximize the coverage rate of targets. On the other side, "targets" are mobile agents that aim to transport cargo between multiple randomly assigned warehouses while minimizing the exposure to the camera sensor networks. To showcase the practicality of MATE, we benchmark the multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms from different aspects, including cooperation, communication, scalability, robustness, and asymmetric self-play. We start by reporting results for cooperative tasks using MARL algorithms (MAPPO, IPPO, QMIX, MADDPG) and the results after augmenting with multi-agent communication protocols (TarMAC, I2C). We then evaluate the effectiveness of the popular self-play techniques (PSRO, fictitious self-play) in an asymmetric zero-sum competitive game. This process of co-evolution between cameras and targets helps to realize a less exploitable camera network. We also observe the emergence of different roles of the target agents while incorporating I2C into target-target communication. MATE is written purely in Python and integrated with OpenAI Gym API to enhance user-friendliness. Our project is released at https://github.com/UnrealTracking/mate.
