paragraphs: MATE is a simulated environment for studying groups of learning agents with both cooperative and competitive goals. One team controls directional cameras and tries to maximize coverage of moving targets. The other team transports cargo between randomly assigned warehouses while trying to minimize exposure to those cameras.

The teams have different capabilities and objectives, creating an asymmetric game. The authors use this setting to examine cooperation, communication, scalability, robustness, and self-play. They benchmark several multi-agent reinforcement learning methods, add communication protocols, and evaluate self-play techniques in the zero-sum competition between cameras and targets. The environment therefore supports several related research questions within one task structure.

The paper reports that co-evolution through self-play helps produce a camera network that is less exploitable. It also observes distinct roles emerging among target agents when they communicate using I2C. MATE is implemented in Python and integrates with the OpenAI Gym interface. Its contribution combines a reusable benchmark with evidence about communication and competitive training in target coverage.
summary.tldr: MATE benchmarks multi-agent learning through competing camera and cargo-transport teams, revealing benefits from communication and self-play.

title: MATE: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Distributed Target Coverage Control

abstract: In stereo vision, self-similar or bland regions can make it difficult to match patches between two images. Active stereo-based methods mitigate this problem by projecting a pseudo-random pattern on the scene so that each patch of an image pair can be identified without ambiguity. However, the projected pattern significantly alters the appearance of the image. If this pattern acts as a form of adversarial noise, it could negatively impact the performance of deep learning-based methods, which are now the de-facto standard for dense stereo vision. In this paper, we propose the Active-Passive SimStereo dataset and a corresponding benchmark to evaluate the performance gap between passive and active stereo images for stereo matching algorithms. Using the proposed benchmark and an additional ablation study, we show that the feature extraction and matching modules of a selection of twenty selected deep learning-based stereo matching methods generalize to active stereo without a problem. However, the disparity refinement modules of three of the twenty architectures (ACVNet, CascadeStereo, and StereoNet) are negatively affected by the active stereo patterns due to their reliance on the appearance of the input images.

paragraphs: Stereo vision depends on matching corresponding regions in two images. Repetitive or nearly textureless surfaces make this difficult. Active stereo adds a projected pseudo-random pattern to make regions easier to distinguish, but that pattern also changes image appearance. The paper investigates whether this change disrupts deep learning methods developed for stereo matching.

The authors introduce the Active-Passive SimStereo dataset and a benchmark for comparing performance on images with and without active patterns. They also conduct an ablation study to examine which parts of stereo architectures respond poorly to the appearance change. This makes the investigation more specific than a comparison of final predictions alone.

Across twenty selected methods, feature extraction and matching modules generalize successfully to active stereo. However, disparity refinement is negatively affected in ACVNet, CascadeStereo, and StereoNet because those modules depend on input appearance. The findings locate a particular vulnerability within the tested architectures: the projected pattern can support matching while still interfering with later refinement.
summary.tldr: A new stereo benchmark finds that active patterns transfer well through tested feature and matching modules but harm refinement in three architectures.

title: Active-Passive SimStereo - Benchmarking the Cross-Generalization Capabilities of Deep Learning-based Stereo Methods

abstract: We observe that given two (compatible) classes of functions $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{H}$ with small capacity as measured by their uniform covering numbers, the capacity of the composition class $\mathcal{H} \circ \mathcal{F}$ can become prohibitively large or even unbounded. We then show that adding a small amount of Gaussian noise to the output of $\mathcal{F}$ before composing it with $\mathcal{H}$ can effectively control the capacity of $\mathcal{H} \circ \mathcal{F}$, offering a general recipe for modular design. To prove our results, we define new notions of uniform covering number of random functions with respect to the total variation and Wasserstein distances. We instantiate our results for the case of multi-layer sigmoid neural networks. Preliminary empirical results on MNIST dataset indicate that the amount of noise required to improve over existing uniform bounds can be numerically negligible (i.e., element-wise i.i.d. Gaussian noise with standard deviation $10^{-240}$)

We then show that adding a small amount of Gaussian noise to the output of $\mathcal{F}$ before composing it with $\mathcal{H}$ can effectively control the capacity of $\mathcal{H} \circ \mathcal{F}$, offering a general recipe for modular design. To prove our results, we define new notions of uniform covering number of random functions with respect to the total variation and Wasserstein distances. Preliminary empirical results on MNIST dataset indicate that the amount of noise required to improve over existing uniform bounds can be numerically negligible (i.e., element-wise i.i.d. Gaussian noise with standard deviation $10^{-240}$)

paragraphs: Combining two individually manageable families of functions can create a much more complex family. This paper studies that problem using uniform covering numbers, a measure of how many representative functions are needed to approximate a class. Even when each component has a small covering number, passing one component's output into another can produce prohibitively large or unbounded capacity.

The proposed remedy is to add a small amount of Gaussian noise between the components. The authors show that this can control the capacity of the combined class, offering a way to reason about systems assembled from separate modules. Their proofs introduce covering numbers for random functions measured using total variation and Wasserstein distances.

The authors apply the theory to multilayer sigmoid networks. Preliminary MNIST results indicate that noise with an elementwise standard deviation as small as 10^-240 can improve on existing uniform bounds. This finding concerns the mathematical bounds: the stated empirical result does not claim that such tiny noise improves predictive accuracy. Its significance is that capacity control may require numerically negligible perturbations.
summary.tldr: Adding Gaussian noise between function classes can control the complexity that otherwise grows sharply when they are composed.

title: Benefits of Additive Noise in Composing Classes with Bounded Capacity

abstract: Pruning techniques have been successfully used in neural networks to trade accuracy for sparsity. However, the impact of network pruning is not uniform: prior work has shown that the recall for underrepresented classes in a dataset may be more negatively affected. In this work, we study such relative distortions in recall by hypothesizing an intensification effect that is inherent to the model. Namely, that pruning makes recall relatively worse for a class with recall below accuracy and, conversely, that it makes recall relatively better for a class with recall above accuracy. In addition, we propose a new pruning algorithm aimed at attenuating such effect. Through statistical analysis, we have observed that intensification is less severe with our algorithm but nevertheless more pronounced with relatively more difficult tasks, less complex models, and higher pruning ratios. More surprisingly, we conversely observe a de-intensification effect with lower pruning ratios.

In this work, we study such relative distortions in recall by hypothesizing an intensification effect that is inherent to the model. In addition, we propose a new pruning algorithm aimed at attenuating such effect. Through statistical analysis, we have observed that intensification is less severe with our algorithm but nevertheless more pronounced with relatively more difficult tasks, less complex models, and higher pruning ratios. More surprisingly, we conversely observe a de-intensification effect with lower pruning ratios.

paragraphs: Pruning removes parts of a neural network to increase sparsity, often at some cost to accuracy. That cost need not be shared equally across classes. This paper examines changes in class recall, the share of examples from a class that are recognized correctly, and asks how pruning alters existing differences in recognition performance.

The authors hypothesize an intensification effect: classes whose recall is below overall accuracy become relatively worse after pruning, while those above accuracy become relatively better. They propose Undecayed Pruning to reduce this effect. The hypothesis centers on a class's starting performance relative to overall accuracy, extending the investigation beyond class underrepresentation alone.

Statistical analysis finds less severe intensification with the proposed algorithm. It also finds stronger intensification for more difficult tasks, less complex models, and higher pruning ratios. At lower pruning ratios, the authors observe the opposite pattern, a reduction in the disparity. These findings make the relationship conditional on the pruning setting and show why aggregate accuracy alone cannot describe the changes studied.
summary.tldr: The paper studies how pruning changes relative class recall and proposes Undecayed Pruning to attenuate observed disparity intensification.

title: Recall Distortion in Neural Network Pruning and the Undecayed Pruning Algorithm

abstract: We present the problem of reinforcement learning with exogenous termination. We define the Termination Markov Decision Process (TerMDP), an extension of the MDP framework, in which episodes may be interrupted by an external non-Markovian observer. This formulation accounts for numerous real-world situations, such as a human interrupting an autonomous driving agent for reasons of discomfort. We learn the parameters of the TerMDP and leverage the structure of the estimation problem to provide state-wise confidence bounds. We use these to construct a provably-efficient algorithm, which accounts for termination, and bound its regret. Motivated by our theoretical analysis, we design and implement a scalable approach, which combines optimism (w.r.t. termination) and a dynamic discount factor, incorporating the termination probability. We deploy our method on high-dimensional driving and MinAtar benchmarks. Additionally, we test our approach on human data in a driving setting. Our results demonstrate fast convergence and significant improvement over various baseline approaches.

This formulation accounts for numerous real-world situations, such as a human interrupting an autonomous driving agent for reasons of discomfort. We learn the parameters of the TerMDP and leverage the structure of the estimation problem to provide state-wise confidence bounds. We use these to construct a provably-efficient algorithm, which accounts for termination, and bound its regret. Motivated by our theoretical analysis, we design and implement a scalable approach, which combines optimism (w.r.t. termination) and a dynamic discount factor, incorporating the termination probability. We deploy our method on high-dimensional driving and MinAtar benchmarks. Additionally, we test our approach on human data in a driving setting. Our results demonstrate fast convergence and significant improvement over various baseline approaches.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning episode may end because an outside observer interrupts it. For example, a human might stop an autonomous driving agent because its behavior feels uncomfortable. This paper formalizes such situations with a Termination Markov Decision Process, allowing the external observer’s decision to depend on history rather than only the current state.

The authors learn the parameters of this model and exploit the estimation problem’s structure to obtain confidence bounds for individual states. They use these bounds to construct a provably efficient learning algorithm that explicitly accounts for termination, with a regret bound. External interruption is therefore incorporated into the decision problem instead of being left outside its formal description.

The theory also motivates a scalable method combining optimism about termination with a dynamic discount factor that incorporates termination probability. Evaluations cover high-dimensional driving tasks, MinAtar benchmarks, and human data in a driving setting. The reported results show fast convergence and significant gains over several baselines, supporting the practical value of modeling an external observer’s ability to stop an episode.
summary.tldr: Modeling external, history-dependent interruptions leads to a theoretically supported reinforcement-learning algorithm and a scalable method with strong reported results.

title: Reinforcement Learning with a Terminator

abstract: We propose learnable polyphase sampling (LPS), a pair of learnable down/upsampling layers that enable truly shift-invariant and equivariant convolutional networks. LPS can be trained end-to-end from data and generalizes existing handcrafted downsampling layers. It is widely applicable as it can be integrated into any convolutional network by replacing down/upsampling layers. We evaluate LPS on image classification and semantic segmentation. Experiments show that LPS is on-par with or outperforms existing methods in both performance and shift consistency. For the first time, we achieve true shift-equivariance on semantic segmentation (PASCAL VOC), i.e., 100% shift consistency, outperforming baselines by an absolute 3.3%.

LPS can be trained end-to-end from data and generalizes existing handcrafted downsampling layers. It is widely applicable as it can be integrated into any convolutional network by replacing down/upsampling layers. We evaluate LPS on image classification and semantic segmentation. Experiments show that LPS is on-par with or outperforms existing methods in both performance and shift consistency. For the first time, we achieve true shift-equivariance on semantic segmentation (PASCAL VOC), i.e., 100% shift consistency, outperforming baselines by an absolute 3.3%.

paragraphs: Moving an image should have a predictable effect on a vision model. For classification, the predicted category should remain unchanged; for segmentation, the pixel-level output should move with the image. These are shift invariance and shift equivariance, respectively. The paper addresses both through the layers that reduce and restore spatial resolution.

Learnable polyphase sampling, or LPS, provides paired downsampling and upsampling layers that can be trained end to end. The approach generalizes existing handcrafted downsampling layers and can be integrated into convolutional networks by replacing their sampling layers. This makes the sampling operation itself a learned part of obtaining consistent behavior under image shifts.

Experiments cover image classification and semantic segmentation. LPS matches or exceeds existing methods in both task performance and shift consistency. On PASCAL VOC segmentation, the authors report 100% shift consistency, an absolute improvement of 3.3% over the baselines, and describe this as the first achievement of true shift equivariance for that task. The result ties the architectural change to both prediction quality and predictable spatial behavior.
summary.tldr: Learnable sampling layers enable shift-consistent convolutional networks, achieving 100% shift consistency in the reported PASCAL VOC segmentation evaluation.

title: Learnable Polyphase Sampling for Shift Invariant and Equivariant Convolutional Networks

abstract: This paper proposes a new easy-to-implement parameter-free gradient-based optimizer: DoWG (Distance over Weighted Gradients). We prove that DoWG is efficient---matching the convergence rate of optimally tuned gradient descent in convex optimization up to a logarithmic factor without tuning any parameters, and universal---automatically adapting to both smooth and nonsmooth problems. While popular algorithms following the AdaGrad framework compute a running average of the squared gradients, DoWG maintains a new distance-based weighted version of the running average, which is crucial to achieve the desired properties. To complement our theory, we also show empirically that DoWG trains at the edge of stability, and validate its effectiveness on practical machine learning tasks.
originalAbstract: This paper proposes a new easy-to-implement parameter-free gradient-based optimizer: DoWG (Distance over Weighted Gradients). We prove that DoWG is efficient---matching the convergence rate of optimally tuned gradient descent in convex optimization up to a logarithmic factor without tuning any parameters, and universal---automatically adapting to both smooth and nonsmooth problems. While popular algorithms following the AdaGrad framework compute a running average of the squared gradients, DoWG maintains a new distance-based weighted version of the running average, which is crucial to achieve the desired properties. To complement our theory, we also show empirically that DoWG trains at the edge of stability, and validate its effectiveness on practical machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Gradient-based optimization often requires choosing parameters carefully to obtain good convergence. DoWG, short for Distance over Weighted Gradients, is designed to remove that tuning requirement. The paper presents an easy-to-implement optimizer and analyzes whether it can achieve rates comparable to gradient descent whose parameters have already been optimally chosen.

Its key mechanism changes how past gradients are accumulated. Algorithms in the AdaGrad family commonly maintain a running average of squared gradients. DoWG uses a distance-based weighting of that history. The authors identify this weighting as essential to obtaining both efficient convergence and automatic adaptation to smooth and nonsmooth optimization problems.

For convex optimization, the paper proves that DoWG matches the convergence rate of optimally tuned gradient descent up to a logarithmic factor, without parameter tuning. Practical machine-learning experiments complement this guarantee and show training behavior described as operating at the edge of stability. The theoretical claim is specifically about convex problems, while the experiments provide separate evidence of practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: DoWG uses distance-weighted gradient history to avoid tuning while nearly matching optimally tuned gradient descent’s convex convergence rate.

title: DoWG Unleashed: An Efficient Universal Parameter-Free Gradient Descent Method

abstract: Although there has been work to develop ex-post private mechanisms from Ligett et al. '17 and Whitehouse et al '22 that seeks to provide privacy guarantees subject to a target level of accuracy, there was not a way to use them in conjunction with differentially private mechanisms. Furthermore, there has yet to be work in developing a theory for how these ex-post privacy mechanisms compose, so that we can track the accumulated privacy over several mechanisms. We develop privacy filters that allow an analyst to adaptively switch between differentially private mechanisms and ex-post private mechanisms subject to an overall privacy loss guarantee. We show that using a particular ex-post private mechanism --- noise reduction mechanisms --- can substantially outperform baseline approaches that use existing privacy loss composition bounds. We use the common task of returning as many counts as possible subject to a relative error guarantee and an overall privacy budget as a motivating example.
originalAbstract: Although there has been work to develop ex-post private mechanisms from Ligett et al. '17 and Whitehouse et al '22 that seeks to provide privacy guarantees subject to a target level of accuracy, there was not a way to use them in conjunction with differentially private mechanisms. Furthermore, there has yet to be work in developing a theory for how these ex-post privacy mechanisms compose, so that we can track the accumulated privacy over several mechanisms. We develop privacy filters that allow an analyst to adaptively switch between differentially private mechanisms and ex-post private mechanisms subject to an overall privacy loss guarantee. We show that using a particular ex-post private mechanism --- noise reduction mechanisms --- can substantially outperform baseline approaches that use existing privacy loss composition bounds. We use the common task of returning as many counts as possible subject to a relative error guarantee and an overall privacy budget as a motivating example.

paragraphs: Privacy protection becomes harder to track when an analysis runs several mechanisms in sequence. Accuracy-first mechanisms seek a specified accuracy level and provide an ex-post privacy guarantee. The paper addresses a gap in how these mechanisms can be combined with ordinary differentially private mechanisms while accounting for the total privacy loss.

The authors develop privacy filters that let an analyst adaptively switch between the two kinds of mechanisms under an overall privacy guarantee. This matters because the analyst need not commit to using only one kind throughout an analysis. The contribution is an accounting framework for the combined process, including choices made as the analysis proceeds.

The paper uses releasing counts as its motivating application: return as many counts as possible while meeting both a relative-error requirement and a total privacy budget. It shows that a particular accuracy-first approach, noise reduction, can substantially outperform baselines using existing composition bounds. The result supports more effective use of a privacy budget in this setting without abandoning an overall guarantee.
summary.tldr: Privacy filters enable adaptive combinations of accuracy-first and differentially private mechanisms while maintaining an overall privacy guarantee.

title: Adaptive Privacy Composition for Accuracy-first Mechanisms

abstract: We aim to investigate whether end-to-end learning of visual reasoning can be achieved with general-purpose neural networks, with the help of visual pretraining. A positive result would refute the common belief that explicit visual abstraction (e.g. object detection) is essential for compositional generalization on visual reasoning, and confirm the feasibility of a neural network ''generalist'' to solve visual recognition and reasoning tasks. We propose a simple and general self-supervised framework which ''compresses'' each video frame into a small set of tokens with a transformer network, and reconstructs the remaining frames based on the compressed temporal context. To minimize the reconstruction loss, the network must learn a compact representation for each image, as well as capture temporal dynamics and object permanence from temporal context. We perform evaluation on two visual reasoning benchmarks, CATER and ACRE. We observe that pretraining is essential to achieve compositional generalization for end-to-end visual reasoning. Our proposed framework outperforms traditional supervised pretraining, including image classification and explicit object detection, by large margins.

A positive result would refute the common belief that explicit visual abstraction (e.g. object detection) is essential for compositional generalization on visual reasoning, and confirm the feasibility of a neural network ''generalist'' to solve visual recognition and reasoning tasks. We propose a simple and general self-supervised framework which ''compresses'' each video frame into a small set of tokens with a transformer network, and reconstructs the remaining frames based on the compressed temporal context. To minimize the reconstruction loss, the network must learn a compact representation for each image, as well as capture temporal dynamics and object permanence from temporal context. We perform evaluation on two visual reasoning benchmarks, CATER and ACRE. We observe that pretraining is essential to achieve compositional generalization for end-to-end visual reasoning. Our proposed framework outperforms traditional supervised pretraining, including image classification and explicit object detection, by large margins.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a general-purpose neural network can learn visual reasoning directly from images without an explicit object-detection stage. The central issue is compositional generalization: using learned visual knowledge in new combinations. Success would challenge the view that a separately designed visual abstraction step is essential for this ability.

The authors propose self-supervised video pretraining. A transformer compresses each frame into a small collection of tokens and uses this compressed temporal context to reconstruct other frames. This objective encourages compact image representations while requiring the network to capture changes over time and object permanence, the persistence of objects through changes in what is visible.

Evaluations on CATER and ACRE show that pretraining is essential for compositional generalization in the studied end-to-end setup. The proposed approach substantially outperforms supervised pretraining based on image classification or explicit object detection. These findings support temporal reconstruction as a useful preparation for visual reasoning, with the evidence grounded in the two evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised video reconstruction enables strong end-to-end visual reasoning and outperforms supervised visual pretraining on two benchmarks.

title: Does Visual Pretraining Help End-to-End Reasoning?

abstract: The efficient frontier (EF) is a fundamental resource allocation problem where one has to find an optimal portfolio maximizing a reward at a given level of risk. This optimal solution is traditionally found by solving a convex optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce NeuralEF: a fast neural approximation framework that robustly forecasts the result of the EF convex optimizations problems with respect to heterogeneous linear constraints and variable number of optimization inputs. By reformulating an optimization problem as a sequence to sequence problem, we show that NeuralEF is a viable solution to accelerate large-scale simulation while handling discontinuous behavior.
originalAbstract: The efficient frontier (EF) is a fundamental resource allocation problem where one has to find an optimal portfolio maximizing a reward at a given level of risk. This optimal solution is traditionally found by solving a convex optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce NeuralEF: a fast neural approximation framework that robustly forecasts the result of the EF convex optimizations problems with respect to heterogeneous linear constraints and variable number of optimization inputs. By reformulating an optimization problem as a sequence to sequence problem, we show that NeuralEF is a viable solution to accelerate large-scale simulation while handling discontinuous behavior.

paragraphs: An efficient-frontier problem asks how to allocate resources to maximize reward at a specified level of risk. Traditionally, the answer comes from solving a convex optimization problem. NeuralEF learns to approximate the outputs of those optimizations, targeting situations where many such solutions are needed as part of a larger simulation.

The framework reformulates the optimization task as a sequence-to-sequence prediction problem. Its stated capabilities include handling heterogeneous linear constraints and a variable number of optimization inputs. Those features matter because the learning task must accommodate changes in both the restrictions imposed on a portfolio and the size of the problem being presented.

The authors show that NeuralEF can accelerate large-scale simulation while handling discontinuous behavior in the optimization results. The contribution is a neural approximation framework for forecasting solutions across varying problem instances. Its practical purpose is to make repeated efficient-frontier calculations faster, with flexibility across input counts and constraints forming a central part of that proposal. The predicted output remains an approximation to the optimization result.
summary.tldr: NeuralEF approximates efficient-frontier optimization solutions across varying constraints and input sizes to accelerate large-scale simulation.

title: Learning the Efficient Frontier

abstract: Embodied AI is a crucial frontier in robotics, capable of planning and executing action sequences for robots to accomplish long-horizon tasks in physical environments.In this work, we introduce EmbodiedGPT, an end-to-end multi-modal foundation model for embodied AI, empowering embodied agents with multi-modal understanding and execution capabilities. To achieve this, we have made the following efforts: (i) We craft a large-scale embodied planning dataset, termed EgoCOT. The dataset consists of carefully selected videos from the Ego4D dataset, along with corresponding high-quality language instructions. Specifically, we generate a sequence of sub-goals with the "Chain of Thoughts" mode for effective embodied planning.(ii) We introduce an efficient training approach to EmbodiedGPT for high-quality plan generation, by adapting a 7B large language model (LLM) to the EgoCOT dataset via prefix tuning. (iii) We introduce a paradigm for extracting task-related features from LLM-generated planning queries to form a closed loop between high-level planning and low-level control.Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of EmbodiedGPT on embodied tasks, including embodied planning, embodied control, visual captioning, and visual question answering.Notably, EmbodiedGPT significantly enhances the success rate of the embodied control task by extracting more effective features. It has achieved a remarkable 1.6 times increase in success rate on the Franka Kitchen benchmark and a 1.3 times increase on the Meta-World benchmark, compared to the BLIP-2 baseline fine-tuned with the Ego4D dataset.

paragraphs: EmbodiedGPT connects multimodal understanding, high-level planning, and low-level control for embodied tasks. Its motivation is that carrying out a long task requires both a sequence of useful subgoals and features that help an agent execute those plans. The proposed system is an end-to-end multimodal foundation model.

The authors construct EgoCOT from selected Ego4D videos and corresponding language instructions, including sequences of planning subgoals. They adapt a seven-billion-parameter language model to this dataset using prefix tuning. They also extract task-related features from model-generated planning queries, forming a closed loop between planning and control.

Experiments cover embodied planning, control, visual captioning, and visual question answering. For control, the authors report success rates 1.6 times those of the comparison system on Franka Kitchen and 1.3 times on Meta-World. That comparison uses BLIP-2 fine-tuned on Ego4D. These results support the usefulness of the extracted planning-related features in the evaluated control tasks, alongside the model's broader multimodal capabilities.
summary.tldr: EmbodiedGPT uses video-derived subgoal training and planning-related features to connect language-based planning with embodied control.

title: EmbodiedGPT: Vision-Language Pre-Training via Embodied Chain of Thought

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are widely used for modeling complex interactions between entities represented as vertices of a graph. Despite recent efforts to theoretically analyze the expressive power of GNNs, a formal characterization of their ability to model interactions is lacking. The current paper aims to address this gap. Formalizing strength of interactions through an established measure known as separation rank, we quantify the ability of certain GNNs to model interaction between a given subset of vertices and its complement, i.e. between the sides of a given partition of input vertices. Our results reveal that the ability to model interaction is primarily determined by the partition's walk index --- a graph-theoretical characteristic defined by the number of walks originating from the boundary of the partition. Experiments with common GNN architectures corroborate this finding. As a practical application of our theory, we design an edge sparsification algorithm named Walk Index Sparsification (WIS), which preserves the ability of a GNN to model interactions when input edges are removed. WIS is simple, computationally efficient, and in our experiments has markedly outperformed alternative methods in terms of induced prediction accuracy. More broadly, it showcases the potential of improving GNNs by theoretically analyzing the interactions they can model.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks model relationships among entities, but their ability to represent interactions needs a more precise account than general statements about expressive power. This paper studies interactions across a partition of the graph: one group of vertices on one side and all remaining vertices on the other.

The authors quantify interaction strength using separation rank. For the GNNs covered by their analysis, interaction capacity is primarily governed by the partition’s walk index, a graph property based on walks originating at the partition boundary. Experiments with common GNN architectures support this connection. The result links a model’s ability to combine information across groups to a concrete feature of graph structure.

The authors turn the theory into Walk Index Sparsification, an algorithm for removing edges while preserving interaction-modeling capacity. They describe it as simple and computationally efficient, and report markedly better resulting prediction accuracy than alternative sparsification methods in their experiments. This application shows how an analysis of interactions can guide practical decisions about which graph connections to retain.
summary.tldr: A graph’s walk index helps characterize GNN interaction capacity and guides an effective edge-sparsification algorithm.

title: On the Ability of Graph Neural Networks to Model Interactions Between Vertices

abstract: Generative models produce unbounded outputs, necessitating the use of refusal techniques to confine their output space. Employing generative refusals is crucial in upholding the ethical and copyright integrity of synthesized content, particularly when working with widely adopted diffusion models. "Concept negation'' presents a promising paradigm to achieve generative refusals, as it effectively defines and governs the model's output space based on concepts, utilizing natural language interfaces that are readily comprehensible to humans. However, despite the valuable contributions of prior research to the field of concept negation, it still suffers from significant limitations. The existing concept negation methods, which operate based on the composition of score or noise predictions from the diffusion process, are limited to independent concepts (e.g., ``a blonde girl`` without ``glasses``) and fail to consider the interconnected nature of concepts in reality (e.g., ``Mickey mouse eats ice cream`` without ``Disney characters``). Keeping the limitations in mind, we propose a novel framework, called $ProtoRe$, to improve the flexibility of concept negation via test-time negative concept identification along with purification in the feature space. $ProtoRe$ works by incorporating CLIP's language-contrastive knowledge to identify the prototype of negative concepts, extract the negative features from outputs using the prototype as a prompt, and further refine the attention maps by retrieving negative features. Our evaluation on multiple benchmarks shows that $ProtoRe$ outperforms state-of-the-art methods under various settings, in terms of the effectiveness of purification and the fidelity of generative images.

paragraphs: Concept negation aims to keep specified concepts out of generated images through natural-language instructions. The paper identifies a difficulty with existing methods that combine diffusion score or noise predictions: they handle independent concepts but fail to account for relationships between concepts. Excluding a broad category can require recognizing its connection to a specifically named subject.

ProtoRe addresses this issue during generation by identifying unwanted concepts and removing their influence in feature space. It uses CLIP’s language-contrastive knowledge to identify a prototype of a negative concept. That prototype guides the extraction of negative features from outputs, and retrieving these features helps refine the model’s attention maps.

This approach makes concept negation depend on the unwanted concept’s representation and connections, improving flexibility beyond independent exclusions. Across multiple benchmarks and settings, the authors report better purification effectiveness and image fidelity than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the proposed test-time mechanism as a way to improve generative refusals while retaining the quality of the resulting images.
summary.tldr: ProtoRe uses CLIP-derived concept prototypes and feature-space purification to improve test-time exclusion of interconnected concepts from generated images.

title: Towards Test-Time Refusals via Concept Negation

abstract: Extending recent advances in Learning from Demonstration (LfD) frameworks to multi-robot settings poses critical challenges such as environment non-stationarity due to partial observability which is detrimental to the applicability of existing methods. Although prior work has shown that enabling communication among agents of a robot team can alleviate such issues, creating inter-agent communication under existing Multi-Agent LfD (MA-LfD) frameworks requires the human expert to provide demonstrations for both environment actions and communication actions, which necessitates an efficient communication strategy on a known message spaces. To address this problem, we propose Mixed-Initiative Multi-Agent Apprenticeship Learning (MixTURE). MixTURE enables robot teams to learn from a human expert-generated data a preferred policy to accomplish a collaborative task, while simultaneously learning emergent inter-agent communication to enhance team coordination. The key ingredient to MixTURE's success is automatically learning a communication policy, enhanced by a mutual-information maximizing reverse model that rationalizes the underlying expert demonstrations without the need for human generated data or an auxiliary reward function. MixTURE outperforms a variety of relevant baselines on diverse data generated by human experts in complex heterogeneous domains. MixTURE is the first MA-LfD framework to enable learning multi-robot collaborative policies directly from real human data, resulting in ~44% less human workload, and ~46% higher usability score.

paragraphs: Teaching a robot team from demonstrations is difficult when each robot observes only part of the environment. Communication can improve coordination, but existing multi-agent demonstration frameworks may require experts to demonstrate both task actions and communication actions. This adds the burden of specifying how robots should communicate within a known message space.

MixTURE learns collaborative behavior from human expert data while also learning communication among the robots. Its key component is an automatically learned communication policy supported by a reverse model that maximizes mutual information. This model helps account for the expert demonstrations without requiring human-generated communication data or an auxiliary reward function.

The authors report that MixTURE outperforms relevant baselines across diverse human-generated data in complex heterogeneous domains. They also report approximately 44% lower human workload and a 46% higher usability score. These findings support the practical value of learning communication alongside task behavior: experts can demonstrate how to accomplish a collaborative task while the framework takes on more of the work of developing coordination.
summary.tldr: MixTURE learns robot-team behavior and communication from human task demonstrations, reducing expert workload in the reported evaluation.

title: Mixed-Initiative Multiagent Apprenticeship Learning for Human Training of Robot Teams

abstract: Inductive Conformal Prediction (ICP) provides a practical and effective approach for equipping deep learning models with uncertainty estimates in the form of set-valued predictions which are guaranteed to contain the ground truth with high probability.Despite the appeal of this coverage guarantee, these sets may not be efficient: the size and contents of the prediction sets are not directly controlled, and instead depend on the underlying model and choice of score function.To remedy this, recent work has proposed learning model and score function parameters using data to directly optimize the efficiency of the ICP prediction sets.While appealing, the generalization theory for such an approach is lacking: direct optimization of empirical efficiency may yield prediction sets that are either no longer efficient on test data, or no longer obtain the required coverage on test data.In this work, we use PAC-Bayes theory to obtain generalization bounds on both the coverage and the efficiency of set-valued predictors which can be directly optimized to maximize efficiency while satisfying a desired test coverage.In contrast to prior work, our framework allows us to utilize the entire calibration dataset to learn the parameters of the model and score function, instead of requiring a separate hold-out set for obtaining test-time coverage guarantees.We leverage these theoretical results to provide a practical algorithm for using calibration data to simultaneously fine-tune the parameters of a model and score function while guaranteeing test-time coverage and efficiency of the resulting prediction sets.We evaluate the approach on regression and classification tasks, and outperform baselines calibrated using a Hoeffding bound-based PAC guarantee on ICP, especially in the low-data regime.

paragraphs: Inductive conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible answers with a high-probability coverage guarantee. Useful sets should also be efficient in their size and contents. Learning model and scoring parameters to improve those properties creates a challenge: gains on calibration data may fail to preserve efficiency or coverage on test data.

This paper uses PAC-Bayes theory to derive generalization bounds for both coverage and efficiency. Those bounds can be optimized to improve efficiency while satisfying a desired test-coverage requirement. The framework permits using the entire calibration dataset to learn model and score parameters, avoiding the separate holdout set required by the compared approach.

The authors turn the theory into an algorithm that jointly fine-tunes the prediction model and score function using calibration data. Evaluations on regression and classification tasks outperform baselines using a Hoeffding-bound-based PAC guarantee, especially when data are scarce. The contribution brings the optimization objective and its statistical guarantees together, making calibration data useful for learning efficient prediction sets while retaining guarantees about their test-time behavior.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayes bounds enable learning more efficient conformal prediction sets from the full calibration dataset while certifying test-time coverage and efficiency.

title: PAC-Bayes Generalization Certificates for Learned Inductive Conformal Prediction

abstract: We propose a theoretical framework for studying behavior cloning of complex expert demonstrations using generative modeling.Our framework invokes low-level controllers - either learned or implicit in position-command control - to stabilize imitation around expert demonstrations. We show that with (a) a suitable low-level stability guarantee and (b) a powerful enough generative model as our imitation learner, pure supervised behavior cloning can generate trajectories matching the per-time step distribution of essentially arbitrary expert trajectories in an optimal transport cost. Our analysis relies on a stochastic continuity property of the learned policy we call "total variation continuity" (TVC). We then show that TVC can be ensured with minimal degradation of accuracy by combining a popular data-augmentation regimen with a novel algorithmic trick: adding augmentation noise at execution time. We instantiate our guarantees for policies parameterized by diffusion models and prove that if the learner accurately estimates the score of the (noise-augmented) expert policy, then the distribution of imitator trajectories is close to the demonstrator distribution in a natural optimal transport distance. Our analysis constructs intricate couplings between noise-augmented trajectories, a technique that may be of independent interest. We conclude by empirically validating our algorithmic recommendations, and discussing implications for future research directions for better behavior cloning with generative modeling.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning learns to imitate demonstrations through supervised learning. This paper develops a theoretical framework for complex expert behavior using generative models, with low-level controllers stabilizing execution around demonstrations. Those controllers may be learned or already implicit in position-command control.

The main guarantee requires suitable low-level stability and a sufficiently expressive generative learner. Under those conditions, behavior cloning can match the per-time-step distributions of essentially arbitrary expert trajectories in an optimal transport cost. The analysis uses a policy property called total variation continuity. The authors show how data augmentation combined with augmentation noise during execution can ensure this property with little loss of accuracy.

For diffusion-based policies, the paper further proves closeness between imitator and expert trajectory distributions when the learner accurately estimates the noise-augmented expert policy’s score. Experiments validate the algorithmic recommendations. The work explains how stable low-level execution and expressive high-level imitation can jointly support distributional guarantees, while keeping the required stability and estimation conditions explicit.
summary.tldr: Under stability and modeling conditions, generative behavior cloning receives distributional guarantees strengthened by adding augmentation noise during execution.

title: Provable Guarantees for Generative Behavior Cloning: Bridging Low-Level Stability and High-Level Behavior

abstract: A prominent goal of representation learning research is to achieve representations which are factorized in a useful manner with respect to the ground truth factors of variation. The fields of disentangled and equivariant representation learning have approached this ideal from a range of complimentary perspectives; however, to date, most approaches have proven to either be ill-specified or insufficiently flexible to effectively separate all realistic factors of interest in a learned latent space. In this work, we propose an alternative viewpoint on such structured representation learning which we call Flow Factorized Representation Learning, and demonstrate it to learn both more efficient and more usefully structured representations than existing frameworks. Specifically, we introduce a generative model which specifies a distinct set of latent probability paths that define different input transformations. Each latent flow is generated by the gradient field of a learned potential following dynamic optimal transport. Our novel setup brings new understandings to both \textit{disentanglement} and \textit{equivariance}. We show that our model achieves higher likelihoods on standard representation learning benchmarks while simultaneously being closer to approximately equivariant models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transformations learned by our model are flexibly composable and can also extrapolate to new data, implying a degree of robustness and generalizability approaching the ultimate goal of usefully factorized representation learning.

paragraphs: Structured representation learning aims to separate meaningful factors of variation within a model’s internal representation. The paper argues that existing disentangled and equivariant approaches can be insufficiently specified or flexible for realistic factors. It proposes organizing representations around distinct transformations expressed as flows through latent space.

The generative model defines separate probability paths for different input transformations. Each flow follows the gradient field of a learned potential under dynamic optimal transport. This provides a way to describe how a representation changes under a transformation, connecting the separation of factors with the goal of having latent changes correspond to changes in the input.

On standard representation-learning benchmarks, the model achieves higher likelihoods while moving closer to approximate equivariance. The authors also demonstrate that learned transformations can be composed flexibly and extrapolated to new data. These findings suggest a degree of robustness and generalizability, alongside a more useful organization of the learned representation. The claim concerns the demonstrated structure and transfer, rather than complete separation of every possible factor.
summary.tldr: The method structures latent representations through learned transformation flows that compose flexibly and show improved likelihood and approximate equivariance.

title: Flow Factorized Representation Learning

abstract: Current perceptual similarity metrics operate at the level of pixels and patches. These metrics compare images in terms of their low-level colors and textures, but fail to capture mid-level similarities and differences in image layout, object pose, and semantic content. In this paper, we develop a perceptual metric that assesses images holistically. Our first step is to collect a new dataset of human similarity judgments over image pairs that are alike in diverse ways. Critical to this dataset is that judgments are nearly automatic and shared by all observers. To achieve this we use recent text-to-image models to create synthetic pairs that are perturbed along various dimensions. We observe that popular perceptual metrics fall short of explaining our new data, and we introduce a new metric, DreamSim, tuned to better align with human perception. We analyze how our metric is affected by different visual attributes, and find that it focuses heavily on foreground objects and semantic content while also being sensitive to color and layout. Notably, despite being trained on synthetic data, our metric generalizes to real images, giving strong results on retrieval and reconstruction tasks. Furthermore, our metric outperforms both prior learned metrics and recent large vision models on these tasks. Our project page: https://dreamsim-nights.github.io/

paragraphs: Two images can resemble one another in object pose, composition, and meaning even when their local colors or textures differ. This paper argues that existing perceptual similarity metrics miss important aspects of that broader resemblance. It introduces DreamSim, a metric trained to bring image comparisons into closer agreement with human visual judgments.

The authors first use text-to-image models to generate synthetic image pairs that differ along varied visual dimensions. They collect human similarity judgments on these pairs, aiming for comparisons that people make readily and consistently. Existing metrics struggle to explain this dataset, so the authors tune a new metric using the judgments. Their analysis finds that DreamSim emphasizes foreground objects and semantic content while remaining sensitive to color and layout.

Although its training data are synthetic, DreamSim transfers to real images in the reported retrieval and reconstruction tasks. It outperforms previous learned metrics and recent large vision models on those tasks. The findings show that deliberately generated comparisons can provide useful supervision for a more holistic similarity measure, with benefits extending beyond the synthetic images used to train it.
summary.tldr: DreamSim learns from human judgments of synthetic image pairs to measure broader visual similarity and transfers successfully to real-image tasks.

title: DreamSim: Learning New Dimensions of Human Visual Similarity using Synthetic Data

abstract: Neural collapse (NC) refers to the surprising structure of the last layer of deep neural networks in the terminal phase of gradient descent training. Recently, an increasing amount of experimental evidence has pointed to the propagation of NC to earlier layers of neural networks. However, while the NC in the last layer is well studied theoretically, much less is known about its multi-layered counterpart - deep neural collapse (DNC). In particular, existing work focuses either on linear layers or only on the last two layers at the price of an extra assumption. Our work fills this gap by generalizing the established analytical framework for NC - the unconstrained features model - to multiple non-linear layers. Our key technical contribution is to show that, in a deep unconstrained features model, the unique global optimum for binary classification exhibits all the properties typical of DNC. This explains the existing experimental evidence of DNC. We also empirically show that (i) by optimizing deep unconstrained features models via gradient descent, the resulting solution agrees well with our theory, and (ii) trained networks recover the unconstrained features suitable for the occurrence of DNC, thus supporting the validity of this modeling principle.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a distinctive structure that appears in a network’s final layer late in training. Experiments have also found related structure in earlier layers, a phenomenon called deep neural collapse. Explaining that multilayer pattern is harder: earlier theoretical work addressed linear layers or only the final two layers with an additional assumption.

The paper extends the unconstrained features model, an existing framework for analyzing neural collapse, to multiple nonlinear layers. Within this deep version of the framework, the authors prove that the unique global optimum for binary classification has the properties associated with deep neural collapse. The binary classification setting and the analytical model are essential to the scope of this result.

Two empirical checks support the theory. Gradient descent on the deep unconstrained features model produces solutions that agree well with the prediction, and trained networks recover features suitable for deep neural collapse. Together, these findings connect the mathematical framework to observed network behavior and support its use in explaining why collapse can extend beyond the final layer.
summary.tldr: For binary classification in a deep unconstrained features model, the authors prove that the unique global optimum exhibits deep neural collapse.

title: Deep Neural Collapse Is Provably Optimal for the Deep Unconstrained Features Model

abstract: In this paper, we develop an active learning framework for the bipartite ranking problem.Motivated by numerous applications, ranging from supervised anomaly detection to credit-scoring through the design of medical diagnosis support systems, and usually formulated as the problem of optimizing (a scalar summary of) the ROC curve, bipartite ranking has been the subject of much attention in the passive context. Various dedicated algorithms have been recently proposed and studied by the machine-learning community. In contrast, active bipartite ranking rule is poorly documented in the literature. Due to its global nature, a strategy for labeling sequentially data points that are difficult to rank w.r.t. to the others is required. This learning task is much more complex than binary classification, for which many active algorithms have been designed. It is the goal of this article to provide a rigorous formulation of such a selective sampling approach. We propose a dedicated algorithm, referred to as active-rank, which aims to minimise the distance between the ROC curve of the ranking function built and the optimal one, w.r.t. the sup norm. We show that, for a fixed confidence level $\epsilon$ and probability $\delta$, active-rank is PAC$(\epsilon,\delta)$. In addition, we provide a problem dependent upper bound on the expected sampling time of active-rank and also demonstrate a problem dependent lower bound on the expected sampling time of any PAC$(\epsilon,\delta)$ algorithm. Beyond the theoretical analysis carried out, numerical results are presented, providing strong empirical evidence of the performance of the algorithm proposed, which compares favorably with more naive approaches.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we develop an active learning framework for the bipartite ranking problem.Motivated by numerous applications, ranging from supervised anomaly detection to credit-scoring through the design of medical diagnosis support systems, and usually formulated as the problem of optimizing (a scalar summary of) the ROC curve, bipartite ranking has been the subject of much attention in the passive context. Various dedicated algorithms have been recently proposed and studied by the machine-learning community. In contrast, active bipartite ranking rule is poorly documented in the literature. Due to its global nature, a strategy for labeling sequentially data points that are difficult to rank w.r.t. to the others is required. This learning task is much more complex than binary classification, for which many active algorithms have been designed. It is the goal of this article to provide a rigorous formulation of such a selective sampling approach. We propose a dedicated algorithm, referred to as active-rank, which aims to minimise the distance between the ROC curve of the ranking function built and the optimal one, w.r.t. the sup norm. We show that, for a fixed confidence level $\epsilon$ and probability $\delta$, active-rank is PAC$(\epsilon,\delta)$. In addition, we provide a problem dependent upper bound on the expected sampling time of active-rank and also demonstrate a problem dependent lower bound on the expected sampling time of any PAC$(\epsilon,\delta)$ algorithm. Beyond the theoretical analysis carried out, numerical results are presented, providing strong empirical evidence of the performance of the algorithm proposed, which compares favorably with more naive approaches.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking learns to order examples from two classes, as needed in applications such as anomaly detection and credit scoring. Its quality is often assessed through the ROC curve. The paper studies an active version of this problem, where the learner chooses which examples to label instead of simply accepting a supplied labeled dataset.

Selecting useful labels is challenging because ranking quality depends on an example's position relative to other examples. The proposed active-rank algorithm addresses this global structure directly. It aims to bring its learned ROC curve close to the optimal curve under the supremum norm, which measures their largest discrepancy rather than only an average or scalar summary.

The authors prove that active-rank satisfies a probably approximately correct guarantee for specified accuracy and probability parameters. They also bound its expected sampling time and establish a problem-dependent lower bound for any algorithm meeting the same guarantee. Numerical results favor active-rank over more naive approaches, complementing the theory with evidence that selective labeling can be useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Active-rank selectively requests labels to learn a ranking with a provable ROC-curve accuracy guarantee.

title: Active Bipartite Ranking

abstract: Offline model-based optimization aims to find a design that maximizes a property of interest using only an offline dataset, with applications in robot, protein, and molecule design, among others. A prevalent approach is gradient ascent, where a proxy model is trained on the offline dataset and then used to optimize the design. This method suffers from an out-of-distribution issue, where the proxy is not accurate for unseen designs. To mitigate this issue, we explore using a pseudo-labeler to generate valuable data for fine-tuning the proxy. Specifically, we propose $\textit{\textbf{I}mportance-aware \textbf{C}o-\textbf{T}eaching for Offline Model-based Optimization}~(\textbf{ICT})$. This method maintains three symmetric proxies with their mean ensemble as the final proxy, and comprises two steps. The first step is $\textit{pseudo-label-driven co-teaching}$. In this step, one proxy is iteratively selected as the pseudo-labeler for designs near the current optimization point, generating pseudo-labeled data. Subsequently, a co-teaching process identifies small-loss samples as valuable data and exchanges them between the other two proxies for fine-tuning, promoting knowledge transfer. This procedure is repeated three times, with a different proxy chosen as the pseudo-labeler each time, ultimately enhancing the ensemble performance.To further improve accuracy of pseudo-labels, we perform a secondary step of $\textit{meta-learning-based sample reweighting}$,which assigns importance weights to samples in the pseudo-labeled dataset and updates them via meta-learning. ICT achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple design-bench tasks, achieving the best mean rank $3.1$ and median rank $2$ among $15$ methods.Our source code can be accessed here.

paragraphs: Offline model-based optimization searches for a high-performing design using an existing dataset. A common approach trains a proxy for the desired property and then optimizes against it. The difficulty is that optimization can reach unfamiliar designs where the proxy's predictions are inaccurate. ICT addresses this by generating and selectively using pseudo-labeled data near the current search point.

ICT maintains three proxy models and uses their average prediction as the final proxy. One model generates pseudo-labels while the other two select small-loss examples and exchange them for fine-tuning. Each model takes a turn as pseudo-labeler. This co-teaching process is intended to transfer useful knowledge and improve the ensemble during optimization.

A second component assigns importance weights to pseudo-labeled samples and updates those weights through meta-learning to improve pseudo-label accuracy. Across multiple Design-Bench tasks, ICT reports state-of-the-art results, including the best mean rank of 3.1 and median rank of 2 among 15 methods. The findings support adapting the proxy around the search trajectory while controlling which generated examples influence it.
summary.tldr: ICT improves offline design optimization by having three proxy models exchange selected pseudo-labeled examples and learn their importance weights.

title: Importance-aware Co-teaching for Offline Model-based Optimization

abstract: Goal-conditioned policies are generally understood to be "feed-forward" circuits, in the form of neural networks that map from the current state and the goal specification to the next action to take. However, under what circumstances such a policy can be learned and how efficient the policy will be are not well understood. In this paper, we present a circuit complexity analysis for relational neural networks (such as graph neural networks and transformers) representing policies for planning problems, by drawing connections with serialized goal regression search (S-GRS). We show that there are three general classes of planning problems, in terms of the growth of circuit width and depth as a function of the number of objects and planning horizon, providing constructive proofs. We also illustrate the utility of this analysis for designing neural networks for policy learning.

paragraphs: A goal-conditioned policy maps the current state and a desired goal to the next action. Representing that mapping as a feed-forward neural network raises a structural question: how large or deep must the network become as planning problems grow? This paper studies that question for relational networks, including graph neural networks and transformers.

The authors connect neural policy representations to serialized goal regression search. They use this connection to analyze circuit complexity, focusing on how network width and depth grow with the number of objects and the planning horizon. Their analysis identifies three general classes of planning problems and supplies constructive proofs, showing how the relevant representations can be built.

The work also illustrates how this analysis can guide network design for policy learning. Its significance is that planning structure can inform architectural requirements rather than leaving network size entirely to trial and error. The stated results concern representation and circuit scaling; they provide a way to reason about neural policies without asserting that every representable policy will be easy to learn.
summary.tldr: A circuit-complexity analysis classifies planning problems by how relational neural policy width and depth scale with objects and planning horizon.

title: What Planning Problems Can A Relational Neural Network Solve?

abstract: Generative transformer models have become increasingly complex, with large numbers of parameters and the ability to process multiple input modalities. Current methods for explaining their predictions are resource-intensive. Most crucially, they require prohibitively large amounts of additional memory, since they rely on backpropagation which allocates almost twice as much GPU memory as the forward pass. This makes it difficult, if not impossible, to use explanations in production. We present AtMan that provides explanations of generative transformer models at almost no extra cost. Specifically, AtMan is a modality-agnostic perturbation method that manipulates the attention mechanisms of transformers to produce relevance maps for the input with respect to the output prediction. Instead of using backpropagation, AtMan applies a parallelizable token-based search method relying on cosine similarity neighborhood in the embedding space. Our exhaustive experiments on text and image-text benchmarks demonstrate that AtMan outperforms current state-of-the-art gradient-based methods on several metrics while being computationally efficient. As such, AtMan is suitable for use in large model inference deployments.

paragraphs: Explaining a large generative transformer can require substantial memory beyond what is needed to produce its prediction. The paper identifies backpropagation as a major source of this overhead in existing explanation methods. AtMan aims to make explanations practical during inference by estimating which input elements matter to an output without running backward through the model.

AtMan perturbs the transformer’s attention mechanisms and uses the resulting behavior to construct input relevance maps for a prediction. Its search operates on tokens and uses neighborhoods defined by cosine similarity in embedding space. Because this search can be parallelized and does not depend on a specific input modality, the method can be applied to both text and multimodal inputs.

Experiments on text and image-text benchmarks report better performance than leading gradient-based explanation methods on several metrics, alongside computational efficiency. These findings support the proposed use of AtMan in large-model inference deployments where explanation memory costs are a concern. Its contribution is an attention-manipulation procedure for producing relevance maps, with the reported advantage tied to the evaluated benchmarks and metrics.
summary.tldr: AtMan explains transformer predictions by manipulating attention, producing relevance maps without memory-intensive backpropagation.

title: ATMAN: Understanding Transformer Predictions Through Memory Efficient Attention Manipulation

abstract: A Top Two sampling rule for bandit identification is a method which selects the next arm to sample from among two candidate arms, a *leader* and a *challenger*. Due to their simplicity and good empirical performance, they have received increased attention in recent years. However, for fixed-confidence best arm identification, theoretical guarantees for Top Two methods have only been obtained in the asymptotic regime, when the error level vanishes. In this paper, we derive the first non-asymptotic upper bound on the expected sample complexity of a Top Two algorithm, which holds for any error level. Our analysis highlights sufficient properties for a regret minimization algorithm to be used as leader. These properties are satisfied by the UCB algorithm, and our proposed UCB-based Top Two algorithm simultaneously enjoys non-asymptotic guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks a learning algorithm to determine which option has the highest expected reward while controlling its probability of error. A Top Two sampling rule chooses each new observation from two candidates, a leader and a challenger. These methods are simple and perform well empirically, but their earlier guarantees concerned the limiting case where the allowed error approaches zero.

This paper derives an upper bound on expected sample complexity that applies at any error level. That makes the guarantee non-asymptotic: it addresses a selected confidence requirement directly rather than relying only on behavior in a limit. The analysis also identifies sufficient properties that allow a regret-minimization algorithm to supply the leader.

The authors show that UCB satisfies those properties and use it to construct a Top Two algorithm. The resulting method combines the new sample-complexity guarantee with competitive experimental performance. The broader value is a theoretical route from a suitable leader-selection procedure to finite-confidence guarantees; the stated properties are sufficient conditions, not a claim that every valid leader must satisfy them.
summary.tldr: A UCB-based Top Two algorithm gains an expected sample-complexity guarantee valid at any error level while remaining empirically competitive.

title: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of a UCB-based Top Two Algorithm

abstract: We introduce Back-Modality, a novel data augmentation schema predicated on modal transformation. Data from an initial modality undergoes transformation to an intermediate modality, followed by a reverse transformation. This framework serves dual roles. On one hand, it operates as a general data augmentation strategy. On the other hand, it allows for other augmentation techniques, suitable for the intermediate modality, to enhance the initial modality. For instance, data augmentation methods applicable to pure text can be employed to augment images, thereby facilitating the cross-modality of data augmentation techniques. To validate the viability and efficacy of our framework, we proffer three instantiations of Back-Modality: back-captioning, back-imagination, and back-speech. Comprehensive evaluations across tasks such as image classification, sentiment classification, and textual entailment demonstrate that our methods consistently enhance performance under data-scarce circumstances.

paragraphs: Back-Modality proposes a general way to create additional training examples by moving data between modalities. An example begins in one form, passes through an intermediate form, and is then converted back. This round trip supplies a framework for producing variations of data through transformations across different forms of representation.

The framework has two uses. The transformation cycle itself acts as data augmentation, and the intermediate modality provides a place to apply other augmentation methods. For example, an image can benefit from augmentation techniques designed for text when text serves as the intermediate representation. This allows techniques developed for one modality to contribute to learning in another.

The authors demonstrate three versions, called back-captioning, back-imagination, and back-speech. They evaluate the framework on image classification, sentiment classification, and textual entailment, reporting consistent performance improvements when training data is scarce. The findings support cross-modal transformation as a useful augmentation strategy in those settings, with the intermediate representation becoming an active part of how new training examples are generated.
summary.tldr: Back-Modality augments data by converting it into another modality and back, improving evaluated tasks when training data is scarce.

title: Back-Modality: Leveraging Modal Transformation for Data Augmentation

abstract: The aim of this paper is to make clear and precise the relationship between the Rubin causal model (RCM) and structural causal model (SCM) frameworks for causal inference. Adopting a neutral logical perspective, and drawing on previous work, we show what is required for an RCM to be representable by an SCM. A key result then shows that every RCM---including those that violate algebraic principles implied by the SCM framework---emerges as an abstraction of some representable RCM. Finally, we illustrate the power of this ameliorative perspective by pinpointing an important role for SCM principles in classic applications of RCMs; conversely, we offer a characterization of the algebraic constraints implied by a graph, helping to substantiate further comparisons between the two frameworks.
originalAbstract: The aim of this paper is to make clear and precise the relationship between the Rubin causal model (RCM) and structural causal model (SCM) frameworks for causal inference. Adopting a neutral logical perspective, and drawing on previous work, we show what is required for an RCM to be representable by an SCM. A key result then shows that every RCM---including those that violate algebraic principles implied by the SCM framework---emerges as an abstraction of some representable RCM. Finally, we illustrate the power of this ameliorative perspective by pinpointing an important role for SCM principles in classic applications of RCMs; conversely, we offer a characterization of the algebraic constraints implied by a graph, helping to substantiate further comparisons between the two frameworks.

paragraphs: Causal inference uses multiple mathematical frameworks, and their relationship can be obscured by differences in how they express assumptions. This paper compares the Rubin causal model, associated with potential outcomes, and the structural causal model framework. It adopts a logical perspective to state precisely when a model in the first framework can be represented in the second.

The central result distinguishes direct representation from representation through abstraction. Some Rubin causal models violate algebraic principles required by structural causal models and therefore do not admit the same direct representation. Nevertheless, the authors show that every Rubin causal model can arise as an abstraction of a Rubin model that is representable by a structural causal model.

This result offers a way to understand apparent incompatibilities through the level of description used by a model. The paper also identifies roles for structural-model principles in classic potential-outcome applications and characterizes the algebraic constraints imposed by a graph. Together, these contributions make comparisons more precise without treating direct representability and abstraction as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: The paper clarifies when causal frameworks agree directly and proves that every Rubin causal model can arise through abstraction from a structurally representable model.

title: Comparing Causal Frameworks: Potential Outcomes, Structural Models, Graphs, and Abstractions

abstract: With the scale of vision Transformer-based models continuing to grow, finetuning these large-scale pretrained models for new tasks has become increasingly parameter-intensive. Visual prompt tuning is introduced as a parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) method to this trend. Despite its successes, a notable research challenge persists within almost all PEFT approaches: significant performance degradation is observed when there is a substantial disparity between the datasets applied in pretraining and finetuning phases. To address this challenge, we draw inspiration from human visual cognition, and propose the Visual Fourier Prompt Tuning (VFPT) method as a general and effective solution for adapting large-scale transformer-based models. Our approach innovatively incorporates the Fast Fourier Transform into prompt embeddings and harmoniously considers both spatial and frequency domain information. Apart from its inherent simplicity and intuitiveness, VFPT exhibits superior performance across all datasets, offering a general solution to dataset challenges, irrespective of data disparities. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art baselines on two benchmarks, with low parameter usage (e.g., 0.57% of model parameters on VTAB-1k) and notable performance enhancements (e.g., 73.20% of mean accuracy on VTAB-1k). Our code is avaliable at https://github.com/runtsang/VFPT.

Visual prompt tuning offers a more parameter-efficient route, but performance can deteriorate when pretraining and adaptation datasets differ substantially. Visual Fourier Prompt Tuning addresses this gap by changing the information represented in the learned prompts.

VFPT incorporates the Fast Fourier Transform into prompt embeddings so that adaptation considers both spatial and frequency-domain information. The design draws inspiration from human visual cognition and is presented as a simple way to adapt large Transformer-based vision models. Its central idea is to enrich prompt representations while keeping the number of adaptation parameters small.
