On VTAB-1k, they report 73.20% mean accuracy while using 0.57% of the model's parameters. These results support the usefulness of combining spatial and frequency information within prompts, particularly for the paper's motivating challenge of adapting a pretrained model when the target data differs from its original training data.
summary.tldr: VFPT adds Fourier information to visual prompts to improve parameter-efficient adaptation across differing datasets.

title: Visual Fourier Prompt Tuning

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) plays a crucial role in addressing distribution shifts in machine learning. In this work, we improve the theoretical foundations of UDA proposed in Acuna et al. (2021) by refining their $f$-divergence-based discrepancy and additionally introducing a new measure, $f$-domain discrepancy ($f$-DD). By removing the absolute value function and incorporating a scaling parameter, $f$-DD obtains novel target error and sample complexity bounds, allowing us to recover previous KL-based results and bridging the gap between algorithms and theory presented in Acuna et al. (2021). Using a localization technique, we also develop a fast-rate generalization bound. Empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of $f$-DD-based learning algorithms over previous works in popular UDA benchmarks.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses learning when the distribution encountered at deployment differs from the source distribution. This paper improves a theoretical framework that measures such differences using f-divergences. Its central contribution is a revised discrepancy measure intended to connect adaptation algorithms more closely with guarantees about their behavior.

The authors refine an existing discrepancy and introduce f-domain discrepancy, abbreviated f-DD. The new formulation removes an absolute value operation and adds a scaling parameter. These changes lead to new bounds on target error and sample complexity, recover earlier KL-based results, and address a gap between algorithms and theory in the previous framework.

The analysis also uses localization to establish a fast-rate generalization bound. Experiments on commonly used unsupervised adaptation benchmarks report better performance for algorithms based on f-DD than for previous approaches. The paper therefore contributes both a theoretical revision and an empirically useful learning criterion: changing how domain discrepancy is measured improves the available analysis and supports stronger results in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A revised f-divergence discrepancy yields new domain adaptation guarantees and improved performance on standard benchmarks.

title: On $f$-Divergence Principled Domain Adaptation: An Improved Framework

abstract: We consider a clustering problem where a learner seeks to partition a finite set by querying a faulty oracle. This models applications where learners crowdsource information from non-expert human workers or conduct noisy experiments to determine group structure. The learner aims to exactly recover a partition by submitting queries of the form ``are $u$ and $v$ in the same group?'' for any pair of elements $u$ and $v$ in the set. Moreover, because the learner only has access to faulty sources of information, they require an error-tolerant algorithm for this task: i.e. they must fully recover the correct partition, even if up to $\ell$ answers are incorrect, for some error-tolerance parameter $\ell$. We study the question: for any given error-tolerance $\ell$, what is the minimum number of queries needed to learn a finite set partition of $n$ elements into $k$ groups? We design algorithms for this task and prove that they achieve optimal query complexity. To analyze our algorithms, we first highlight a connection between this task and correlation clustering. We then use this connection to build a Rényi-Ulam style analytical framework for this problem, which yields matching lower bounds. Our analysis also reveals an inherent asymmetry between the query complexity necessary to be robust against false negative errors as opposed to false positive errors.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to discover the groups in a finite set by asking whether two elements belong to the same group. Answers may be wrong, as can happen with non-expert human judgments or noisy experiments. The learner must recover the entire partition correctly despite up to a specified number of incorrect answers.

The central question is how many pairwise queries are necessary for a set of n elements divided into k groups, given an error allowance of ℓ. The authors design algorithms and prove that their query counts are optimal. Matching lower bounds establish that the required number of queries cannot be reduced within the problem setting.

To obtain these results, the analysis connects partition recovery to correlation clustering and develops a Rényi-Ulam-style framework for reasoning about faulty answers. It also reveals that false negatives and false positives impose inherently different query requirements. Thus, confusing members of the same group with separate groups is not equivalent in query cost to incorrectly joining elements from different groups.
summary.tldr: The paper gives query-optimal algorithms for exactly recovering groups from pairwise answers despite a bounded number of errors.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Learning Partitions with Faulty Oracles

abstract: The study of modern machine learning models often necessitates storing vast quantities of gradients or Hessian vector products (HVPs). Traditional sketching methods struggle to scale under these memory constraints. We present a novel framework for scalable gradient and HVP sketching, tailored for modern hardware. We provide theoretical guarantees and demonstrate the power of our methods in applications like training data attribution, Hessian spectrum analysis, and intrinsic dimension computation for pre-trained language models. Our work sheds new light on the behavior of pre-trained language models, challenging assumptions about their intrinsic dimensionality and Hessian properties.

paragraphs: Understanding a trained machine-learning model can require storing large collections of gradients or Hessian-vector products. These quantities support analysis of how training examples affect a model and how its loss behaves around its parameters. Their storage requirements become a major obstacle for modern models, and conventional sketching methods struggle under those constraints.

The paper introduces a framework for scalable sketching of both types of quantities, tailored to modern hardware. Sketching provides compact representations for these analyses, addressing the burden of retaining the original large objects. The authors accompany the framework with theoretical guarantees and demonstrate its use in several investigations of pretrained language models.

Those applications include training-data attribution, analysis of the Hessian spectrum, and computation of intrinsic dimension. Together, they connect the storage method to questions about training influence, loss geometry, and the dimensional structure of models. The authors report findings that challenge assumptions about language models’ intrinsic dimensionality and Hessian properties. The contribution therefore combines an analysis-enabling computational method with new observations obtained through its use.
summary.tldr: Hardware-oriented gradient and Hessian-vector sketches make language-model attribution and loss-landscape analysis more scalable.

title: Efficient Sketches for Training Data Attribution and Studying the Loss Landscape

abstract: Matrix factorization models have been extensively studied as a valuable test-bed for understanding the implicit biases of overparameterized models. Although both low nuclear norm and low rank regularization have been studied for these models, a unified understanding of when, how, and why they achieve different implicit regularization effects remains elusive. In this work, we systematically investigate the implicit regularization of matrix factorization for solving matrix completion problems. We empirically discover that the connectivity of observed data plays a key role in the implicit bias, with a transition from low nuclear norm to low rank as data shifts from disconnected to connected with increased observations. We identify a hierarchy of intrinsic invariant manifolds in the loss landscape that guide the training trajectory to evolve from low-rank to higher-rank solutions. Based on this finding, we theoretically characterize the training trajectory as following the hierarchical invariant manifold traversal process, generalizing the characterization of Li et al.(2020) to include the disconnected case. Furthermore, we establish conditions that guarantee minimum nuclear norm, closely aligning with our experimental findings, and we provide a dynamics characterization condition for ensuring minimum rank. Our work reveals the intricate interplay between data connectivity, training dynamics, and implicit regularization in matrix factorization models.
originalAbstract: Matrix factorization models have been extensively studied as a valuable test-bed for understanding the implicit biases of overparameterized models. Although both low nuclear norm and low rank regularization have been studied for these models, a unified understanding of when, how, and why they achieve different implicit regularization effects remains elusive. In this work, we systematically investigate the implicit regularization of matrix factorization for solving matrix completion problems. We empirically discover that the connectivity of observed data plays a key role in the implicit bias, with a transition from low nuclear norm to low rank as data shifts from disconnected to connected with increased observations. We identify a hierarchy of intrinsic invariant manifolds in the loss landscape that guide the training trajectory to evolve from low-rank to higher-rank solutions. Based on this finding, we theoretically characterize the training trajectory as following the hierarchical invariant manifold traversal process, generalizing the characterization of Li et al.(2020) to include the disconnected case. Furthermore, we establish conditions that guarantee minimum nuclear norm, closely aligning with our experimental findings, and we provide a dynamics characterization condition for ensuring minimum rank. Our work reveals the intricate interplay between data connectivity, training dynamics, and implicit regularization in matrix factorization models.

paragraphs: Matrix completion reconstructs missing entries from the entries that are observed. Matrix factorization provides a useful setting for studying implicit regularization: the tendency of training to favor particular solutions without explicitly requesting them. This paper investigates why training can favor either low nuclear norm or low rank, two distinct measures of matrix simplicity.

The authors empirically identify the connectivity of observed data as an important influence. As additional observations move the data from disconnected to connected, they observe a shift from low nuclear norm toward low rank. To explain the training process, they identify a hierarchy of invariant manifolds, structured regions of the optimization landscape that guide movement from lower-rank toward higher-rank solutions.

Their theoretical account characterizes training as traversal through this hierarchy and includes the disconnected case. They also establish conditions guaranteeing minimum nuclear norm and give a condition on the dynamics for ensuring minimum rank. These conditional results connect the observed data pattern to the solutions training favors, rather than assigning matrix factorization one universal implicit bias.
summary.tldr: The connectivity of observed entries helps explain when matrix factorization favors low nuclear norm or low rank during matrix completion.

title: Connectivity Shapes Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization Models for Matrix Completion

abstract: Transferring visual-language knowledge from large-scale foundation models for video recognition has proved to be effective. To bridge the domain gap, additional parametric modules are added to capture the temporal information. However, zero-shot generalization diminishes with the increase in the number of specialized parameters, making existing works a trade-off between zero-shot and close-set performance. In this paper, we present MoTE, a novel framework that enables generalization and specialization to be balanced in one unified model. Our approach tunes a mixture of temporal experts to learn multiple task views with various degrees of data fitting. To maximally preserve the knowledge of each expert, we propose Weight Merging Regularization, which regularizes the merging process of experts in weight space. Additionally with temporal feature modulation to regularize the contribution of temporal feature during test. We achieve a sound balance between zero-shot and close-set video recognition tasks and obtain state-of-the-art or competitive results on various datasets, including Kinetics-400 \& 600, UCF, and HMDB. Code is available at https://github.com/ZMHH-H/MoTE.

paragraphs: Transferring knowledge from vision-language foundation models to video recognition requires learning about temporal information. Adding specialized modules helps capture that information, but increasing specialization can weaken zero-shot generalization. MoTE addresses the resulting tension between recognizing the classes used for task-specific training and transferring knowledge to classes outside that training setting.

The framework tunes a mixture of temporal experts that learn different views of the task and fit the training data to different degrees. It introduces Weight Merging Regularization to preserve knowledge from the individual experts as their weights are merged. At test time, temporal feature modulation additionally regulates how much the temporal features contribute to recognition.

Together, these mechanisms allow one model to balance generalization with specialization. The authors report state-of-the-art or competitive performance across zero-shot and closed-set video recognition evaluations on Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600, UCF, and HMDB. The results support controlling both expert combination and temporal feature contribution as a practical way to retain broad transferred knowledge while adapting to video-specific tasks.
summary.tldr: MoTE balances zero-shot transfer and task-specific video recognition through temporal experts, regularized weight merging, and test-time feature modulation.

title: MoTE: Reconciling Generalization with Specialization for Visual-Language to Video Knowledge Transfer

abstract: Transduction is a powerful paradigm that leverages the structure of unlabeled data to boost predictive accuracy. We present TransCLIP, a novel and computationally efficient transductive approach designed for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). TransCLIP is applicable as a plug-and-play module on top of popular inductive zero- and few-shot models, consistently improving their performances. Our new objective function can be viewed as a regularized maximum-likelihood estimation, constrained by a KL divergence penalty that integrates the text-encoder knowledge and guides the transductive learning process. We further derive an iterative Block Majorize-Minimize (BMM) procedure for optimizing our objective, with guaranteed convergence and decoupled sample-assignment updates, yielding computationally efficient transduction for large-scale datasets. We report comprehensive evaluations, comparisons, and ablation studies that demonstrate: (i) Transduction can greatly enhance the generalization capabilities of inductive pretrained zero- and few-shot VLMs; (ii) TransCLIP substantially outperforms standard transductive few-shot learning methods relying solely on vision features, notably due to the KL-based language constraint.

paragraphs: TransCLIP improves vision-language predictions by using the structure of an unlabeled collection of examples. This approach, called transduction, lets information across the collection influence predictions. The method can be added to existing zero-shot and few-shot models, extending models that otherwise make predictions through their previously learned rules.

Its objective combines fitting the unlabeled data with a constraint that preserves guidance from the text encoder. The constraint uses KL divergence to keep the transductive process informed by language knowledge. This matters because a method relying only on visual features would leave out the textual information that helps define a vision-language model’s predictions.

The authors derive an iterative optimization procedure with guaranteed convergence and separate updates for sample assignments, supporting computationally efficient use on large datasets. Their evaluations report consistent improvements to the tested zero-shot and few-shot models. TransCLIP also substantially outperforms evaluated transductive methods based only on vision features, with the language constraint identified as an important contributor. The findings support using unlabeled data and text guidance together.
summary.tldr: TransCLIP improves tested vision-language models by combining unlabeled-data structure with a constraint that preserves text-encoder guidance.

title: Boosting Vision-Language Models with Transduction

abstract: Pre-trained models produce strong generic representations that can be adapted via fine-tuning on specialised datasets. The learned weight difference relative to the pre-trained model, known as a task vector, characterises the direction and stride of fine-tuning that enables the model to capture these specialised representations. The significance of task vectors is such that simple arithmetic operations on them can be used to combine diverse representations from different domains. This paper builds on these properties of task vectors and aims to answer (1) whether components of task vectors, particularly parameter blocks, exhibit similar characteristics, and (2) how such blocks can be used to enhance knowledge composition and transfer. To this end, we introduce aTLAS, an algorithm that linearly combines parameter blocks with different learned coefficients, resulting in anisotropic scaling at the task vector level. We show that such linear combinations explicitly exploit the low intrinsic dimensionality of pre-trained models, with only a few coefficients being the learnable parameters. Furthermore, composition of parameter blocks enables modular learning that effectively leverages the already learned representations, thereby reducing the dependency on large amounts of data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in task arithmetic, few-shot recognition and test-time adaptation, with supervised or unsupervised objectives. In particular, we show that (1) learned anisotropic scaling allows task vectors to be more disentangled, causing less interference in composition; (2) task vector composition excels with scarce or no labelled data and is less prone to domain shift, thus leading to better generalisability; (3) mixing the most informative parameter blocks across different task vectors prior to training can reduce the memory footprint and improve the flexibility of knowledge transfer. Moreover, we show the potential of aTLAS as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, particularly with less data, and demonstrate that it can be easily scaled up for higher performance.

paragraphs: A task vector records how a model's weights change when a pretrained model is fine-tuned for a particular task. Arithmetic on these vectors can combine specialized representations. This paper asks whether different blocks within a task vector should contribute differently when transferring or combining knowledge, and introduces aTLAS to learn those contributions.

aTLAS assigns different learned coefficients to parameter blocks and combines them linearly. This produces anisotropic scaling: different parts of a task vector receive different amounts of emphasis. Only a small number of coefficients need to be learned, exploiting the low intrinsic dimensionality of pretrained models. Reusing already learned blocks also supports modular learning with reduced dependence on large datasets.

Learned block scaling reduces interference among composed task vectors, while composition performs well with few or no labels and shows greater resilience to domain shift. Selecting informative blocks before training can also reduce memory requirements. The authors further demonstrate potential for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and scaling to higher performance.
summary.tldr: aTLAS learns how strongly to combine blocks of task vectors, improving knowledge transfer with relatively few trainable coefficients.

title: Knowledge Composition using Task Vectors with Learned Anisotropic Scaling

abstract: Image retargeting is the task of adjusting the aspect ratio of images to suit different display devices or presentation environments. However, existing retargeting methods often struggle to balance the preservation of key semantics and image quality, resulting in either deformation or loss of important objects, or the introduction of local artifacts such as discontinuous pixels and inconsistent regenerated content. To address these issues, we propose a content-aware retargeting method called PruneRepaint. It incorporates semantic importance for each pixel to guide the identification of regions that need to be pruned or preserved in order to maintain key semantics. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive repainting module that selects image regions for repainting based on the distribution of pruned pixels and the proportion between foreground size and target aspect ratio, thus achieving local smoothness after pruning. By focusing on the content and structure of the foreground, our PruneRepaint approach adaptively avoids key content loss and deformation, while effectively mitigating artifacts with local repainting. We conduct experiments on the public RetargetMe benchmark and demonstrate through objective experimental results and subjective user studies that our method outperforms previous approaches in terms of preserving semantics and aesthetics, as well as better generalization across diverse aspect ratios. Codes will be available at https://github.com/fhshen2022/PruneRepaint.

paragraphs: Changing an image's aspect ratio can damage its content: important objects may disappear or become distorted, and local edits can leave visible discontinuities. PruneRepaint addresses this by treating resizing as a content-sensitive editing problem. It aims to preserve the image's key meaning while maintaining a visually coherent result.

The method assigns semantic importance to individual pixels to guide which regions should be removed and which should remain. After pruning, an adaptive module selects areas to repaint. That selection depends on where pixels were removed and on the relationship between foreground size and the requested aspect ratio, allowing repairs to respond to the particular edit.

Experiments on RetargetMe, including objective evaluations and user studies, report better preservation of meaning and aesthetics than previous approaches. The authors also report better generalization across diverse aspect ratios. The approach matters because content preservation and visual repair are coordinated: decisions about what to remove help determine where repainting is needed to reduce artifacts and protect foreground structure.
summary.tldr: PruneRepaint changes image aspect ratios by preserving semantically important content and adaptively repairing regions affected by pixel removal.

title: Prune and Repaint: Content-Aware Image Retargeting for any Ratio

abstract: Parallel-in-time (PinT) techniques have been proposed to solve systems of time-dependent differential equations by parallelizing the temporal domain. Among them, Parareal computes the solution sequentially using an inaccurate (fast) solver, and then ``corrects'' it using an accurate (slow) integrator that runs in parallel across temporal subintervals. This work introduces RandNet-Parareal, a novel method to learn the discrepancy between the coarse and fine solutions using random neural networks (RandNets). RandNet-Parareal achieves speed gains up to x125 and x22 compared to the fine solver run serially and Parareal, respectively. Beyond theoretical guarantees of RandNets as universal approximators, these models are quick to train, allowing the PinT solution of partial differential equations on a spatial mesh of up to $10^5$ points with minimal overhead, dramatically increasing the scalability of existing PinT approaches. RandNet-Parareal's numerical performance is illustrated on systems of real-world significance, such as the viscous Burgers' equation, the Diffusion-Reaction equation, the two- and three-dimensional Brusselator, and the shallow water equation.

paragraphs: Time-dependent differential equations are often solved by advancing through time in sequence. Parareal creates opportunities for parallel computation by combining a fast, inaccurate sequential solver with accurate corrections computed across time intervals in parallel. This paper introduces RandNet-Parareal, which uses random neural networks to learn the discrepancy between those coarse and fine solutions.

The learned discrepancy supports the correction process, while the networks' quick training keeps the additional work small. The authors connect this choice to theoretical universal-approximation guarantees for random neural networks. They report solving partial differential equations on spatial meshes containing up to 100,000 points with minimal learning overhead, addressing the scalability of parallel-in-time computation.

Reported speed gains reach 125-fold relative to running the fine solver serially and 22-fold relative to Parareal. These are maximum observed gains, rather than fixed speedups for every problem. Numerical demonstrations include viscous Burgers, diffusion-reaction, two- and three-dimensional Brusselator, and shallow-water equations. The results show how a quickly trained correction model can substantially accelerate time-parallel numerical solving in the evaluated systems.
summary.tldr: RandNet-Parareal learns coarse-to-fine solver discrepancies with random neural networks, achieving reported speedups up to 125-fold over serial fine solving.

title: RandNet-Parareal: a time-parallel PDE solver using Random Neural Networks

abstract: As Archimedes famously said, ``Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I shall move the world'', in this study, we propose to use a tiny Language Model (LM), \eg, a Transformer with 67M parameters, to lever much larger Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) with 9B parameters. Specifically, we use this tiny \textbf{Lever-LM} to configure effective in-context demonstration (ICD) sequences to improve the In-Context Learinng (ICL) performance of LVLMs. Previous studies show that diverse ICD configurations like the selection and ordering of the demonstrations heavily affect the ICL performance, highlighting the significance of configuring effective ICD sequences. Motivated by this and by re-considering the the process of configuring ICD sequence, we find this is a mirror process of human sentence composition and further assume that effective ICD configurations may contain internal statistical patterns that can be captured by Lever-LM. Then a dataset with effective ICD sequences is constructed to train Lever-LM. After training, given novel queries, new ICD sequences are configured by the trained Lever-LM to solve vision-language tasks through ICL. Experiments show that these ICD sequences can improve the ICL performance of two LVLMs compared with some strong baselines in Visual Question Answering and Image Captioning, validating that Lever-LM can really capture the statistical patterns for levering LVLMs. The code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Lever-LM-604A/}.

paragraphs: The examples placed in a vision-language model’s prompt can strongly affect its in-context learning performance. Both which demonstrations are selected and their order matter. Lever-LM treats constructing that sequence as a learning problem, using a small language model to configure demonstrations for a much larger vision-language model.

The approach assumes that effective demonstration sequences contain statistical patterns that a language model can learn, drawing an analogy with composing sentences. The authors construct a dataset of effective sequences and train Lever-LM on it. For a new query, the trained model produces a demonstration sequence to support the larger model’s task.

Experiments evaluate this strategy on visual question answering and image captioning using two large vision-language models. The configured sequences outperform several strong baselines, supporting the hypothesis that useful sequence patterns can be learned. The paper illustrates the size contrast with a 67-million-parameter transformer configuring context for models with 9 billion parameters, making prompt construction the smaller model’s substantive contribution.
summary.tldr: Lever-LM learns to select and order demonstrations that improve larger vision-language models’ in-context performance.

title: Lever LM: Configuring In-Context Sequence to Lever Large Vision Language Models

abstract: The rapid progress of Deepfake technology has made face swapping highly realistic, raising concerns about the malicious use of fabricated facial content. Existing methods often struggle to generalize to unseen domains due to the diverse nature of facial manipulations. In this paper, we revisit the generation process and identify a universal principle: Deepfake images inherently contain information from both source and target identities, while genuine faces maintain a consistent identity. Building upon this insight, we introduce DiffusionFake, a novel plug-and-play framework that reverses the generative process of face forgeries to enhance the generalization of detection models. DiffusionFake achieves this by injecting the features extracted by the detection model into a frozen pre-trained Stable Diffusion model, compelling it to reconstruct the corresponding target and source images. This guided reconstruction process constrains the detection network to capture the source and target related features to facilitate the reconstruction, thereby learning rich and disentangled representations that are more resilient to unseen forgeries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffusionFake significantly improves cross-domain generalization of various detector architectures without introducing additional parameters during inference. The code are available in https://github.com/skJack/DiffusionFake.git.

paragraphs: Deepfake detectors often struggle when they encounter facial manipulations outside their training domain. DiffusionFake approaches this problem through the identity information involved in face swapping. The paper's central premise is that a forged face contains information from both source and target identities, whereas a genuine face maintains a consistent identity. It uses this distinction to guide what a detector learns.

During training, features extracted by the detector are supplied to a frozen, pretrained Stable Diffusion model. The diffusion model is tasked with reconstructing the corresponding source and target images. This reconstruction requirement pressures the detector to retain information about both identities and learn representations that separate their contributions, tying detection features to the process that produced the forgery.

Experiments report significantly improved cross-domain generalization across several detector architectures. The framework adds no parameters during inference, so the extra generative machinery shapes training without increasing the detector's parameter count at deployment. The stated benefit is greater resilience to previously unseen forgeries.
summary.tldr: DiffusionFake trains detectors through source-and-target image reconstruction, improving cross-domain detection without adding inference parameters.

title: DiffusionFake: Enhancing Generalization in Deepfake Detection via Guided Stable Diffusion

abstract: Recent advances in AI have been significantly driven by the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems in ways that resemble human thinking. However, there is an ongoing debate about the extent to which LLMs are capable ofactual reasoning. Central to this debate are two key probabilistic concepts that are essential for connecting causesto their effects: the probability of necessity (PN) and the probability of sufficiency (PS). This paper introduces a framework that is both theoretical and practical, aimed at assessing how effectively LLMs are able to replicate real-world reasoning mechanisms using these probabilistic measures. By viewing LLMs as abstract machines that process information through a natural language interface, we examine the conditions under which it is possible to compute suitable approximations of PN and PS. Our research marks an important step towards gaining a deeper understanding of when LLMs are capable of reasoning, as illustrated by a series of math examples.

paragraphs: Language models can produce solutions that resemble human reasoning, but that observation leaves open what kind of reasoning their behavior demonstrates. This paper approaches the question through two causal quantities: the probability of necessity and the probability of sufficiency. These provide a more specific target for analysis than the broad question of whether a model reasons.

Necessity concerns whether a cause was needed for an effect, while sufficiency concerns whether a cause can bring about that effect. The authors develop a framework with theoretical and practical components for assessing language models through these quantities. They treat a model as an abstract information-processing machine accessed through natural language and examine conditions under which suitable approximations can be computed.

Mathematical examples illustrate the framework and its relevance to understanding when language models can reason. The contribution is a way to formulate and investigate that question using causal probabilities. Its claims depend on the conditions for approximating those probabilities; the abstract does not present an unconditional conclusion that reasoning emerges in all language models.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a conditional framework for assessing LLM reasoning through approximations to the probabilities of causal necessity and sufficiency.

title: Does Reasoning Emerge? Examining the Probabilities of Causation in Large Language Models

abstract: LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation enables the robots to obtain fine-grained semantic information of the surrounding environment. Recently, many works project the point cloud onto the 2D image and adopt the 2D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) or vision transformer for LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation. However, since more than one point can be projected onto the same 2D position but only one point can be preserved, the previous 2D projection-based segmentation methods suffer from inevitable quantized information loss, which results in incomplete geometric structure, especially for small objects. To avoid quantized information loss, in this paper, we propose a novel spherical frustum structure, which preserves all points projected onto the same 2D position. Additionally, a hash-based representation is proposed for memory-efficient spherical frustum storage. Based on the spherical frustum structure, the Spherical Frustum sparse Convolution (SFC) and Frustum Farthest Point Sampling (F2PS) are proposed to convolve and sample the points stored in spherical frustums respectively. Finally, we present the Spherical Frustum sparse Convolution Network (SFCNet) to adopt 2D CNNs for LiDAR point cloud semantic segmentation without quantized information loss. Extensive experiments on the SemanticKITTI and nuScenes datasets demonstrate that our SFCNet outperforms previous 2D projection-based semantic segmentation methods based on conventional spherical projection and shows better performance on small object segmentation by preserving complete geometric structure. Codes will be available at https://github.com/IRMVLab/SFCNet.

Keeping only one discards geometric information, which can be especially damaging when representing small objects.

SFCNet replaces that single-point storage with a spherical frustum structure that retains all points mapped to each position. A hash-based representation makes this storage more memory-efficient. The authors also introduce sparse convolution and farthest-point sampling operations adapted to the frustums, allowing the network to process and sample the retained points while using two-dimensional convolutional networks.

On SemanticKITTI and nuScenes, SFCNet outperforms earlier projection-based segmentation methods using conventional spherical projection. It also reports better small-object segmentation, linked to preserving more complete geometry. The contribution targets a specific information loss caused by projection collisions: its representation keeps the points that conventional projection would discard before the segmentation network can use them.
summary.tldr: SFCNet retains all LiDAR points sharing a projected position, improving reported segmentation performance, particularly for small objects.

title: Spherical Frustum Sparse Convolution Network for LiDAR Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Scaling machine learning models significantly improves their performance. However, such gains come at the cost of inference being slow and resource-intensive. Early-exit neural networks (EENNs) offer a promising solution: they accelerate inference by allowing intermediate layers to exit and produce a prediction early. Yet a fundamental issue with EENNs is how to determine when to exit without severely degrading performance. In other words, when is it 'safe' for an EENN to go 'fast'? To address this issue, we investigate how to adapt frameworks of risk control to EENNs. Risk control offers a distribution-free, post-hoc solution that tunes the EENN's exiting mechanism so that exits only occur when the output is of sufficient quality. We empirically validate our insights on a range of vision and language tasks, demonstrating that risk control can produce substantial computational savings, all the while preserving user-specified performance goals.

paragraphs: Early-exit neural networks can produce a prediction from an intermediate layer instead of processing every input through the entire network. This offers a way to reduce the inference cost of large models. The difficult decision is when to stop: exiting earlier saves computation, but an unsuitable exit can lower prediction quality.

This paper adapts risk-control frameworks to tune the exiting mechanism after training. The approach is distribution-free and connects the decision to exit with a specified level of output quality. It turns the speed-versus-performance choice into a controlled selection problem, with the user's performance requirement guiding how aggressively the network can exit.

Experiments across vision and language tasks show substantial computational savings while preserving user-specified performance goals. These findings support risk control as a practical way to choose an early-exit policy. The paper's use of safety refers to controlling prediction risk against those goals; the reported contribution is a method for accelerating inference while maintaining the targeted level of performance.
summary.tldr: Post-training risk control tunes early exits to save computation while preserving user-specified prediction performance.

title: Fast yet Safe: Early-Exiting with Risk Control

abstract: Instrumental variables (IVs) provide a powerful strategy for identifying causal effects in the presence of unobservable confounders. Within the nonparametric setting (NPIV), recent methods have been based on nonlinear generalizations of Two-Stage Least Squares and on minimax formulations derived from moment conditions or duality. In a novel direction, we show how to formulate a functional stochastic gradient descent algorithm to tackle NPIV regression by directly minimizing the populational risk. We provide theoretical support in the form of bounds on the excess risk, and conduct numerical experiments showcasing our method's superior stability and competitive performance relative to current state-of-the-art alternatives. This algorithm enables flexible estimator choices, such as neural networks or kernel based methods, as well as non-quadratic loss functions, which may be suitable for structural equations beyond the setting of continuous outcomes and additive noise. Finally, we demonstrate this flexibility of our framework by presenting how it naturally addresses the important case of binary outcomes, which has received far less attention by recent developments in the NPIV literature.

paragraphs: Instrumental-variable regression provides a strategy for identifying causal effects when unobserved factors confound the relationship of interest. In the nonparametric setting, the relationship can take flexible forms. Recent approaches have used nonlinear versions of two-stage least squares or minimax objectives; this paper develops a different optimization formulation.

The authors construct functional stochastic gradient descent that directly minimizes population risk. They provide excess-risk bounds as theoretical support and allow flexible estimator choices, including neural networks and kernel methods. The framework also accepts non-quadratic losses, which may suit structural equations beyond continuous outcomes with additive noise.

Numerical experiments show greater stability and competitive performance relative to current state-of-the-art alternatives. The paper further demonstrates how the framework handles binary outcomes, an application that has received less attention in recent nonparametric instrumental-variable work. Its contribution is therefore both an optimization route with theoretical support and a flexible modeling framework whose usefulness extends to the demonstrated binary-outcome setting.
summary.tldr: A functional stochastic-gradient approach offers stable, flexible nonparametric instrumental-variable regression, including a formulation for binary outcomes.

title: Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Regression through Stochastic Approximate Gradients

abstract: Modern recurrent architectures, such as xLSTM and Mamba, have recently challenged the Transformer in language modeling. However, their structure constrains their applicability to sequences only or requires processing multi-dimensional data structures, such as images or molecular graphs, in a pre-defined sequential order. In contrast, Multi-Dimensional RNNs (MDRNNs) are well suited for data with a higher level structure, like 2D grids, trees, and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). In this work, we extend the notion of multi-dimensionality to linear RNNs. We introduce parallelizable Linear Source Transition Mark networks (pLSTMs) using Source, Transition, and Mark gates that act on the linegraph of a general DAG. This enables parallelization in analogy to parallel associative scans and the chunkwise-recurrent form of sequential linear RNNs, but for DAGs. For regular grids (1D and 2D), like images, this scheme can be efficiently implemented using einsum operations, concatenations, and padding in logarithmic time. pLSTMs tackle the vanishing/exploding activation/gradient problem for long distances in DAGs via two distinct modes: a directed propagation mode (P-mode) and a diffusive distribution mode (D-mode). To showcase the long-range capabilities of pLSTM, we introduce arrow-pointing extrapolation as a synthetic computer vision task that contains long-distance directional information. We demonstrate that pLSTMs generalize well to larger image sizes, whereas Transformers struggle to extrapolate. On established molecular graph and computer vision benchmarks, pLSTMs also show strong performance. The complete code is available at https://github.com/ml-jku/plstm_experiments.

title: pLSTM: parallelizable Linear Source Transition Mark networks

abstract: Scaling test-time compute is crucial for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically employ reinforcement learning (RL) to maximize a verifiable reward obtained at the end of reasoning traces. However, such methods optimize only the final performance under a large and fixed token budget, which hinders efficiency in both training and deployment. In this work, we present **AnytimeReasoner**, a novel framework for optimizing reasoning performance under varying thinking budget constraints. To achieve this, we truncate the complete thinking process to fit within sampled token budgets from a prior distribution, compelling the model to summarize the optimal answer for each truncated thinking for verification. This introduces verifiable dense rewards into the reasoning process, facilitating more effective credit assignment in RL optimization. We then optimize the thinking and summary policies in a decoupled manner to maximize the cumulative reward. Additionally, we introduce a novel variance reduction technique, **Budget Relative Policy Optimization (BRPO)**, to enhance the robustness and efficiency of the learning process when reinforcing the thinking policy. Empirical results in mathematical reasoning tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms GRPO across all thinking budgets under various prior distributions, enhancing both training and token efficiency.

paragraphs: A reasoning model may have a generous thinking budget in one deployment and a tight budget in another. Training only for correctness at the end of a long reasoning trace does not directly reward useful answers at earlier stopping points. AnytimeReasoner trains models to perform well across a distribution of thinking budgets.

The method samples token budgets, truncates a complete thinking process to each budget, and requires the model to summarize an answer from the available reasoning. Verifying those answers supplies rewards at multiple stages, making it easier to assign credit within the reasoning process. The thinking policy and answer-summary policy are optimized separately toward cumulative reward. Budget Relative Policy Optimization adds a variance-reduction technique for training the thinking policy.

Mathematical-reasoning experiments show consistent improvements over GRPO at every tested thinking budget under several prior budget distributions. The authors also report better training and token efficiency. The findings support explicitly rewarding intermediate usefulness when a model must operate under varying computational constraints, rather than judging its reasoning solely by the answer available after a fixed, lengthy process.
summary.tldr: AnytimeReasoner rewards answers at sampled thinking budgets, while BRPO stabilizes training to improve mathematical reasoning across tested budget levels.

title: Optimizing Anytime Reasoning via Budget Relative Policy Optimization

abstract: Recent advances in large multimodal models have significantly advanced video comprehension, yet their performance remains limited in first-person scenarios. The interactive nature of egocentric videos is critical for applications like embodied intelligence, but introduces complex visual contexts that conventional models struggle to capture. To bridge this gap, we introduce OpenMMEgo with innovations across three dimensions: data, model, and training strategy. To provide rich spatiotemporal visual knowledge, we curate a large-scale, high-quality dataset named OME10M, comprising over 8.2M egocentric video QA pairs synthesized from Ego4D series. We also establish OMEBench, a comprehensive benchmark for rigorous egocentric understanding assessment. To alleviate the frequent viewpoint shifts inherent in egocentric videos, we implement semantic-aware visual token compression. Further, a curriculum learning strategy is complemented to foster stable learning across various data complexities. OpenMMEgo consistently improves the performance of LMMs on egocentric benchmarks without sacrificing general video understanding performance. Notably, Qwen2.5-VL tuned with OpenMMEgo substantially outperforms other models of the same size in egocentric video understanding. The data, weights and training code will be put at https://github.com/BeingBeyond/OpenMMEgo.

The planned release of data, weights, and training code also makes the approach available as an open research foundation.
summary.tldr: OpenMMEgo combines large-scale first-person video training data, semantic token compression, and curriculum learning to improve egocentric understanding.

title: OpenMMEgo: Enhancing Egocentric Understanding for LMMs with Open Weights and Data

abstract: Occupancy prediction infers fine-grained 3D geometry and semantics from camera images of the surrounding environment, making it a critical perception task for autonomous driving. Existing methods either adopt dense grids as scene representation which is difficult to scale to high resolution, or learn the entire scene using a single set of sparse queries, which is insufficient to handle the various object characteristics. In this paper, we present ODG, a hierarchical dual sparse Gaussian representation to effectively capture complex scene dynamics. Building upon the observation that driving scenes can be universally decomposed into static and dynamic counterparts, we define dual Gaussian queries to better model the diverse scene objects. We utilize a hierarchical Gaussian transformer to predict the occupied voxel centers and semantic classes along with the Gaussian parameters. Leveraging the real-time rendering capability of 3D Gaussian Splatting, we also impose rendering supervision with available depth and semantic map annotations injecting pixel-level alignment to boost occupancy learning. Extensive experiments on the Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo benchmarks demonstrate our proposed method sets new state-of-the-art results while maintaining low inference cost.

paragraphs: ODG predicts which parts of a surrounding three-dimensional scene are occupied and what those regions contain, using camera images. Dense scene grids become difficult to scale to high resolution. A single collection of sparse queries, meanwhile, can struggle to represent objects with different characteristics.

The method separates driving scenes into static and dynamic components and assigns them dual sets of sparse Gaussian queries. A hierarchical Gaussian transformer predicts occupied voxel centers, semantic classes, and Gaussian parameters. This representation gives the model distinct ways to handle the different components while maintaining a sparse description of the scene.

ODG also uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to render predictions and compare them with available depth and semantic annotations. This adds pixel-level alignment signals to occupancy learning. Experiments on Occ3D-nuScenes and Occ3D-Waymo achieve state-of-the-art results while retaining low inference cost. The reported findings support combining a structured sparse representation with image-level supervision to improve detailed three-dimensional perception efficiently.
summary.tldr: ODG combines separate static and dynamic Gaussian representations with rendering supervision for accurate, low-cost 3D occupancy prediction.

title: ODG: Occupancy Prediction Using Dual Gaussians

abstract: We present a three-stage framework for training deep learning models specializing in antibody sequence-structure co-design. We first pre-train a language model using millions of antibody sequence data. Then, we employ the learned representations to guide the training of a diffusion model for joint optimization over both sequence and structure of antibodies. During the final alignment stage, we optimize the model to favor antibodies with low repulsion and high attraction to the antigen binding site, enhancing the rationality and functionality of the designs. To mitigate conflicting energy preferences, we extend AbDPO (Antibody Direct Preference Optimization) to guide the model toward Pareto optimality under multiple energy-based alignment objectives. Furthermore, we adopt an iterative learning paradigm with temperature scaling, enabling the model to benefit from diverse online datasets without requiring additional data. In practice, our proposed methods achieve high stability and efficiency in producing a better Pareto front of antibody designs compared to top samples generated by baselines and previous alignment techniques. Through extensive experiments, we showcase the superior performance of our methods in generating nature-like antibodies with high binding affinity.

paragraphs: Antibody design involves choosing both a molecular sequence and its structure, while balancing interaction preferences at an antigen's binding site. This paper develops a three-stage framework that first learns from millions of antibody sequences. Those learned representations then guide a diffusion model that jointly optimizes antibody sequences and structures.

The final stage aligns generation toward lower repulsion and greater attraction at the binding site. Because energy objectives can conflict, the authors extend Antibody Direct Preference Optimization to pursue Pareto-optimal tradeoffs across multiple objectives. An iterative learning procedure with temperature scaling allows the model to benefit from diverse online datasets without requiring additional data.

Experiments report stable, efficient generation and a better Pareto front than top samples from baselines and earlier alignment methods. A better front represents improved tradeoffs among the energy objectives, rather than a single score that hides their tensions. summary.tldr: A three-stage antibody-design framework aligns joint sequence-and-structure generation toward better tradeoffs among competing binding-energy objectives.

title: Pareto-Optimal Energy Alignment for Designing Nature-Like Antibodies

abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has achieved state-of-the-art rendering results. However, its efficiency relies on simplifications that disregard the thickness of Gaussian primitives and their overlapping interactions. These simplifications can lead to popping artifacts due to inaccurate sorting, thereby affecting the rendering quality. In this paper, we propose Screen-Aligned Primitives (SAP), an anisotropic kernel that generates primitives parallel to the image plane for each view. Our rasterization pipeline enables full per-pixel ordering in real time. Since the primitives are parallel for a given viewpoint, a single global sorting operation suffices for correct per-pixel depth ordering. We formulate 3D reconstruction as a combination of a 3D-consistent decoder and 2D view-specific primitives, and further propose a highly efficient decoder to ensure 3D consistency. Moreover, within our framework, the primitive function values remain consistent between view space and screen space, allowing arbitrary radial basis functions (RBFs) to represent the scene without introducing projection errors. Experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality while maintaining real-time performance.

paragraphs: Gaussian splatting renders scenes efficiently, but simplifying the thickness and overlap of its primitives can produce incorrect depth ordering. Those errors can appear as popping artifacts. SAP changes the representation so that the primitives generated for each viewpoint lie parallel to the image plane, making ordering easier to handle correctly.

Because the primitives are parallel within a view, one global sorting operation is sufficient to obtain correct depth ordering at every pixel. The framework combines view-specific two-dimensional primitives with an efficient decoder that maintains three-dimensional consistency. This pairing connects a convenient rendering representation to a coherent reconstruction of the underlying scene.

The authors also show that primitive function values remain consistent between view space and screen space. Within their framework, this permits arbitrary radial basis functions without projection errors. Experiments on diverse datasets report state-of-the-art rendering quality at real-time speed. The central contribution is a representation whose geometry supports exact sorting while retaining efficient rendering and consistency across viewpoints.
summary.tldr: SAP uses screen-aligned primitives so one global sort provides correct per-pixel depth ordering for high-quality real-time rendering.

title: SAP: Exact Sorting in Splatting via Screen-Aligned Primitives

abstract: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) aims to quickly fine-tune the model during the test phase so that it can adapt to multiple unknown downstream domain distributions without pre-acquiring downstream domain data. To this end, existing advanced CTTA methods mainly reduce the catastrophic forgetting of historical knowledge caused by irregular switching of downstream domain data by restoring the initial model or reusing historical models. However, these methods are usually accompanied by serious insufficient learning of new knowledge and interference from potentially harmful historical knowledge, resulting in severe performance degradation. To this end, we propose a class-aware domain Knowledge Fusion and Fission method for continual test-time adaptation, called KFF, which adaptively expands and merges class-aware domain knowledge in old and new domains according to the test-time data from different domains, where discriminative historical knowledge can be dynamically accumulated. Specifically, considering the huge domain gap within streaming data, a domain Knowledge FIssion (KFI) module is designed to adaptively separate new domain knowledge from a paired class-aware domain prompt pool, alleviating the impact of negative knowledge brought by old domains that are distinct from the current domain. Besides, to avoid the cumulative computation and storage overheads from continuously fissioning new knowledge, a domain Knowledge FUsion (KFU) module is further designed to merge the fissioned new knowledge into the existing knowledge pool with minimal cost, where a greedy knowledge dynamic merging strategy is designed to improve the compatibility of new and old knowledge while keeping the computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Continual test-time adaptation updates a model as it encounters unfamiliar data distributions during use. Retaining previous knowledge can prevent forgetting, but historical knowledge can also interfere when the current domain is very different. The paper proposes KFF to manage this tension while learning from a changing stream of test data.

KFF stores class-aware domain knowledge in a paired prompt pool. Its knowledge fission module separates new domain knowledge adaptively, aiming to reduce harmful influence from distinct older domains. This gives the system a way to accommodate differences between domains instead of forcing all incoming information immediately into the same stored representation.

Repeated separation could make the knowledge pool increasingly expensive to maintain. KFF therefore adds a knowledge fusion module that merges newly separated knowledge back into the existing pool. A greedy dynamic merging strategy aims to improve compatibility between old and new knowledge while keeping computation efficient. The contribution is a mechanism for expanding and consolidating domain knowledge, designed to balance adaptation, historical knowledge retention, and storage costs.
summary.tldr: KFF separates and merges class-aware domain knowledge to support continual adaptation while limiting harmful historical interference and growing overhead.

title: Class-aware Domain Knowledge Fusion and Fission for Continual Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Recent studies suggest that context-aware low-rank approximation is a useful tool for compression and fine-tuning of modern large-scale neural networks. In this type of approximation, a norm is weighted by a matrix of input activations, significantly improving metrics over the unweighted case. Nevertheless, existing methods for neural networks suffer from numerical instabilities due to their reliance on classical formulas involving explicit Gram matrix computation and their subsequent inversion. We demonstrate that this can degrade the approximation quality or cause numerically singular matrices. To address these limitations, we propose a novel _inversion-free regularized framework_ that is based entirely on stable decompositions and overcomes the numerical pitfalls of prior art. Our method can handle all possible challenging scenarios: (1) when calibration matrices exceed GPU memory capacity, (2) when input activation matrices are nearly singular, and even (3) when insufficient data prevents unique approximation. For the latter, we prove that our solution converges to a desired approximation and derive explicit error bounds.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation reduces the complexity of neural network components for compression or fine-tuning. Context-aware versions weight approximation errors using input activations, so the approximation reflects how the network is used. The paper addresses a numerical problem in existing methods: explicitly forming and inverting Gram matrices can degrade approximation quality or produce matrices that are numerically singular.

COALA replaces those calculations with an inversion-free, regularized framework built from stable decompositions. The aim is to retain the benefits of activation-weighted approximation while avoiding unstable intermediate calculations. This makes numerical reliability a central part of the approximation procedure.

The framework handles calibration matrices too large for GPU memory, activation matrices close to singularity, and data shortages that prevent a unique approximation. For the insufficient-data case, the authors prove convergence to a desired approximation and provide explicit error bounds. These results matter because the usefulness of context-aware compression depends on obtaining a reliable approximation even when the available activation data are computationally or mathematically challenging.
summary.tldr: COALA makes context-aware low-rank approximation more numerically reliable through regularization and stable, inversion-free calculations.

title: COALA: Numerically Stable and Efficient Framework for Context-Aware Low-Rank Approximation

abstract: Participating in efforts to endow generative AI with the 3D physical world perception, we propose I2-NeRF, a novel neural radiance field framework that enhances isometric and isotropic metric perception under media degradation. While existing NeRF models predominantly rely on object-centric sampling, I2-NeRF introduces a reverse-stratified upsampling strategy to achieve near-uniform sampling across 3D space, thereby preserving isometry. We further present a general radiative formulation for media degradation that unifies emission, absorption, and scattering into a particle model governed by the Beer–Lambert attenuation law. By matting direct and media-induced in-scatter radiance, this formulation extends naturally to complex media environments such as underwater, haze, and even low-light scenes. By treating light propagation uniformly in both vertical and horizontal directions, I2-NeRF enables isotropic metric perception and can even estimate medium properties such as water depth. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves both reconstruction fidelity and physical plausibility compared to existing approaches. The source code will be released.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a scene becomes harder when the surrounding medium changes how light reaches the camera. I2-NeRF addresses this problem by combining a different spatial sampling strategy with a physical model of light interacting with matter. Its goal is to improve geometric perception and reconstruction under conditions such as underwater imaging, haze, and low light.

The framework uses reverse-stratified upsampling to distribute samples nearly uniformly throughout three-dimensional space, helping preserve spatial distance relationships. It also unifies emission, absorption, and scattering in a particle-based formulation governed by Beer–Lambert attenuation. Separating direct radiance from light scattered into the view by the medium makes these effects explicit in the reconstruction model.

Light propagation is treated consistently across vertical and horizontal directions, supporting direction-independent metric perception. The method can also estimate medium-related properties such as water depth. Experiments on real-world datasets report significant improvements in reconstruction fidelity and physical plausibility over existing approaches. Together, the results support modeling both the scene’s spatial structure and the medium’s effects on observed light.
summary.tldr: I2-NeRF combines near-uniform spatial sampling with physical light–medium modeling to improve reconstruction in degraded imaging conditions.

title: I2-NeRF: Learning Neural Radiance Fields Under Physically-Grounded Media Interactions

abstract: Military weapon systems and command-and-control infrastructure augmented by artificial intelligence (AI) have seen rapid development and deployment in recent years. However, the sociotechnical impacts of AI on combat systems, military decision-making, and the norms of warfare have been understudied. We focus on a specific subset of lethal autonomous weapon systems (LAWS) that use AI for targeting or battlefield decisions. We refer to this subset as AI-powered lethal autonomous weapon systems (AI-LAWS) and argue that they introduce novel risks—including unanticipated escalation, poor reliability in unfamiliar environments, and erosion of human oversight—all of which threaten both military effectiveness and the openness of AI research.These risks cannot be addressed by high-level policy alone; effective regulation must be grounded in the technical behavior of AI models. We argue that AI researchers must be involved throughout the regulatory lifecycle.Thus, we propose a clear, behavior-based definition of AI-LAWS—systems that introduce unique risks through their use of modern AI—as a foundation for technically grounded regulation, given that existing frameworks do not distinguish them from conventional LAWS.Using this definition, we propose several technically-informed policy directions and invite greater participation from the AI research community in military AI policy discussions.

paragraphs: This paper argues that regulating military AI requires attention to how AI systems actually behave. It focuses on lethal autonomous weapons that use AI for targeting or battlefield decisions, naming this subset AI-LAWS. The authors distinguish these systems from the broader category of autonomous weapons because they argue that modern AI introduces distinctive risks.

Those risks include unexpected escalation, unreliable behavior in unfamiliar environments, and weakened human oversight. The paper connects them to both military effectiveness and the openness of AI research. Its central policy argument is that high-level principles alone cannot adequately address behavior that depends on technical properties of the underlying models.

The authors propose a behavior-based definition of AI-LAWS as a foundation for technically informed regulation. They argue that existing frameworks do not sufficiently distinguish this subset from conventional autonomous weapons. Building on their definition, they propose policy directions and call for AI researchers to participate throughout the regulatory lifecycle. The contribution is a conceptual and policy framework for making technical expertise part of how these systems are defined and governed.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates a behavior-based definition of AI-powered autonomous weapons and sustained AI-researcher involvement in technically informed regulation.

title: Military AI Needs Technically-Informed Regulation to Safeguard AI Research and its Applications

abstract: In the classic expert problem, $\Phi$-regret measures the gap between the learner's total loss and that achieved by applying the best action transformation $\phi \in \Phi$. A recent work by Lu et al., [2025] introduced an adaptive algorithm whose regret against a comparator $\phi$ depends on a certain sparsity-based complexity measure of $\phi$, recovering and interpolating optimal bounds for standard regret notions such as external, internal, and swap regret. In this work, we propose a general idea to achieve an even better comparator-adaptive $\Phi$-regret bound via much simpler algorithms compared to Lu et al., [2025]. Specifically, we discover a prior distribution over all possible binary transformations and show that it suffices to achieve prior-dependent regret against these transformations. Then, we propose two concrete and efficient algorithms to achieve so, where the first one combines multiple copies of the kernelized Hedge algorithm of Farina et al., [2022], and the second one combines multiple copies of a variant of the BM-reduction [Blum and Mansour, 2007]. To further showcase the power of our methods and the advantages over Lu et al., [2025] besides the simplicity and better regret bounds, we also show that our second approach can be extended to the game setting to achieve accelerated and adaptive convergence rate to $\Phi$-equilibria for a class of general-sum games. When specified to the special case of correlated equilibria, our bound improves over the existing ones from Anagnostides et al., [2022a,b].

paragraphs: In online learning, regret compares the learner’s accumulated loss with what an alternative decision rule would have achieved. Phi-regret allows that alternative to transform the learner’s actions. This paper studies guarantees that adapt to the particular transformation used for comparison, building on earlier bounds tied to a sparsity-based measure of transformation complexity.

The central contribution is a prior distribution over binary transformations. The authors show that obtaining regret guarantees dependent on this prior is sufficient to obtain their improved comparator-adaptive bound. They then give two efficient constructions: one combines copies of kernelized Hedge, while the other combines copies of a variant of the Blum–Mansour reduction. Both simplify the algorithmic route to the guarantee.

The second construction also extends to a class of general-sum games, where it yields accelerated, adaptive convergence to Phi-equilibria. For correlated equilibria, a special case, the reported bound improves on existing results. The contribution therefore links stronger individual learning guarantees with improved convergence guarantees in the stated game setting.
summary.tldr: A prior over action transformations yields simpler algorithms with improved adaptive regret bounds and stronger equilibrium-convergence guarantees for a class of games.

title: Comparator-Adaptive $\Phi$-Regret: Improved Bounds, Simpler Algorithms, and Applications to Games

abstract: Continual Learning (CL) aims to enable models to continuously acquire new knowledge from a sequence of tasks with avoiding the forgetting of learned information. However, existing CL methods only rely on the parameters of the most recent task for inference, which makes them susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. Inspired by the recent success of model merging techniques, we propose Perturb-and-Merge (P\&M), a novel continual learning framework that integrates model merging into the CL paradigm to mitigate forgetting. Specifically, after training on each task, P\&M constructs a new model by forming a convex combination of the previous model and the newly trained task-specific model. Through theoretical analysis, We minimize the total loss increase across all tasks and derive a closed-form solution for the merging coefficient under mild assumptions. To further improve the performance of the merged model, we observe that the degradation introduced during merging can be alleviated by a regularization term composed of the task vector and the Hessian matrix of the loss function. Interestingly, we show that this term can be efficiently approximated using second-order symmetric finite differences, and a stochastic perturbation strategy along the task vector direction is accordingly devised which incurs no additional forward or backward passes while providing an effective approximation of the regularization term. Finally, we combine P\&M with LoRA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, to reduce memory overhead. Our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on several continual learning benchmark datasets. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/qhmiao/P-M-for-Continual-Learning}.

summary.tldr: Perturb-and-Merge prepares task models for parameter merging during training, then combines old and new models to reduce continual-learning forgetting.

title: Train with Perturbation, Infer after Merging: A Two-Stage Framework for Continual Learning

abstract: Visual-spatial understanding, the ability to infer object relationships and layouts from visual input, is fundamental to downstream tasks such as robotic navigation and embodied interaction. However, existing methods face spatial uncertainty and data scarcity, limiting the 3D spatial reasoning capability of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs). To address these challenges, we present a unified framework for enhancing 3D spatial reasoning in pre-trained VLMs without modifying their architecture. This framework combines SpatialMind, a structured prompting strategy that decomposes complex scenes and questions into interpretable reasoning steps, with ScanForgeQA, a scalable question-answering dataset built from diverse 3D simulation scenes through an automated construction process designed for fine-tuning. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate the individual and combined effectiveness of our prompting and fine-tuning strategies, and yield insights that may inspire future research on visual-spatial understanding.

paragraphs: Understanding spatial relationships from visual input means inferring how objects are arranged and related in three dimensions. This ability matters for tasks such as navigation and embodied interaction. The paper identifies spatial uncertainty and limited training data as obstacles for pretrained vision-language models, then addresses both within a framework that preserves their existing architecture.

The first component, SpatialMind, structures the model's prompting process. It breaks complex scenes and questions into interpretable reasoning steps, giving spatial analysis a more explicit organization. The second component, ScanForgeQA, supplies question-answering data constructed automatically from diverse three-dimensional simulation scenes. This scalable dataset is designed for fine-tuning models on spatial understanding.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate benefits from the prompting strategy and the fine-tuning strategy individually, as well as from their combination. The findings support improving spatial reasoning through both the way a question is approached and the examples used to train the model. Together, these components offer a route to enhancing pretrained models without redesigning their architecture.
summary.tldr: Structured spatial prompts and automatically generated simulation questions improve pretrained vision-language models' spatial reasoning without architectural changes.

title: Spatial Understanding from Videos: Structured Prompts Meet Simulation Data

abstract: In explainable AI, DNN gradients are used to interpret the prediction; in safety-critical control systems, gradients could encode safety constraints; in scientific-computing applications, gradients could encode physical invariants. While recent work on provable editing of DNNs has focused on input-output constraints, the problem of enforcing hard constraints on DNN gradients remains unaddressed. We present ProGrad, the first efficient approach for editing the parameters of a DNN to provably enforce hard constraints on the DNN gradients. Given a DNN $\mathcal{N}$ with parameters $\theta$, and a set $\mathcal{S}$ of pairs $(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{Q})$ of input $\mathrm{x}$ and corresponding linear gradient constraints $\mathrm{Q}$, ProGrad finds new parameters $\theta'$ such that $\bigwedge_{(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{Q}) \in \mathcal{S}} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathrm{x}}\mathcal{N}(\mathrm{x}; \theta') \in \mathrm{Q}$ while minimizing the changes $\lVert\theta' - \theta\rVert$. The key contribution is a novel *conditional variable gradient* of DNNs, which relaxes the NP-hard provable gradient editing problem to a linear program (LP), enabling ProGrad to use an LP solver to efficiently and effectively enforce the gradient constraints. We experimentally evaluated ProGrad via enforcing (i) hard Grad-CAM constraints on ImageNet ResNet DNNs; (ii) hard Integrated Gradients constraints on Llama 3 and Qwen 3 LLMs; (iii) hard gradient constraints in training a DNN to approximate a target function as a proxy for safety constraints in control systems and physical invariants in scientific applications. The results highlight the unique capability of ProGrad in enforcing hard constraints on DNN gradients.

paragraphs: ProGrad edits a neural network so that its input gradients satisfy specified hard constraints. Gradients describe how outputs respond to input changes, making them relevant to attribution methods and potentially to physical or safety requirements. The paper addresses constraints on these sensitivities, extending the editing problem beyond conditions imposed directly on outputs.

The input to ProGrad includes a network and a collection of inputs paired with linear gradient constraints. It seeks adjusted parameters that satisfy all those supplied constraints while minimizing parameter changes. A new construction called the conditional variable gradient relaxes the NP-hard editing problem into a linear program, allowing an LP solver to perform the constrained edit.
