The last setting serves as a proxy for safety and physical-invariant applications. The reported results demonstrate hard gradient enforcement in these settings, with the guarantee attached to the supplied input-and-constraint specification.
summary.tldr: ProGrad uses a linear-programming relaxation to edit network parameters and provably enforce specified linear gradient constraints.

title: Provable Gradient Editing of Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Addressing intricate real-world problems necessitates in-depth information seeking and multi-step reasoning. Recent progress in agentic systems, exemplified by Deep Research, underscores the potential for autonomous multi-step research. In this work, we present a cohesive paradigm for building end-to-end agentic information seeking agents from a data-centric and training-stage perspective. Our approach consists of four key stages: (1) browsing data construction, (2) trajectories sampling, (3) supervised fine-tuning for effective cold start, and (4) reinforcement learning for enhanced generalisation. We instantiate this framework in a web agent based on the ReAct format, WebDancer. Empirical evaluations on the challenging GAIA and WebWalkerQA benchmarks demonstrate the strong performance of WebDancer, achieving considerable results and highlighting the efficacy of our training paradigm. Further analysis of agent training provides valuable insights and actionable, systematic pathways for developing more capable agentic models.

The paper focuses on how to build and train an end-to-end agent for that process. Its contribution is a coordinated development paradigm that connects the construction of browsing data with successive stages of model training.

The framework has four stages: constructing browsing data, sampling trajectories, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Supervised fine-tuning provides an effective starting point for the agent, while reinforcement learning is used to improve generalization. Organizing these stages together makes the data and training process a central part of the agent design.

The authors instantiate the approach as WebDancer, a web agent using the ReAct format. The stated contribution therefore includes both the working agent and an organized approach to training autonomous information-seeking behavior.
summary.tldr: WebDancer combines browsing-data construction, trajectory sampling, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning to train an autonomous information-seeking web agent.

title: WebDancer: Towards Autonomous Information Seeking Agency

abstract: The essence of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training is to smartly allocate Gaussian primitives, expressing complex regions with more primitives and vice versa. Prior researches typically mark out under-reconstructed regions in a rendering-loss-driven manner. However, such a loss-driven strategy is often dominated by low-frequency regions, which leads to insufficient modeling of high-frequency details in texture-rich regions. As a result, it yields a suboptimal spatial allocation of Gaussian primitives. This inspires us to excavate the loss-agnostic visual prior in training views to identify complex regions that need more primitives to model. Based on this insight, we propose Complexity-Density Consistent Gaussian Splatting (CDC-GS), which allocates primitives based on the consistency between visual complexity of training views and the density of primitives. Specifically, primitives involved in rendering high visual complexity areas are categorized as modeling high complexity regions, where we leverage the high frequency wavelet components of training views to measure the visual complexity. And the density of a primitive is computed with the inverse of geometric mean of its distance to the neighboring primitives. Guided by the positive correlation between primitive complexity and density, we determine primitives to be densified as well as pruned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our CDC-GS surpasses the baseline methods in rendering quality by a large margin using the same amount of Gaussians. And we provide insightful analysis to reveal that our method serves perpendicularly to rendering loss in guiding Gaussian primitive allocation.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting must decide where to place more primitives and where fewer will suffice. The paper argues that allocating them mainly through rendering loss can favor low-frequency regions, leaving fine texture insufficiently modeled. CDC-GS introduces a separate signal based on visual complexity to guide that allocation.

The method measures complexity using high-frequency wavelet components from the training images. Gaussians contributing to visually complex image regions are treated as representing complex scene regions. It estimates each primitive's local density using the inverse geometric mean of distances to neighboring primitives. Comparing complexity with density then guides which primitives should be densified or pruned.

The intended relationship is that more complex regions receive a higher concentration of primitives. Experiments report substantially better rendering quality than baselines using the same number of Gaussians, making spatial allocation central to the improvement. The accompanying analysis indicates that this complexity-based signal provides guidance complementary to rendering loss, helping direct representational capacity toward fine detail that loss alone can underemphasize.
summary.tldr: CDC-GS allocates Gaussian primitives according to visual complexity and local density, improving rendering quality at the same primitive count.

title: Reframing Gaussian Splatting Densification with Complexity-Density Consistency of Primitives

abstract: Node tokenized graph Transformers (GTs) have shown promising performance in node classification. The generation of token sequences is the key module in existing tokenized GTs which transforms the input graph into token sequences, facilitating the node representation learning via Transformer. In this paper, we observe that the generations of token sequences in existing GTs only focus on the first-order neighbors on the constructed similarity graphs, which leads to the limited usage of nodes to generate diverse token sequences, further restricting the potential of tokenized GTs for node classification. To this end, we propose a new method termed SwapGT. SwapGT first introduces a novel token swapping operation based on the characteristics of token sequences that fully leverages the semantic relevance of nodes to generate more informative token sequences. Then, SwapGT leverages a Transformer-based backbone to learn node representations from the generated token sequences. Moreover, SwapGT develops a center alignment loss to constrain the representation learning from multiple token sequences, further enhancing the model performance. Extensive empirical results on various datasets showcase the superiority of SwapGT for node classification. Code is available at https://github.com/JHL-HUST/SwapGT.

paragraphs: SwapGT studies how graph Transformers build token sequences for node classification. These sequences determine which graph information reaches the Transformer. The authors observe that existing methods focus on immediate neighbors in constructed similarity graphs, restricting the nodes used to create diverse sequences and limiting the resulting representations.

The proposed method introduces token swapping to use semantic relationships among nodes more fully. This operation produces more informative token sequences, which a Transformer backbone then converts into node representations. A center alignment loss adds a constraint across representations learned from multiple sequences, tying the sequence-generation mechanism to the representation-learning objective.

Experiments across various datasets show that SwapGT outperforms the compared approaches for node classification. The findings emphasize that the construction of Transformer inputs is a consequential part of graph learning. Here, improving the diversity and semantic relevance of those inputs, together with aligning the resulting representations, provides the route to stronger classification performance.
summary.tldr: SwapGT improves node classification through semantically informed token swapping and alignment of representations learned from multiple token sequences.

title: Rethinking Tokenized Graph Transformers for Node Classification

abstract: Generative models are spearheading recent progress in deep learning, showcasing strong promise for trajectory sampling in dynamical systems as well. However, whereas latent space modeling paradigms have transformed image and video generation, similar approaches are more difficult for most dynamical systems. Such systems -- from chemical molecule structures to collective human behavior -- are described by interactions of entities, making them inherently linked to connectivity patterns, entity conservation, and the traceability of entities over time. Our approach, LaM-SLidE (Latent Space Modeling of Spatial Dynamical Systems via Linked Entities), bridges the gap between: (1) keeping the traceability of individual entities in a latent system representation, and (2) leveraging the efficiency and scalability of recent advances in image and video generation, where pre-trained encoder and decoder enable generative modeling directly in latent space. The core idea of LaM-SLidE is the introduction of identifier representations (IDs) that enable the retrieval of entity properties and entity composition from latent system representations, thus fostering traceability. Experimentally, across different domains, we show that LaM-SLidE performs favorably in terms of speed, accuracy, and generalizability. Code is available at https://github.com/ml-jku/LaM-SLidE.
originalAbstract: Generative models are spearheading recent progress in deep learning, showcasing strong promise for trajectory sampling in dynamical systems as well. However, whereas latent space modeling paradigms have transformed image and video generation, similar approaches are more difficult for most dynamical systems. Such systems -- from chemical molecule structures to collective human behavior -- are described by interactions of entities, making them inherently linked to connectivity patterns, entity conservation, and the traceability of entities over time. Our approach, LaM-SLidE (Latent Space Modeling of Spatial Dynamical Systems via Linked Entities), bridges the gap between: (1) keeping the traceability of individual entities in a latent system representation, and (2) leveraging the efficiency and scalability of recent advances in image and video generation, where pre-trained encoder and decoder enable generative modeling directly in latent space. The core idea of LaM-SLidE is the introduction of identifier representations (IDs) that enable the retrieval of entity properties and entity composition from latent system representations, thus fostering traceability. Experimentally, across different domains, we show that LaM-SLidE performs favorably in terms of speed, accuracy, and generalizability. Code is available at https://github.com/ml-jku/LaM-SLidE.

paragraphs: LaM-SLidE brings latent-space generation to systems made of interacting entities, such as molecules or groups of people. Compressing these systems into a latent representation creates a particular challenge: the model must still track individual entities over time and retain information about their composition and connections. Efficient generation alone does not address that requirement.

These identifiers allow retrieval of entity properties and composition from the latent representation, supporting traceability. The contribution is the connection between efficient latent modeling and explicit access to the entities being modeled. It shows a way to use a compressed system representation while retaining the ability to recover information about its individual components throughout a generated trajectory.
summary.tldr: LaM-SLidE uses entity identifiers to preserve traceability while generating dynamical-system trajectories in latent space.

title: LaM-SLidE: Latent Space Modeling of Spatial Dynamical Systems via Linked Entities

abstract: This paper presents JavisGPT, the first unified multimodal large language model (MLLM) for Joint Audio-Video (JAV) comprehension and generation. JavisGPT adopts a concise encoder–LLM–decoder architecture, featuring a SyncFusion module for spatio-temporal audio- video fusion and synchrony-aware learnable queries to bridge a pretrained JAV-DiT generator. This design enables temporally coherent video-audio understanding and generation from multimodal instructions. We design an effective three-stage training pipeline consisting of multimodal pretraining, audio-video fine-tuning, and large-scale instruction-tuning, to progressively build multimodal comprehension and generation from existing vision-language models. To support this, we further construct JavisInst-Omni, a high-quality instruction dataset with over 200K GPT-4o-curated audio-video-text dialogues that span diverse and multi-level comprehension and generation scenarios. Extensive experiments on JAV comprehension and generation benchmarks show that JavisGPT outperforms existing MLLMs, particularly in complex and temporally synchronized settings.

This matters for instructions that require the model to interpret or produce an audiovisual event as a temporally connected whole.

The system uses an encoder–language-model–decoder architecture. A SyncFusion module combines audio and video information across space and time, while synchrony-aware learned queries connect the language model to a pretrained joint audio-video generator. Training progresses through multimodal pretraining, audio-video fine-tuning, and large-scale instruction tuning, building these abilities from existing vision-language models.

Evaluations on joint audio-video benchmarks show that JavisGPT outperforms existing multimodal language models, particularly in complex settings requiring temporal synchronization. The findings support combining explicit synchronization mechanisms with staged training and instruction data to develop a unified model for understanding and producing sounding video.
summary.tldr: JavisGPT unifies audio-video understanding and generation through synchronization-aware architecture, staged training, and a large instruction dataset.

title: JavisGPT: A Unified Multi-modal LLM for Sounding-Video Comprehension and Generation

abstract: Test-time adaptation with pre-trained vision-language models shows impressive zero-shot classification abilities, and training-free methods further improve the performance without any optimization burden. However, existing training-free test-time adaptation methods typically rely on entropy criteria to select the visual features and update the visual caches, while ignoring the generalizable factors, such as shape-sensitive and style-insensitive factors. In this paper, we propose a novel shape and style guidance method (SSG) for training-free test-time adaptation in vision-language models, aiming to highlight the shape-sensitive (SHS) and style-insensitive (STI) factors in addition to entropy criteria. Specifically, SSG perturbs the raw test image with shape and style corruption operations, and measures the prediction difference between the raw and corrupted one as perturbed prediction difference (PPD). Based on the PPD measurement, SSG reweights the high-confidence visual features and corresponding predictions, aiming to highlight the effect of SHS and STI factors during the test-time procedure. Furthermore, SSG takes both PPD and entropy into consideration to update the visual cache, aiming to maintain the stored sample with high entropy and generalizable factors. Extensive experimental results on out-of-distribution and cross-domain benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed SSG consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods while also exhibiting promising computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Shape and Style Guidance, or SSG, improves training-free test-time adaptation for vision-language models. Existing methods commonly use prediction entropy to select visual features and update a cache of test examples. The paper argues that this overlooks factors that may generalize better, particularly sensitivity to shape and insensitivity to style.

SSG applies shape and style corruptions to each test image, then measures how predictions change relative to the original image. This perturbed prediction difference becomes a signal for reweighting high-confidence visual features and their predictions. The intended effect is to emphasize features whose behavior reflects the desired shape-sensitive and style-insensitive properties during adaptation.

The cache update combines the perturbation measure with entropy, aiming to retain samples with high entropy and generalizable factors. This adds information about responses to image changes to the criteria used for storing examples. Across out-of-distribution and cross-domain benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods and promising computational efficiency. The results support perturbation-guided adaptation without an optimization stage at test time.
summary.tldr: SSG uses prediction changes under shape and style corruptions to guide training-free adaptation of vision-language models.

title: Training-Free Test-Time Adaptation via Shape and Style Guidance for Vision-Language Models

abstract: This paper provides an analysis of error propagation in Approximate Dynamic Programming applied to zero-sum two-player Stochastic Games. We provide a novel and unified error propagation analysis in L_p-norm of three well-known algorithms adapted to Stochastic Games (namely Approximate Value Iteration, Approximate Policy Iteration and Approximate Generalized Policy Iteration). We show that we can achieve a stationary policy which is \frac2γ(1 - γ)^2 ε+ \frac1(1 - γ)^2ε’-optimal, where εis the value function approximation error and ε’ is the approximate greedy operator error. In addition, we provide a practical algorithm (AGPI-Q) to solve infinite horizon γ-discounted two-player zero-sum stochastic games in a batch setting. It is an extension of the Fitted-Q algorithm (which solves Markov Decisions Processes in a batch setting) and can be non-parametric. Finally, we demonstrate experimentally the performance of AGPI-Q on a simultaneous two-player game, namely Alesia.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum stochastic game, learning a good strategy requires accounting for an opponent whose interests conflict with yours. This paper studies what happens when dynamic programming calculations for such games are approximate. Its central question is how errors in intermediate computations affect the quality of the strategy ultimately obtained.

The authors give a unified error analysis for approximate value iteration, policy iteration, and generalized policy iteration adapted to stochastic games. The analysis uses Lp norms and distinguishes errors in estimating values from errors in the approximate greedy operation. It bounds the suboptimality of an achievable stationary policy in terms of both errors and the discount factor.

The paper also introduces AGPI-Q, a practical batch algorithm for infinite-horizon discounted games. It extends the Fitted-Q approach from Markov decision processes to the two-player setting and permits a nonparametric implementation. Experiments on the simultaneous game Alesia demonstrate its performance, connecting the theoretical treatment of approximation errors to an implemented game-solving method.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds approximation-error propagation in two-player zero-sum games and introduces a batch learning algorithm called AGPI-Q.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming for Two-Player Zero-Sum Markov Games

abstract: We show that the widely used Kendall tau correlation coefficient is a positive definite kernel for permutations. It offers a computationally attractive alternative to more complex kernels on the symmetric group to learn from rankings, or to learn to rank. We show how to extend it to partial rankings or rankings with uncertainty, and demonstrate promising results on high-dimensional classification problems in biomedical applications.

It offers a computationally attractive alternative to more complex kernels on the symmetric group to learn from rankings, or to learn to rank. We show how to extend it to partial rankings or rankings with uncertainty, and demonstrate promising results on high-dimensional classification problems in biomedical applications.

paragraphs: Rankings describe an ordering of items, so a learning method needs a way to compare those orderings. This paper shows that the familiar Kendall tau correlation coefficient is a positive definite kernel on permutations. That mathematical property allows the ranking similarity measure to serve as a kernel for learning from ordered data.

The result provides a computationally attractive alternative to more complex kernels defined over the set of permutations. The authors position it for both learning from rankings and learning to rank. Its importance is that a widely used ranking comparison gains a formal role within kernel-based learning, connecting an existing measure to predictive methods.

The paper also extends the construction to partial rankings and rankings with uncertainty. This broadens its applicability beyond complete, fully specified orderings. Experiments on high-dimensional biomedical classification problems produce promising results. These findings support the practical potential of the ranking kernel and its extensions, while the core theoretical contribution establishes Kendall tau's validity as a positive definite kernel.
summary.tldr: Kendall tau is shown to be a positive definite ranking kernel, with extensions to partial and uncertain rankings.

title: The Kendall and Mallows Kernels for Permutations

abstract: Clustering is the task of grouping a set of examples so that similar examples are grouped into the same cluster while dissimilar examples are in different clusters. The quality of a clustering depends on two problem-dependent factors which are i) the chosen similarity metric and ii) the data representation. Supervised clustering approaches, which exploit labeled partitioned datasets have thus been proposed, for instance to learn a metric optimized to perform clustering. However, most of these approaches assume that the representation of the data is fixed and then learn an appropriate linear transformation. Some deep supervised clustering learning approaches have also been proposed. However, they rely on iterative methods to compute gradients resulting in high algorithmic complexity. In this paper, we propose a deep supervised clustering metric learning method that formulates a novel loss function. We derive a closed-form expression for the gradient that is efficient to compute: the complexity to compute the gradient is linear in the size of the training mini-batch and quadratic in the representation dimensionality. We further reveal how our approach can be seen as learning spectral clustering. Experiments on standard real-world datasets confirm state-of-the-art Recall@K performance.

paragraphs: Clustering quality depends on both how examples are represented and how similarity is measured. This paper studies supervised clustering learning, where labeled partitions provide information about which examples belong together. Its goal is to learn a deep similarity representation that supports good grouping, rather than treating the original representation as fixed.

The authors introduce a new loss function for deep supervised clustering metric learning. A central contribution is a closed-form expression for its gradient, avoiding the iterative gradient computations used by some earlier deep approaches. Computing this gradient scales linearly with training mini-batch size and quadratically with representation dimensionality. These dependencies explain where the method's computational savings arise and which dimensions still affect its cost.

The paper also establishes an interpretation of the method as learning spectral clustering, linking its training objective to that clustering framework. Experiments on standard real-world datasets report state-of-the-art Recall@K performance. The stated contribution combines a learned representation and similarity measure with an efficiently computable training gradient, supported by the reported evaluation results.
summary.tldr: A new deep clustering loss enables closed-form gradient computation and achieves reported state-of-the-art Recall@K performance.

title: Deep Spectral Clustering Learning

abstract: Making inferences from data streams is a pervasive problem in many modern data analysis applications. But it requires to address the problem of continuous model updating, and adapt to changes or drifts in the underlying data generating distribution. In this paper, we approach these problems from a Bayesian perspective covering general conjugate exponential models. Our proposal makes use of non-conjugate hierarchical priors to explicitly model temporal changes of the model parameters. We also derive a novel variational inference scheme which overcomes the use of non-conjugate priors while maintaining the computational efficiency of variational methods over conjugate models. The approach is validated on three real data sets over three latent variable models.

In this paper, we approach these problems from a Bayesian perspective covering general conjugate exponential models. paragraphs: Learning from a data stream involves more than repeatedly adding observations to a fixed dataset. The model must keep updating while the process producing the data may itself change. This paper develops a Bayesian approach to those linked problems, covering a general class of conjugate exponential models.

The approach explicitly represents changes in model parameters over time through hierarchical priors. Those priors are non-conjugate, meaning they do not preserve the convenient mathematical relationships that make inference straightforward in the underlying conjugate models. This introduces a computational challenge alongside the benefit of directly modeling temporal change.

The authors derive a variational inference scheme that handles these priors while maintaining the computational efficiency associated with variational methods for conjugate models. They validate the approach on three real datasets using three latent-variable models. The contribution is therefore both a way to express changing stream behavior and an inference procedure intended to make that flexibility practical for continuous model updating.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical priors model temporal changes in streaming data while a new variational scheme keeps inference computationally efficient.

title: Bayesian Models of Data Streams with Hierarchical Power Priors

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have shown extraordinary performance in a number of applications, but they are usually of heavy design for the accuracy reason. Beyond compressing the filters in CNNs, this paper focuses on the redundancy in the feature maps derived from the large number of filters in a layer. We propose to extract intrinsic representation of the feature maps and preserve the discriminability of the features. Circulant matrix is employed to formulate the feature map transformation, which only requires O(dlog d) computation complexity to embed a d-dimensional feature map. The filter is then re-configured to establish the mapping from original input to the new compact feature map, and the resulting network can preserve intrinsic information of the original network with significantly fewer parameters, which not only decreases the online memory for launching CNN but also accelerates the computation speed. Experiments on benchmark image datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can be costly to store and run because their designs prioritize accuracy. This paper approaches compression by examining redundancy in the feature maps produced by a layer's filters. The goal is to retain the information that helps distinguish inputs while representing the layer's output more compactly.

The authors construct a feature-map transformation using a circulant matrix. This structure permits embedding a d-dimensional feature map with O(d log d) computation. They then reconfigure the filters so that the original input maps directly to the new compact representation. Thus, compression changes the network's internal mapping as well as the representation of its features.

The resulting network can preserve intrinsic information from the original model while using substantially fewer parameters. The authors report lower memory requirements for running the network and faster computation. Experiments on benchmark image datasets show advantages over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The broader contribution is to make feature-map redundancy an explicit target for portable network design.
summary.tldr: Compressing redundant feature maps and reconfiguring filters yields smaller, faster convolutional networks while preserving useful information.

title: Beyond Filters: Compact Feature Map for Portable Deep Model

abstract: We propose a novel algorithmic framework of Variable Metric Over-Relaxed Hybrid Proximal Extra-gradient (VMOR-HPE) method with a global convergence guarantee for the maximal monotone operator inclusion problem. Its iteration complexities and local linear convergence rate are provided, which theoretically demonstrate that a large over-relaxed step-size contributes to accelerating the proposed VMOR-HPE as a byproduct. Specifically, we find that a large class of primal and primal-dual operator splitting algorithms are all special cases of VMOR-HPE. Hence, the proposed framework offers a new insight into these operator splitting algorithms. In addition, we apply VMOR-HPE to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) generalized equation of linear equality constrained multi-block composite convex optimization, yielding a new algorithm, namely nonsymmetric Proximal Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers with a preconditioned Extra-gradient step in which the preconditioned metric is generated by a blockwise Barzilai-Borwein line search technique (PADMM-EBB). We also establish iteration complexities of PADMM-EBB in terms of the KKT residual. Finally, we apply PADMM-EBB to handle the nonnegative dual graph regularized low-rank representation problem. Promising results on synthetic and real datasets corroborate the efficacy of PADMM-EBB.

paragraphs: This paper introduces VMOR-HPE, a framework for solving maximal monotone operator inclusions. It brings variable metrics and over-relaxed steps into a hybrid proximal extra-gradient method. The framework covers a broad class of primal and primal-dual operator splitting algorithms, providing a shared perspective on methods that might otherwise be analyzed separately.

The authors establish global convergence, iteration complexity results, and a local linear convergence rate. Their analysis also supports the role of larger over-relaxed steps in accelerating the framework. These results connect algorithm design to convergence behavior: the choice of step and metric is part of the theoretical explanation for progress.

Applying the framework to optimality equations for equality-constrained, multi-block composite convex optimization produces PADMM-EBB. This algorithm combines a nonsymmetric proximal alternating direction method with a preconditioned extra-gradient step and a blockwise line search for its metric. The paper bounds complexity through the KKT residual and reports promising synthetic and real-data results on nonnegative dual graph regularized low-rank representation.
summary.tldr: VMOR-HPE unifies operator splitting methods with convergence guarantees and yields a new algorithm for constrained composite convex optimization.

title: An Algorithmic Framework of Variable Metric Over-Relaxed Hybrid Proximal Extra-Gradient Method

abstract: Black-box explanation is the problem of explaining how a machine learning model – whose internal logic is hidden to the auditor and generally complex – produces its outcomes. Current approaches for solving this problem include model explanation, outcome explanation as well as model inspection. While these techniques can be beneficial by providing interpretability, they can be used in a negative manner to perform fairwashing, which we define as promoting the false perception that a machine learning model respects some ethical values. In particular, we demonstrate that it is possible to systematically rationalize decisions taken by an unfair black-box model using the model explanation as well as the outcome explanation approaches with a given fairness metric. Our solution, LaundryML, is based on a regularized rule list enumeration algorithm whose objective is to search for fair rule lists approximating an unfair black-box model. We empirically evaluate our rationalization technique on black-box models trained on real-world datasets and show that one can obtain rule lists with high fidelity to the black-box model while being considerably less unfair at the same time.

paragraphs: An explanation of a black-box model can influence whether an auditor considers its decisions fair. This paper studies fairwashing: creating a misleading impression that a model respects ethical values. The concern is that an interpretable explanation may look substantially fairer than the hidden model whose behavior it is supposed to describe.

The authors demonstrate this possibility for both explanations of an overall model and explanations of individual outcomes, using a specified fairness metric. Their method, LaundryML, searches for rule lists that approximate an unfair black-box model while appearing fairer. It uses regularized rule-list enumeration to pursue these two properties together: agreement with the model and lower measured unfairness.

Experiments with black-box models trained on real-world datasets produce rule lists that closely match model decisions while being considerably less unfair. High agreement therefore can coexist with an important fairness discrepancy between a model and its explanation. The result exposes a risk in treating an explanation’s measured fairness as evidence about the underlying model: an explanation can rationalize its behavior without faithfully conveying its unfairness.
summary.tldr: LaundryML shows that explanations can closely mimic an unfair model while appearing much fairer, creating a misleading impression of ethical behavior.

title: Fairwashing: the risk of rationalization

abstract: Tournament procedures, recently introduced in the literature, offer an appealing alternative, from a theoretical perspective at least, to the principle of Empirical Risk Minimization in machine learning. Statistical learning by Median-of-Means (MoM) basically consists in segmenting the training data into blocks of equal size and comparing the statistical performance of every pair of candidate decision rules on each data block: that with highest performance on the majority of the blocks is declared as the winner. In the context of nonparametric regression, functions having won all their duels have been shown to outperform empirical risk minimizers w.r.t. the mean squared error under minimal assumptions, while exhibiting robustness properties. It is the purpose of this paper to extend this approach, in order to address other learning problems in particular, for which the performance criterion takes the form of an expectation over pairs of observations rather than over one single observation, as may be the case in pairwise ranking, clustering or metric learning. Precisely, it is proved here that the bounds achieved by MoM are essentially conserved when the blocks are built by means of independent sampling without replacement schemes instead of a simple segmentation. These results are next extended to situations where the risk is related to a pairwise loss function and its empirical counterpart is of the form of a $U$-statistic. Beyond theoretical results guaranteeing the performance of the learning/estimation methods proposed, some numerical experiments provide empirical evidence of their relevance in practice.

paragraphs: Median-of-means learning compares candidate decision rules across blocks of training data. A rule wins a comparison when it performs better on most blocks, giving a tournament-style alternative to choosing the best overall empirical average. Prior results motivate this approach through robustness and strong mean-squared-error performance under minimal assumptions in nonparametric regression.

This paper extends the framework in two directions. First, blocks can be formed through independent sampling without replacement rather than a single segmentation of the dataset. The authors prove that the existing median-of-means bounds are essentially preserved under this randomized construction, broadening the ways data can be organized for comparisons.

Second, the analysis extends to objectives defined over pairs of observations, whose empirical forms are U-statistics. Such objectives arise in ranking, clustering, and metric learning. This makes the tournament approach relevant beyond losses attached to individual examples. The paper supplies theoretical performance guarantees for the proposed learning and estimation methods, with numerical experiments providing additional evidence of practical relevance.
summary.tldr: Median-of-means guarantees largely survive randomized block construction and extend to learning objectives based on pairs of observations.

title: On Medians of (Randomized) Pairwise Means

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel setting for Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), namely "Learning from a Learner" (LfL). As opposed to standard IRL, it does not consist in learning a reward by observing an optimal agent but from observations of another learning (and thus sub-optimal) agent. To do so, we leverage the fact that the observed agent’s policy is assumed to improve over time. The ultimate goal of this approach is to recover the actual environment’s reward and to allow the observer to outperform the learner. To recover that reward in practice, we propose methods based on the entropy-regularized policy iteration framework. We discuss different approaches to learn solely from trajectories in the state-action space. We demonstrate the genericity of our method by observing agents implementing various reinforcement learning algorithms. Finally, we show that, on both discrete and continuous state/action tasks, the observer’s performance (that optimizes the recovered reward) can surpass those of the observed agent.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a novel setting for Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), namely "Learning from a Learner" (LfL). As opposed to standard IRL, it does not consist in learning a reward by observing an optimal agent but from observations of another learning (and thus sub-optimal) agent. To do so, we leverage the fact that the observed agent’s policy is assumed to improve over time. The ultimate goal of this approach is to recover the actual environment’s reward and to allow the observer to outperform the learner. To recover that reward in practice, we propose methods based on the entropy-regularized policy iteration framework. We discuss different approaches to learn solely from trajectories in the state-action space. We demonstrate the genericity of our method by observing agents implementing various reinforcement learning algorithms. Finally, we show that, on both discrete and continuous state/action tasks, the observer’s performance (that optimizes the recovered reward) can surpass those of the observed agent.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks to infer a reward from observed behavior. This paper introduces a setting in which the observed agent is still learning and is therefore suboptimal. The observer uses changes in that agent’s behavior as evidence, with the explicit assumption that the observed policy improves over time.

The goal is to recover the environment’s actual reward and then use it to learn behavior that can outperform the observed agent. The authors propose practical methods based on entropy-regularized policy iteration and discuss approaches that use only trajectories through states and actions. The informative signal is thus the learner’s progression, rather than a requirement to observe an already optimal policy.

The methods are evaluated by observing agents that use various reinforcement learning algorithms. On tasks with both discrete and continuous states or actions, an observer optimizing the recovered reward can surpass the observed learner’s performance. These results demonstrate that an improving but imperfect agent can provide useful supervision for learning a stronger policy.
summary.tldr: An observer can infer rewards from an improving, suboptimal learner and sometimes learn a policy that surpasses it.

title: Learning from a Learner

abstract: This work presents Dynamic Normalization (DN), which is able to learn arbitrary normalization operations for different convolutional layers in a deep ConvNet. Unlike existing normalization approaches that predefined computations of the statistics (mean and variance), DN learns to estimate them. DN has several appealing benefits. First, it adapts to various networks, tasks, and batch sizes. Second, it can be easily implemented and trained in a differentiable end-to-end manner with merely small number of parameters. Third, its matrix formulation represents a wide range of normalization methods, shedding light on analyzing them theoretically. Extensive studies show that DN outperforms its counterparts in CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Normalization methods in convolutional networks usually prescribe how to compute the means and variances used to transform activations. Dynamic Normalization makes those estimates learnable. The aim is to let different convolutional layers acquire appropriate normalization operations as part of training, instead of fixing the statistical computations in advance.

The proposed method is differentiable and can be trained end to end with a small number of additional parameters. The authors describe it as adaptable across networks, tasks, and batch sizes. Its matrix formulation also represents a broad range of normalization methods, providing a common mathematical language for examining their relationships and supporting theoretical analysis.

Studies on CIFAR10 and ImageNet show Dynamic Normalization outperforming the comparison methods. The result supports learning the normalization operation as a useful component of representation learning in those evaluations. The contribution combines a practical training mechanism with a broader formulation: the network can learn its statistical estimates, while existing normalization approaches can be viewed within the same representational framework.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Normalization learns layer-specific normalization statistics end to end and outperforms comparison methods on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

title: Differentiable Dynamic Normalization for Learning Deep Representation

abstract: The Optimal Transport (a.k.a. Wasserstein) distance is an increasingly popular similarity measure for rich data domains, such as images or text documents. This raises the necessity for fast nearest neighbor search algorithms according to this distance, which poses a substantial computational bottleneck on massive datasets. In this work we introduce Flowtree, a fast and accurate approximation algorithm for the Wasserstein-1 distance. We formally analyze its approximation factor and running time. We perform extensive experimental evaluation of nearest neighbor search algorithms in the W_1 distance on real-world dataset. Our results show that compared to previous state of the art, Flowtree achieves up to 7.4 times faster running time.

paragraphs: Finding similar images or documents can use the Wasserstein distance, also known as an optimal transport distance. However, nearest-neighbor search under this measure becomes computationally demanding on massive datasets. This paper addresses that bottleneck by introducing Flowtree, an approximation algorithm for the Wasserstein-1 distance intended to combine fast computation with accurate similarity estimates.

The authors formally analyze both the approximation factor and the running time. These two aspects address different requirements: how the approximated distance relates to the target distance, and how much computation the algorithm needs. Studying them together gives a theoretical basis for using an approximation within nearest-neighbor search, where expensive distance comparisons can dominate the workload.

Extensive experiments evaluate Wasserstein-1 nearest-neighbor search on real-world data. Compared with the previous state of the art, Flowtree achieves running-time improvements of up to 7.4 times. This is the largest reported speedup rather than a promise for every search. The contribution combines analysis of the approximation with empirical evidence that it can substantially reduce the computational burden of this similarity measure.
summary.tldr: Flowtree approximates Wasserstein-1 distance for nearest-neighbor search and reports speedups of up to 7.4 times over prior state of the art.

title: Scalable Nearest Neighbor Search for Optimal Transport

abstract: We introduce T-Basis, a novel concept for a compact representation of a set of tensors, each of an arbitrary shape, which is often seen in Neural Networks. Each of the tensors in the set is modeled using Tensor Rings, though the concept applies to other Tensor Networks. Owing its name to the T-shape of nodes in diagram notation of Tensor Rings, T-Basis is simply a list of equally shaped three-dimensional tensors, used to represent Tensor Ring nodes. Such representation allows us to parameterize the tensor set with a small number of parameters (coefficients of the T-Basis tensors), scaling logarithmically with each tensor’s size in the set and linearly with the dimensionality of T-Basis. We evaluate the proposed approach on the task of neural network compression and demonstrate that it reaches high compression rates at acceptable performance drops. Finally, we analyze memory and operation requirements of the compressed networks and conclude that T-Basis networks are equally well suited for training and inference in resource-constrained environments and usage on the edge devices. Project website: obukhov.ai/tbasis.

paragraphs: T-Basis provides a compact way to represent a collection of tensors, the multidimensional arrays used in neural networks. The tensors in that collection can have different shapes. The approach represents each tensor using a Tensor Ring, giving the collection a structure that can be described through smaller components.

The central idea is to use a shared list of three-dimensional tensors, all with the same shape, to represent the nodes of those Tensor Rings. This list is the T-Basis. Coefficients associated with its tensors provide a compact parameterization of the collection. The authors also state that the concept applies to other Tensor Networks.

The number of coefficients scales logarithmically with each represented tensor’s size and linearly with the dimensionality of the T-Basis. In neural network compression experiments, the method achieves high compression with performance decreases the authors describe as acceptable. Their analysis of memory and operation requirements further supports their conclusion that T-Basis networks are suited to both training and inference under resource constraints, including use on edge devices.
summary.tldr: T-Basis compactly represents neural network tensors through shared Tensor Ring components, achieving high compression with performance drops the authors describe as acceptable.

title: T-Basis: a Compact Representation for Neural Networks

abstract: Generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL) demonstrates tremendous success in practice, especially when combined with neural networks. Different from reinforcement learning, GAIL learns both policy and reward function from expert (human) demonstration. Despite its empirical success, it remains unclear whether GAIL with neural networks converges to the globally optimal solution. The major difﬁculty comes from the nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization structure. To bridge the gap between practice and theory, we analyze a gradient-based algorithm with alternating updates and establish its sublinear convergence to the globally optimal solution. To the best of our knowledge, our analysis establishes the global optimality and convergence rate of GAIL with neural networks for the ﬁrst time.

Despite its empirical success, it remains unclear whether GAIL with neural networks converges to the globally optimal solution. The major difﬁculty comes from the nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization structure. To bridge the gap between practice and theory, we analyze a gradient-based algorithm with alternating updates and establish its sublinear convergence to the globally optimal solution. To the best of our knowledge, our analysis establishes the global optimality and convergence rate of GAIL with neural networks for the ﬁrst time.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial imitation learning, or GAIL, learns a policy and a reward function from expert demonstrations. Neural networks have made this approach successful in practice, but empirical success leaves a theoretical question: can the learning procedure reach a globally optimal solution? This paper addresses that question through analysis of the optimization process.

The difficulty is that the policy and reward are learned through a minimax problem whose neural-network formulation is nonconvex and nonconcave. That structure makes global convergence difficult to establish. The authors analyze a gradient-based algorithm that alternates updates, tracking how the coupled optimization progresses toward its solution.

Their result establishes sublinear convergence to a global optimum for the algorithm they study. It therefore provides both a destination guarantee and a characterization of convergence speed, rather than merely evidence that training performs well in examples. The contribution connects neural GAIL’s practical use with formal optimization theory; it concerns the analyzed procedure, not a blanket guarantee for every neural imitation-learning implementation.
summary.tldr: The paper proves sublinear convergence to a global optimum for an alternating gradient algorithm for neural-network GAIL.

title: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning with Neural Network Parameterization: Global Optimality and Convergence Rate

abstract: The difficulty in specifying rewards for many real-world problems has led to an increased focus on learning rewards from human feedback, such as demonstrations. However, there are often many different reward functions that explain the human feedback, leaving agents with uncertainty over what the true reward function is. While most policy optimization approaches handle this uncertainty by optimizing for expected performance, many applications demand risk-averse behavior. We derive a novel policy gradient-style robust optimization approach, PG-BROIL, that optimizes a soft-robust objective that balances expected performance and risk. To the best of our knowledge, PG-BROIL is the first policy optimization algorithm robust to a distribution of reward hypotheses which can scale to continuous MDPs. Results suggest that PG-BROIL can produce a family of behaviors ranging from risk-neutral to risk-averse and outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning algorithms when learning from ambiguous demonstrations by hedging against uncertainty, rather than seeking to uniquely identify the demonstrator’s reward function.

paragraphs: Demonstrations often leave several reward functions consistent with the observed behavior. An imitation learner therefore faces uncertainty about what should be rewarded, even after observing human feedback. Optimizing only expected performance across those possibilities may be unsuitable when the application calls for behavior that is more cautious about unfavorable outcomes.

The paper introduces PG-BROIL, a policy-gradient-style method that optimizes a soft-robust objective balancing expected performance and risk. It works with a distribution of reward hypotheses, allowing a policy to hedge across plausible explanations of the demonstrations. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first policy optimization algorithm with this kind of reward-distribution robustness that scales to continuous Markov decision processes.

The results suggest that PG-BROIL can generate a range of behaviors from risk-neutral to risk-averse. They also suggest advantages over leading imitation-learning algorithms when demonstrations are ambiguous. The central idea is to make uncertainty part of policy optimization, so useful behavior need not depend on uniquely recovering the demonstrator’s reward function.
summary.tldr: PG-BROIL balances expected performance and risk across uncertain reward hypotheses, with results suggesting benefits for imitation from ambiguous demonstrations.

title: Policy Gradient Bayesian Robust Optimization for Imitation Learning

abstract: A discriminatively trained neural net classifier can fit the training data perfectly if all information about its input other than class membership has been discarded prior to the output layer. Surprisingly, past research has discovered that some extraneous visual detail remains in the unnormalized logits. This finding is based on inversion techniques that map deep embeddings back to images. We explore this phenomenon further using a novel synthesis of methods, yielding a feedforward inversion model that produces remarkably high fidelity reconstructions, qualitatively superior to those of past efforts. When applied to an adversarially robust classifier model, the reconstructions contain sufficient local detail and global structure that they might be confused with the original image in a quick glance, and the object category can clearly be gleaned from the reconstruction. Our approach is based on BigGAN (Brock, 2019), with conditioning on logits instead of one-hot class labels. We use our reconstruction model as a tool for exploring the nature of representations, including: the influence of model architecture and training objectives (specifically robust losses), the forms of invariance that networks achieve, representational differences between correctly and incorrectly classified images, and the effects of manipulating logits and images. We believe that our method can inspire future investigations into the nature of information flow in a neural net and can provide diagnostics for improving discriminative models. We provide pre-trained models and visualizations at \url{https://sites.google.com/view/understanding-invariance/home}.

paragraphs: A classifier can fit its training labels even if it discards all input information unrelated to class membership before its output layer. Yet earlier inversion work found that unnormalized output scores, or logits, retain additional visual detail. This paper develops a feedforward reconstruction model to investigate how much information remains and what it reveals about learned representations.

The model builds on BigGAN, conditioning image generation on logits instead of one-hot class labels. The authors report high-fidelity reconstructions that are qualitatively better than previous efforts. For an adversarially robust classifier, the reconstructions preserve enough local detail and global structure to potentially resemble the original image at a quick glance, with recognizable object categories.

The reconstruction model becomes a tool for studying architecture, robust training objectives, and the forms of invariance classifiers acquire. The authors also examine differences between correctly and incorrectly classified images and the effects of changing logits or inputs. These investigations demonstrate the method’s diagnostic use, while its potential to guide future model improvements is presented as a prospect.
summary.tldr: A BigGAN-based inversion model reconstructs images from classifier logits to investigate retained visual information and learned invariance.

title: Understanding Invariance via Feedforward Inversion of Discriminatively Trained Classifiers

abstract: The focus of disentanglement approaches has been on identifying independent factors of variation in data. However, the causal variables underlying real-world observations are often not statistically independent. In this work, we bridge the gap to real-world scenarios by analyzing the behavior of the most prominent disentanglement approaches on correlated data in a large-scale empirical study (including 4260 models). We show and quantify that systematically induced correlations in the dataset are being learned and reflected in the latent representations, which has implications for downstream applications of disentanglement such as fairness. We also demonstrate how to resolve these latent correlations, either using weak supervision during training or by post-hoc correcting a pre-trained model with a small number of labels.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning has largely focused on identifying independent sources of variation. Real-world causal variables, however, can be statistically correlated. This paper studies what happens when prominent disentanglement methods encounter such correlations, examining whether the dependencies in the training data become dependencies in the learned latent representations.

The authors conduct an empirical study involving 4,260 models and systematically introduce correlations into datasets. They show and quantify that the models learn these correlations and reflect them in their latent representations. This matters for downstream applications such as fairness because the learned representation carries relationships present in the data rather than automatically separating them into independent factors.

The paper also demonstrates two ways to resolve latent correlations using supervision. One introduces weak supervision during training; the other corrects an already trained model using a small number of labels. The findings connect the behavior of disentanglement methods on correlated data with practical interventions available both during learning and after a model has been trained.
summary.tldr: A large empirical study finds that disentanglement models absorb dataset correlations and demonstrates supervision-based ways to resolve them.

title: On Disentangled Representations Learned from Correlated Data

abstract: Data-driven approaches to modeling physical systems fail to generalize to unseen systems that share the same general dynamics with the learning domain, but correspond to different physical contexts. We propose a new framework for this key problem, context-informed dynamics adaptation (CoDA), which takes into account the distributional shift across systems for fast and efficient adaptation to new dynamics. CoDA leverages multiple environments, each associated to a different dynamic, and learns to condition the dynamics model on contextual parameters, specific to each environment. The conditioning is performed via a hypernetwork, learned jointly with a context vector from observed data. The proposed formulation constrains the search hypothesis space for fast adaptation and better generalization across environments with few samples. We theoretically motivate our approach and show state-of-the-art generalization results on a set of nonlinear dynamics, representative of a variety of application domains. We also show, on these systems, that new system parameters can be inferred from context vectors with minimal supervision.

paragraphs: A learned model of a physical system may struggle when a new system follows similar general dynamics under different physical conditions. This paper addresses that transfer problem with context-informed dynamics adaptation, or CoDA. It aims to adapt efficiently using only a few observations from the new environment.

CoDA learns across multiple environments, each with its own dynamics and contextual parameters. A hypernetwork conditions the dynamics model on a context vector, with both learned jointly from observations. The formulation constrains the space of candidate models during adaptation. This restriction is intended to make it easier to find suitable dynamics from limited data while sharing useful structure across environments.

The authors provide a theoretical motivation and report state-of-the-art generalization on a collection of nonlinear dynamical systems spanning different application domains. On those systems, they also show that physical system parameters can be inferred from the learned context vectors with minimal supervision. Thus, the context representation supports both adaptation and extraction of information about the system.
summary.tldr: CoDA uses learned environment contexts to adapt dynamics models to new physical systems from few observations.

title: Generalizing to New Physical Systems via Context-Informed Dynamics Model

abstract: This paper is in the field of stochastic Multi-Armed Bandits (MABs), i.e., those sequential selection techniques able to learn online using only the feedback given by the chosen option (a.k.a. arm). We study a particular case of the rested and restless bandits in which the arms’ expected payoff is monotonically non-decreasing. This characteristic allows designing specifically crafted algorithms that exploit the regularity of the payoffs to provide tight regret bounds. We design an algorithm for the rested case (R-ed-UCB) and one for the restless case (R-less-UCB), providing a regret bound depending on the properties of the instance and, under certain circumstances, of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{\frac{2}{3}})$. We empirically compare our algorithms with state-of-the-art methods for non-stationary MABs over several synthetically generated tasks and an online model selection problem for a real-world dataset. Finally, using synthetic and real-world data, we illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches compared with state-of-the-art algorithms for the non-stationary bandits.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly selects an option and receives feedback only for that choice. This paper studies a changing-reward setting in which each option's expected payoff never decreases. That monotonicity is useful structure: although rewards are non-stationary, their evolution is more constrained than arbitrary changes over time.

The authors design separate algorithms for rested and restless versions of this setting, called R-ed-UCB and R-less-UCB. Their regret guarantees depend on properties of the particular problem instance. Under certain circumstances, the regret grows on the order of the time horizon raised to two-thirds, up to logarithmic factors. The qualification matters because that rate is not stated for every instance.

Experiments compare the algorithms with state-of-the-art non-stationary bandit methods on synthetic tasks and an online model-selection problem using a real-world dataset. The results illustrate the effectiveness of exploiting rising expected payoffs. The contribution combines algorithms tailored to this reward structure with instance-sensitive guarantees and empirical evidence across both constructed tasks and a practical selection problem.
summary.tldr: Algorithms for rested and restless rising bandits exploit non-decreasing expected rewards to obtain instance-dependent regret guarantees.

title: Stochastic Rising Bandits

abstract: We consider the problem of audio voice separation for binaural applications, such as earphones and hearing aids. While today’s neural networks perform remarkably well (separating 4+ sources with 2 microphones) they assume a known or fixed maximum number of sources, K. Moreover, today’s models are trained in a supervised manner, using training data synthesized from generic sources, environments, and human head shapes. This paper intends to relax both these constraints at the expense of a slight alteration in the problem definition. We observe that, when a received mixture contains too many sources, it is still helpful to separate them by region, i.e., isolating signal mixtures from each conical sector around the user’s head. This requires learning the fine-grained spatial properties of each region, including the signal distortions imposed by a person’s head. We propose a two-stage self-supervised framework in which overheard voices from earphones are pre-processed to extract relatively clean personalized signals, which are then used to train a region-wise separation model. Results show promising performance, underscoring the importance of personalization over a generic supervised approach. (audio samples available at our project website: https://uiuc-earable-computing.github.io/binaural). We believe this result could help real-world applications in selective hearing, noise cancellation, and audio augmented reality.

paragraphs: Voice-separation systems commonly assume a known or fixed maximum number of speakers and learn from supervised mixtures built with generic conditions. This paper changes the target to relax both constraints. Instead of requiring an individual output for every voice, it separates mixtures by conical regions around the listener’s head. A region may therefore still contain multiple speakers.

The proposed two-stage framework learns from overheard voices captured through earphones. First, it extracts relatively clean signals personalized to the listener. It then uses those signals to train a model for separating sound by region. This process aims to learn fine spatial distinctions, including the sound distortions introduced by the individual’s head shape.

Results are described as promising and emphasize the value of personalization compared with a generic supervised approach. The change in task definition is consequential: spatial separation can remain useful when there are too many voices to isolate individually. The authors suggest potential applications in selective hearing, noise cancellation, and audio augmented reality, presenting those uses as possibilities rather than established deployment outcomes.
summary.tldr: A personalized self-supervised system separates voices by spatial region, relaxing fixed-speaker-count assumptions by allowing each output to contain a regional mixture.

title: Learning to Separate Voices by Spatial Regions

abstract: Recent work has shown that offline reinforcement learning (RL) can be formulated as a sequence modeling problem (Chen et al., 2021; Janner et al., 2021) and solved via approaches similar to large-scale language modeling. However, any practical instantiation of RL also involves an online component, where policies pretrained on passive offline datasets are finetuned via task-specific interactions with the environment. We propose Online Decision Transformers (ODT), an RL algorithm based on sequence modeling that blends offline pretraining with online finetuning in a unified framework. Our framework uses sequence-level entropy regularizers in conjunction with autoregressive modeling objectives for sample-efficient exploration and finetuning. Empirically, we show that ODT is competitive with the state-of-the-art in absolute performance on the D4RL benchmark but shows much more significant gains during the finetuning procedure.

paragraphs: Sequence modeling provides a way to learn reinforcement learning policies from previously collected data. This paper addresses the next stage: improving such a policy through new interactions with its environment. Online Decision Transformer, or ODT, brings offline pretraining and online fine-tuning into one sequence-modeling framework.

The method combines autoregressive modeling objectives with entropy regularization at the sequence level. These regularizers support exploration during online interaction, while the modeling objective maintains the sequence-based approach used for learning from existing data. The goal is to make the transition from passive data to active experience sample-efficient and to use new interactions effectively for policy improvement.

On the D4RL benchmark, ODT achieves absolute performance competitive with state-of-the-art methods and exhibits substantially larger gains during fine-tuning. Those are related but distinct findings: the final performance is competitive, and the improvement obtained through the online phase is particularly strong. The results support extending sequence-based reinforcement learning beyond offline datasets into a unified process that continues learning from task-specific environmental feedback.
summary.tldr: Online Decision Transformer combines offline sequence-model pretraining with entropy-regularized online learning, producing strong fine-tuning gains on D4RL.

title: Online Decision Transformer

abstract: We consider the problem of subset selection where one is given multiple rankings of items and the goal is to select the highest "quality" subset. Score functions from the multiwinner voting literature have been used to aggregate rankings into quality scores for subsets. We study this setting of subset selection problems when, in addition, rankings may contain systemic or unconscious biases toward a group of items. For a general model of input rankings and biases, we show that requiring the selected subset to satisfy group fairness constraints can improve the quality of the selection with respect to unbiased rankings. Importantly, we show that for fairness constraints to be effective, different multiwinner score functions may require a drastically different number of rankings: While for some functions, fairness constraints need an exponential number of rankings to recover a close-to-optimal solution, for others, this dependency is only polynomial. This result relies on a novel notion of "smoothness" of submodular functions in this setting that quantifies how well a function can "correctly" assess the quality of items in the presence of bias. The results in this paper can be used to guide the choice of multiwinner score functions for the subset selection setting considered here; we additionally provide a tool to empirically enable this.

paragraphs: Selecting a group of items from several rankings becomes difficult when those rankings contain systematic or unconscious group bias. This paper studies selection rules drawn from multiwinner voting, where a score measures the quality of an entire subset. It asks whether group fairness constraints can improve selection quality relative to unbiased rankings.

Under a general model of rankings and bias, the authors show that such constraints can help. However, their effectiveness depends strongly on the scoring function. Some functions require exponentially many rankings for fairness-constrained selection to recover a nearly optimal subset, while others need only polynomially many.

The main implication is that choosing fairness constraints and choosing the underlying scoring function are closely connected decisions.
summary.tldr: Fairness constraints can improve selection from biased rankings, but the scoring function can change the required number of rankings from polynomial to exponential.

title: Subset Selection Based On Multiple Rankings in the Presence of Bias: Effectiveness of Fairness Constraints for Multiwinner Voting Score Functions

abstract: We consider a deep matrix factorization model of covariance matrices trained with the Bures-Wasserstein distance. While recent works have made advances in the study of the optimization problem for overparametrized low-rank matrix approximation, much emphasis has been placed on discriminative settings and the square loss. In contrast, our model considers another type of loss and connects with the generative setting. We characterize the critical points and minimizers of the Bures-Wasserstein distance over the space of rank-bounded matrices. The Hessian of this loss at low-rank matrices can theoretically blow up, which creates challenges to analyze convergence of gradient optimization methods. We establish convergence results for gradient flow using a smooth perturbative version of the loss as well as convergence results for finite step size gradient descent under certain assumptions on the initial weights.

paragraphs: This paper studies a generative model that represents covariance matrices through a deep matrix factorisation. Training compares matrices using the Bures-Wasserstein distance. This changes the optimisation problem from the squared-loss, discriminative settings that have received much of the attention in earlier work on overparameterised low-rank approximation.

The authors characterise critical points and minimisers of this distance when matrices have a bounded rank. Such a characterisation helps explain the landscape through which a training algorithm moves. A central complication is that the Hessian, which describes the loss's local curvature, can become unbounded at low-rank matrices. This makes convergence analysis difficult precisely where low-rank modelling is relevant.

The paper establishes convergence results for gradient flow using a smooth, perturbed version of the loss. It also gives convergence results for gradient descent with a finite step size under assumptions on the initial weights. These results provide a theoretical account of training in this generative setting while retaining the qualifications about smoothing and initialisation that make the guarantees possible.
summary.tldr: The paper characterises Bures-Wasserstein optimisation for deep covariance factorisation and establishes convergence results with smoothing or initial-weight assumptions.

title: Critical Points and Convergence Analysis of Generative Deep Linear Networks Trained with Bures-Wasserstein Loss

abstract: Algorithms for safely improving policies are important to deploy reinforcement learning approaches in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose an algorithm, called MCTS-SPIBB, that computes safe policy improvement online using a Monte Carlo Tree Search based strategy. We theoretically prove that the policy generated by MCTS-SPIBB converges, as the number of simulations grows, to the optimal safely improved policy generated by Safe Policy Improvement with Baseline Bootstrapping (SPIBB), a popular algorithm based on policy iteration. Moreover, our empirical analysis performed on three standard benchmark domains shows that MCTS-SPIBB scales to significantly larger problems than SPIBB because it computes the policy online and locally, i.e., only in the states actually visited by the agent.

paragraphs: Safe policy improvement seeks to improve a reinforcement learning policy while retaining a safety relationship to a baseline. This paper develops MCTS-SPIBB, which applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to compute such improvements online. Its purpose is to make the SPIBB approach usable in larger problems by concentrating computation where the agent needs decisions.

The key change is local planning. MCTS-SPIBB computes policy decisions in states the agent actually visits, using simulations to guide the search. This differs operationally from the policy-iteration approach underlying SPIBB and reduces the need to compute a policy across a much larger collection of states.

The authors prove that, as the number of simulations grows, the generated policy converges to the optimal safely improved policy produced by SPIBB. This is a convergence statement about increasing search effort. Experiments on three standard benchmark domains show that the method scales to significantly larger problems than SPIBB, supporting online, local computation as a practical route to scaling the same safe-improvement objective.
summary.tldr: MCTS-SPIBB scales safe policy improvement through local online search that converges to SPIBB's optimal safely improved policy as simulations increase.

title: Scalable Safe Policy Improvement via Monte Carlo Tree Search

abstract: Denoising diffusion models (DDMs) have recently attracted increasing attention by showing impressive synthesis quality. DDMs are built on a diffusion process that pushes data to the noise distribution and the models learn to denoise. In this paper, we establish the interpretation of DDMs in terms of image restoration (IR). Integrating IR literature allows us to use an alternative objective and diverse forward processes, not confining to the diffusion process. By imposing prior knowledge on the loss function grounded on MAP-based estimation, we eliminate the need for the expensive sampling of DDMs. Also, we propose a multi-scale training, which improves the performance compared to the diffusion process, by taking advantage of the flexibility of the forward process. Experimental results demonstrate that our model improves the quality and efficiency of both training and inference. Furthermore, we show the applicability of our model to inverse problems. We believe that our framework paves the way for designing a new type of flexible general generative model.
