paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce memorized training images, raising privacy and intellectual-property concerns. Some mitigation methods remove weights thought to trigger a particular reproduction. This paper examines the assumption behind that strategy: that memorization can be isolated in a localized set of model weights.

The authors show that small changes to the text embeddings of previously mitigated prompts can bring image replication back after pruning. They also find replication triggers distributed across embedding space, different internal activations for embeddings that reproduce the same image, and disagreement between pruning methods about which weights are responsible. Together, these observations provide multiple indications that memorization is not inherently local.

The paper then demonstrates more robust mitigation through adversarial fine-tuning that bypasses the locality assumption. Its significance is that suppressing a known trigger may leave other routes to the same memorized image intact. The findings support evaluating mitigation beyond its original prompts and developing methods that address the broader behavior revealed by embedding perturbations.
summary.tldr: Small text-embedding changes can restore image replication after pruning, challenging localized accounts of diffusion-model memorization.

title: Finding DoRI: Discovery of Retained Images in Diffusion Models

abstract: We develop a theory of intelligent agency grounded in probabilistic modeling for neural models. Agents are represented as outcome distributions with epistemic utility given by log score, and compositions are defined through weighted logarithmic pooling that strictly improves every member’s welfare. We prove that strict unanimity is impossible under linear pooling or in binary outcome spaces, but possible with three or more outcomes. Our framework admits recursive structure via cloning invariance, continuity, and openness, while tilt-based analysis rules out trivial duplication. Finally, we formalize an agentic alignment phenomenon in LLMs using our theory: eliciting a benevolent persona ("Luigi”) induces an antagonistic counterpart ("Waluigi”), while a manifest-then-suppress Waluigi strategy yields strictly larger first-order misalignment reduction than pure Luigi reinforcement alone. These results clarify how developing a principled mathematical framework for how subagents can coalesce into coherent higher-level entities provides novel implications for alignment in agentic AI systems.

paragraphs: This paper develops a mathematical account of agency within neural models. It represents agents as probability distributions over outcomes and evaluates their epistemic utility using a logarithmic score. The central question is how such agents can combine into a larger entity while strictly improving every constituent’s welfare under that formal definition.

The framework uses weighted logarithmic pooling to define compositions. The authors prove that strict unanimous improvement is impossible with linear pooling or with only two possible outcomes, but possible with three or more outcomes. Cloning invariance, continuity, and openness support recursive compositions, while a tilt-based analysis excludes trivial duplication. These results identify structural conditions relevant to the proposed theory of collective agency.

The authors then formalize an alignment phenomenon involving benevolent and antagonistic language-model personas, called Luigi and Waluigi. Within their theory, eliciting the benevolent persona induces an antagonistic counterpart, and manifesting then suppressing that counterpart gives a strictly greater first-order reduction in misalignment than reinforcing Luigi alone. This is a theoretical comparison within the framework.
summary.tldr: The paper models agents as outcome distributions, characterizes mutually beneficial composition, and derives a theoretical comparison of persona-based alignment strategies.

title: Probabilistic Modeling of Latent Agentic Substructures in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Learning from real-world data is frequently hindered by the compound challenge of long-tailed class distributions and noisy annotations. Existing methods partially address these issues but typically ignore the non-uniform impact of label noise across classes, resulting in ineffective correction for tail classes and over-regularization for head classes. To address this issue, we propose Class-Adaptive Rectification with Experts (CARE), a parameter-efficient framework that leverages three complementary supervision sources from vision-language models (VLM): observed noisy labels, VLM text embeddings, and visual features. CARE introduces a class-adaptive expert consensus mechanism that enforces stricter agreement for tail classes and more permissive agreement for head classes based on class frequency. By aggregating high-confidence predictions across these sources, CARE filters unreliable signals and recalibrates class distributions, yielding more reliable rectification under long-tailed distributions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that CARE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 3.0% performance gains. The source code is available at https://github.com/qwq123-study/CARE.

paragraphs: Training data often contain both incorrect labels and unequal numbers of examples across classes. These problems interact: a correction rule that works for common classes may provide poor guidance for rare ones. CARE addresses this interaction by making the level of agreement required for label correction depend on class frequency.

The parameter-efficient framework combines three supervision sources: the observed labels, text embeddings from a vision-language model, and visual features. Its expert consensus mechanism requires stricter agreement for rare classes and allows more permissive agreement for common classes. It aggregates high-confidence predictions across these sources to filter unreliable information and recalibrate the class distribution used for correction.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with reported performance gains of up to 3.0%. The central finding is that correction benefits from accounting for how label noise affects classes differently. CARE uses agreement among complementary signals to make this adjustment, tying its correction policy to the imbalance already present in the data.
summary.tldr: CARE adapts agreement requirements to class frequency to improve label correction when training data are both imbalanced and noisy.

title: CARE: Class-Adaptive Expert Consensus for Reliable Learning with Long-Tailed Noisy Labels

abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) compresses a large training set into a small synthetic set for efficient training, but most DD methods optimize only clean accuracy and leave robustness uncontrolled. Recent robust DD methods improve robustness, yet they often suffer from a poor accuracy–robustness trade-off because they (i) treat all adversarially perturbed examples uniformly, despite robust risk being dominated by near-zero robust margins, and (ii) do not explicitly increase inter-class separation in the decision boundary where attacks concentrate. We present Contrastive Curriculum for Robust Dataset Distillation (C$^2$R), a framework that couples an attack-aware curriculum with a contrastive robustness objective. From a robust-margin perspective, we derive a perturbation score that approximates each sample’s robust hinge, enabling a curriculum that prioritizes the smallest-margin adversaries that most directly drive robust error. In parallel, a class-balanced contrastive robustness loss enforces adversarial invariance while explicitly widening boundary separation across classes. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, and multiple ImageNet-1K subsets under six attacks show that C$^2$R achieves the best robust accuracy, outperforming prior robust DD by 2.8% on average.

paragraphs: A small synthetic dataset can support good accuracy on ordinary inputs without making the trained model robust to adversarial changes. This paper argues that robust distillation should distinguish between adversarial examples and explicitly improve separation between classes near decision boundaries. Treating every perturbed example equally can allocate attention poorly.

The proposed C²R framework combines an attack-aware curriculum with a contrastive robustness objective. A perturbation score approximates each sample’s robust hinge and prioritizes adversaries with the smallest robust margins—the examples most directly associated with robust error. Alongside this curriculum, a class-balanced contrastive loss encourages stability under attacks and greater separation between classes at their boundaries.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10/100, Tiny-ImageNet, and several ImageNet-1K subsets under six attacks. The authors report the best robust accuracy among compared methods, outperforming previous robust distillation by 2.8% on average. The findings support coordinating which adversarial examples receive emphasis with how classes are separated, rather than optimizing robustness through an undifferentiated collection of perturbed inputs.
summary.tldr: C²R improves robust dataset distillation by prioritizing vulnerable adversarial examples and increasing separation between classes.

title: Mind Your Margin and Boundary: Are Your Distilled Datasets Truly Robust?

abstract: Safety alignment in large language models is typically evaluated under isolated queries, yet real-world use is inherently multi-turn. Although multi-turn jailbreaks are empirically effective, the structure of conversational safety failure remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we study safety failures from a state-space perspective and show that many multi-turn safety failures in current safety-aligned language models arise from contextual state evolution, a regime that is not fully captured by isolated prompt-level analyses alone. We introduce STAR, a state-oriented diagnostic framework that treats dialogue history as a state transition operator and enables controlled analysis of safety behavior along interaction trajectories. Rather than optimizing attack strength, STAR provides a principled probe of how aligned models traverse the safety boundary under autoregressive conditioning. Across multiple frontier language models, we find that systems which appear robust under static evaluation can undergo rapid and reproducible safety collapse under structured multi-turn interaction. Mechanistic analysis reveals monotonic drift away from refusal-related representations and abrupt phase transitions induced by role-conditioned context. Together, these findings motivate viewing language model safety as a dynamic, state-dependent process defined over conversational trajectories.

paragraphs: A model's response to an isolated prompt may not reveal how safely it behaves after an extended conversation. This paper examines safety through the evolution of conversational state. It argues that many multi-turn failures arise from changing context, which prompt-level analysis alone does not fully capture.

STAR is a diagnostic framework that treats dialogue history as an operator changing the model's state. It enables controlled study of safety behavior along interaction trajectories. The purpose is to probe how an aligned model crosses a safety boundary under autoregressive conditioning, rather than to optimize the strength of an attack.

They establish a failure pattern in the studied settings, rather than implying that every extended conversation causes collapse.
summary.tldr: STAR shows how evolving conversational context can produce reproducible safety failures in models that appear robust on isolated prompts.

title: State-Dependent Safety Failures in Multi-Turn Language Model Interaction

abstract: Reconstructing unified continuous dynamics from sparse, non-contiguous, and unpaired point cloud snapshots remains a fundamental challenge in spatiotemporal analysis for computer vision and developmental biology. Existing methods, including scene flow and Optimal Transport-based approaches, are limited either by explicit reliance on point-wise correspondences or by cumulative errors from frame-to-frame propagation and temporal discontinuity, and limited ability to model multi-attribute dynamics such as gene expression and population changes. We propose FlowCloud, a variational Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (Neural ODE) generative framework. FlowCloud aggregates information from all observed time points into a joint latent representation that initializes a Neural ODE $z(t)$ enabling continuous spatiotemporal evolution modeling while mitigating propagation-induced errors and preserving temporal consistency. Training is performed without predefined correspondences using a multi-faceted objective with complementary roles: Sinkhorn distance for global distribution alignment, Chamfer distance for local geometric consistency, trajectory regularization to encourage smooth and physically plausible dynamics, and supervised losses for multi-attribute prediction. Experiments on human motion and developmental biology datasets demonstrate improved interpolation accuracy and promising short-term extrapolation performance. By unifying geometry, attributes, and population dynamics within a continuous latent framework, FlowCloud offers a novel and robust solution for continuous dynamic reconstruction from unstructured spatiotemporal observations.

paragraphs: FlowCloud reconstructs continuous dynamics from sparse point-cloud snapshots that may be separated in time and lack point-to-point matches. This setting arises in human motion and developmental biology. Following individual points or repeatedly propagating estimates between adjacent frames can be problematic when correspondences are unavailable and propagation errors accumulate.

The method combines all observed time points into a joint latent representation that initializes a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation. This provides a continuous evolving state. Training uses several complementary signals: Sinkhorn distance aligns overall distributions, Chamfer distance supports local geometric agreement, trajectory regularization encourages smooth and physically plausible movement, and supervised losses train predictions of additional attributes.

The framework therefore represents geometry together with attributes and population changes, including the kinds of dynamics relevant to gene expression. Experiments on human motion and developmental biology datasets report better interpolation and promising short-term extrapolation. These findings support recovering intermediate states from disconnected observations and extending predictions a short distance beyond them, while the shared continuous representation helps maintain temporal consistency.
summary.tldr: FlowCloud learns continuous geometry, attribute, and population dynamics from sparse snapshots without predefined point correspondences.

title: FlowCloud: Learning Continuous Spatiotemporal Dynamics from Unpaired Sparse Point Cloud Snapshots

abstract: The rapid rise of vlogs as a personalized storytelling medium has created a demand for automated systems to evaluate and refine vlog editing plans. However, vlog assessment is highly subjective and remains challenging due to a lack of standardized criteria, dataset and benchmark, and effective reward models. To address these challenges, we define a comprehensive vlog evaluation framework guided by professional vlog creators and product managers, establishing a taxonomy of six key dimensions, i.e., Creativity, Consistency, Concept Design, Cinematography, Narration, and Pacing. Subsequently, we curate a large-scale dataset of 100k vlog edits and a dedicated benchmark, VRMBench, to evaluate the vlog rewarding capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Finally, we present VlogReward, a robust vlog reward model that can provide both fine-grained multi-dimensional scores and actionable feedback for iterative refinement. Technically, we enhance the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework by introducing an adjustable inter-group comparison reward, which mitigates the "direction blindness" issue of standard GRPO and enables the model to better distinguish varied-quality edits. VlogReward achieves state-of-the-art results that significantly outperform existing MLLMs, including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro. We hope that our study can help vlog creators and foster automated vlog evaluation and refinement systems.

paragraphs: Evaluating a vlog edit involves several subjective judgments, making automated feedback difficult to standardize. The paper develops an evaluation framework with guidance from professional creators and product managers. It separates quality into six dimensions: creativity, consistency, concept design, cinematography, narration, and pacing.

The authors assemble a dataset of 100K vlog edits and introduce VRMBench to assess how well multimodal language models judge editing quality. Their VlogReward model provides scores across the six dimensions alongside actionable feedback for iterative improvement. Its training modifies Group Relative Policy Optimization with an adjustable reward for comparisons between groups, addressing the standard method’s difficulty distinguishing the direction of quality differences.

VlogReward achieves state-of-the-art results and significantly outperforms evaluated multimodal models, including GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro. The contribution links a defined evaluation vocabulary, a dataset and benchmark, and a reward model trained to distinguish varied-quality edits. This makes the intended feedback more useful for refinement: creators can receive judgments about particular aspects of an edit together with guidance for improving it.
summary.tldr: VlogReward evaluates six dimensions of vlog editing and provides actionable feedback using a specialized dataset and modified reward training.

title: VlogReward: Learning Multi-Dimensional Evaluation for Vlog Editing

abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) is fundamental to modern AI applications. Most existing solutions optimize query efficiency but fail to align with the practical requirements of modern workloads. In this paper, we outline six critical demands of modern AI applications: high query efficiency, fast indexing, low memory footprint, scalability to high dimensionality, robustness across varying retrieval sizes, and support for online insertions. To satisfy all these demands, we introduce Projection-Augmented Graph (PAG), a new ANNS framework that integrates projection techniques into a graph index. PAG reduces unnecessary exact distance computations through asymmetric comparisons between exact and approximate distances as guided by projection-based statistical tests. Three key components are designed and integrated into the graph index to optimize indexing and searching. Experiments on six modern datasets demonstrate that PAG consistently achieves superior queries per second (QPS)-recall performance—up to 5x faster than HNSW—while offering fast indexing speed and moderate memory footprint. PAG remains robust as dimensionality and retrieval size increase and naturally supports online insertions. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/KejingLu-810/PAG/.

paragraphs: Approximate nearest neighbor search finds close matches without exhaustively comparing a query with every stored item. This paper treats search speed as one part of a broader engineering problem: useful indexes must also be quick to build, economical in memory, adaptable to high dimensions and different result counts, and able to accept new items.

Projection-Augmented Graph, or PAG, combines a graph index with projection methods. Its central mechanism uses statistical tests based on projections to compare exact and approximate distances asymmetrically. These comparisons reduce unnecessary exact distance calculations. Three components integrate that mechanism into index construction and searching, addressing both stages of the retrieval process.

Experiments on six datasets report a better tradeoff between queries per second and recall, with speedups reaching five times those of HNSW. PAG also provides fast indexing and a moderate memory footprint, remains robust as dimensions and requested result counts increase, and supports online insertions. The contribution is therefore a combination of retrieval performance and operational flexibility across the tested workloads.
summary.tldr: PAG uses projection-based statistical tests inside a graph index to accelerate retrieval while supporting practical indexing and update requirements.

title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for Modern AI: A Projection-Augmented Graph Approach

abstract: The stochastic Polyak step size (SPS) has proven to be a promising choice for stochastic gradient descent (SGD), delivering competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art methods on smooth convex and non-convex optimization problems, including deep neural network training. However, extensions of this approach to non-smooth settings remain in their early stages, often relying on interpolation assumptions or requiring knowledge of the optimal solution. In this work, we propose a novel SPS variant, Safeguarded SPS (SPS$_{safe}$), for the stochastic subgradient method, and provide rigorous convergence guarantees for non-smooth convex optimization with no need for strong assumptions. We further incorporate momentum into the update rule, yielding equally tight theoretical results. Comprehensive experiments on convex benchmarks and deep neural networks corroborate our theory: the proposed step size achieves competitive performance to existing adaptive baselines and exhibits stable behavior across a wide range of problem settings. Finally, in the context of deep neural network training, the gradient norms under our step size do not collapse to (near) zero, indicating robustness to vanishing gradients.

paragraphs: Stochastic Polyak step sizes adapt the size of optimization updates and have performed well on smooth problems. Extending them to non-smooth objectives is harder: existing approaches often depend on interpolation assumptions or information about the optimal solution. The paper introduces Safeguarded SPS for stochastic subgradient optimization to address this setting.

The authors prove convergence guarantees for non-smooth convex optimization without the strong assumptions motivating their critique of earlier extensions. They also add momentum to the update rule and obtain equally tight theoretical results. This places the adaptive step-size method and its momentum version within the same analyzed non-smooth optimization setting.

Experiments cover convex benchmarks and deep neural networks. Safeguarded SPS performs competitively with existing adaptive baselines and behaves stably across a wide range of tested problems. During the reported neural-network training, gradient norms do not collapse toward zero, which the authors interpret as evidence of robustness to vanishing gradients. The theoretical guarantees concern non-smooth convex problems, while the neural-network results provide additional empirical support.
summary.tldr: Safeguarded SPS extends adaptive Polyak step sizes to non-smooth optimization with convergence guarantees and stable empirical behavior.

title: Safeguarded Stochastic Polyak Step Sizes for Non-smooth Optimization: Robust Performance Without Small (Sub)Gradients

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity efficiently by selectively routing inputs to a specialized subset of experts. However, input-expert specialization, the core motivation of MoE, critically depends on whether the router is actually aware of input structure. In practice, MoE routing is typically implemented as a shallow linear projection with limited awareness of input representation, which often leads to unstable routing. We propose STAR, a Structure Aware Routing that rethinks MoE routing as a subspace learning problem by augmenting standard learnable routing with an evolving principal subspace that tracks dominant input structure via Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA). By aligning routing decisions directly with input structure, STAR enables stable expert specialization. We evaluate STAR on controlled synthetic setup and large-scale language and vision tasks, where it consistently improves routing quality and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines. Moreover, optional test-time subspace updates further enhance routing robustness and generalization under input distribution shifts. Code is available at https://github.com/psmiz/STAR.

abstract: The proliferation of recursive training on synthetic data can alleviate data scarcity but risks model collapse, where repeated training erodes distributional tails and homogenizes outputs. Data selection is widely viewed as a remedy, yet its reliability depends critically on the reference distribution used by the verifier. We show that in low-resource verification regimes, where each verifier observes only a small, fragmented, and biased slice of the target manifold, selection itself becomes biased. This situation naturally arises in low-resource data silos such as healthcare consortia or proprietary financial institutions, where raw data cannot be pooled and local references are inherently incomplete. As a result, selection preferentially retains samples aligned with the local manifold while pruning globally relevant tail modes, turning from a safeguard against collapse into a mechanism that precipitates it. We theoretically prove that such siloed selection accelerates collapse and induces power-law diversity decay. As an initial mitigation, we construct Wasserstein proxy references from multiple silos without sharing raw data. Empirical results confirm that local-reference selection fails on skewed distributions, whereas collaborative proxy references mitigate diversity degradation, suggesting that recursive synthetic-data pipelines require particular caution when real-data coverage is fragmented or scarce.

paragraphs: Repeatedly training models on synthetic data can gradually remove rare patterns and make outputs more uniform. Selecting apparently good synthetic examples is often proposed as a safeguard. This paper shows why that safeguard can fail when the verifier’s real-data reference is small, biased, and fragmented across separate institutions.

A verifier with only a local reference preferentially retains examples resembling its own slice of the distribution. It can reject rare patterns that matter globally but are poorly represented locally. Under the studied siloed-selection setting, the authors prove that selection accelerates collapse and produces power-law diversity decay. The issue arises from the reference used to judge samples, so filtering itself can become part of the collapse mechanism.

Experiments show that local-reference selection fails on skewed distributions, while collaborative proxies reduce diversity degradation. These findings qualify the value of synthetic-data filtering: when real-data coverage is fragmented or scarce, broader reference coverage matters for retaining globally relevant diversity.
summary.tldr: Filtering synthetic data against fragmented local references can accelerate model collapse, while collaborative proxy references mitigate diversity loss.

title: When Sample Selection Bias Precipitates Model Collapse

abstract: Automated “LLM-as-a-Judge" frameworks have become the de facto standard for scalable evaluation across natural language processing. For instance, in safety evaluation, these judges are relied upon to evaluate harmfulness in order to benchmark the robustness of safety against adversarial attacks. However, we show that existing validation protocols fail to account for substantial distribution shifts inherent to red-teaming: diverse victim models exhibit distinct generation styles, attacks distort output patterns, and semantic ambiguity varies significantly across jailbreak scenarios. Through a comprehensive audit using 6642 human-verified labels, we reveal that the unpredictable interaction of these shifts often causes judge performance to degrade to near random chance. This stands in stark contrast to the high human agreement reported in prior work. Crucially, we find that many attacks inflate their success rates by exploiting judge insufficiencies rather than eliciting genuinely harmful content. To enable more reliable evaluation, we propose ReliableBench, a benchmark of behaviors that remain more consistently judgeable, and JudgeStressTest, a dataset designed to expose judge failures.

paragraphs: Safety evaluations often ask a language model to judge whether another model’s response is harmful. This makes large evaluations practical, but the judge must cope with changing response styles, attack-induced distortions, and ambiguous cases. The paper examines whether existing validation practices adequately capture these changes in the material judges encounter.

The authors audit judge behavior using 6,642 human-verified labels. They find that interactions among these distribution shifts often reduce judging performance to near chance, despite previously reported strong agreement with humans. A judge that works well on one collection of responses can therefore provide an unreliable measurement under the different conditions created by adversarial testing.

This affects how attack success should be interpreted: many attacks receive inflated success rates by exploiting weaknesses in evaluation rather than producing genuinely harmful responses. The authors introduce ReliableBench, which emphasizes behaviors that remain more consistently judgeable, and JudgeStressTest, which targets judge failures. Together, these contributions address both the choice of evaluation cases and the reliability of the evaluator.
summary.tldr: An audit finds that distribution shifts can make LLM safety judges perform near chance and inflate reported attack success.

title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Adaptive methods like Adam have become the de facto standard for large-scale vector and Euclidean optimization due to their coordinate-wise adaptation with a second-order nature. More recently, matrix-based spectral optimizers like Muon (Jordan et al., 2024b) show the power of treating weight matrices as matrices rather than long vectors. Linking these is hard because many natural generalizations are not feasible to implement, and we also cannot simply move the Adam adaptation to the matrix spectrum. To address this, we reformulate the AdaGrad update and decompose it into a variance adaptation term and a scale-invariant term. This decoupling produces DeVA (Decoupled Variance Adaptation), a framework that bridges between vector-based variance adaptation and matrix spectral optimization, enabling a seamless transition from Adam to adaptive spectral descent. Extensive experiments across language modeling and image classification demonstrate that DeVA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as Muon and SOAP (Vyas et al., 2024), reducing token usage by around 6.6%. Theoretically, we show that the variance adaptation term effectively improves the blockwise smoothness, facilitating faster convergence.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam adjust updates coordinate by coordinate, while spectral optimizers such as Muon exploit the matrix structure of model weights. Combining these ideas is difficult: natural generalizations can be impractical, and Adam's adaptation cannot simply be transferred to a matrix's spectrum. This paper develops a common framework for the two approaches.

The authors begin by rewriting the AdaGrad update as two components: one that adapts to variance and another that is scale-invariant. Separating these functions yields DeVA, short for Decoupled Variance Adaptation. The framework connects vector-based adaptation with matrix spectral optimization, allowing a transition from Adam-style updates to adaptive spectral descent.

Experiments in language modeling and image classification report consistent improvements over methods including Muon and SOAP, along with a reduction in token usage of around 6.6%. The theoretical analysis shows that the variance adaptation component improves blockwise smoothness, helping explain faster convergence. Together, the results connect an algebraic decomposition of updates to both a convergence argument and observed training benefits.
summary.tldr: DeVA separates variance adaptation from scale-invariant updates to connect Adam-style optimization with adaptive matrix spectral descent.

title: Decoupling Variance and Scale-Invariant Updates in Adaptive Gradient Descent for Unified Vector and Matrix Optimization

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models achieve efficient scaling through sparse expert activation, but often suffer from suboptimal routing decisions due to distribution shifts in deployment. While existing test-time adaptation methods could potentially address these issues, they primarily focus on dense models and require access to external data, limiting their practical applicability to MoE architectures. However, we find that, instead of relying on reference data, we can optimize MoE expert selection on-the-fly based only on input context. As such, we propose a data-free, online test-time framework that continuously adapts MoE routing decisions during text generation without external supervision or data. Our method cycles between two phases: During the prefill stage, and later in regular intervals, we optimize the routing decisions of the model using self-supervision based on the already generated sequence. Then, we generate text as normal, maintaining the modified router until the next adaption. We implement this through lightweight additive vectors that only update router logits in selected layers, maintaining computational efficiency while preventing over-adaptation. The results show consistent performance gains on challenging reasoning tasks while maintaining robustness to context shifts. For example, our method achieves a 5.5% improvement on HumanEval with OLMoE. Furthermore, owing to its plug-and-play property, our method complements existing test-time scaling techniques, e.g., achieving 6% average gains when incorporated with self-consistency on DeepSeek-V2-Lite.

This paper proposes adapting expert selection during text generation using only the current input context and the sequence generated so far. It requires no external reference data or supervision.

summary.tldr: Online router adjustments improve Mixture-of-Experts generation using self-supervision from the current context without external data.

title: Rewiring Experts on the Fly: Continuous Rerouting for Better Online Adaptation in Mixture-of-Expert Models

abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on untrusted hardware entails a risk of weight extraction, which can lead to unauthorized replication and misuse of the model. A practical approach is to leverage Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) and protect model security by obfuscating model weights. However, existing obfuscation schemes struggle to simultaneously provide strong security guarantees and high performance: schemes with security guarantees incur substantial overhead due to frequent TEE interactions, whereas schemes that achieve efficient inference are insecure. We propose SLIM, a secure inference framework that exploits the iterative structure of LLMs to let transformed representations cascade through consecutive obfuscated layers, thereby minimizing interactions with the TEE. SLIM introduces a T-Way Mixing algorithm that performs consecutive inter-vector covering using carefully constructed block-diagonal Householder matrices and combines it with successive random permutations, providing thorough weight obfuscation while keeping TEE-side computation lightweight. Evaluations demonstrate that SLIM provides robust security guarantees and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art obfuscation schemes in terms of performance, delivering up to a $13.80\times$ speedup while preserving fidelity.

paragraphs: Running a language model on untrusted hardware creates a risk that its weights will be extracted. Trusted Execution Environments can help protect obfuscated weights, but frequent interactions with the protected environment can slow inference. SLIM addresses the tension between strong weight protection and efficient execution.

The framework exploits the model’s repeated layer structure so transformed representations can pass through consecutive obfuscated layers. This reduces how often computation must interact with the trusted environment. Its T-Way Mixing algorithm combines successive inter-vector covering with random permutations. Carefully constructed block-diagonal Householder matrices provide the mixing operation while keeping work inside the trusted environment lightweight.

Evaluations report robust security guarantees and speedups of up to 13.80 times over prior state-of-the-art obfuscation schemes while preserving fidelity. The architectural insight is that the cost of protection depends on how transformed data move across layers, as well as on the transformations themselves. By letting those representations continue through multiple layers, SLIM reduces a key source of overhead within its TEE-based inference framework.
summary.tldr: SLIM carries transformed representations across obfuscated layers to protect model weights with fewer TEE interactions and up to 13.80-fold faster inference.

title: SLIM: Secure and Efficient Inference for Large Language Models on Untrusted Devices via TEEs

abstract: Adopting pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in Federated Learning (FL) presents a promising avenue for mitigating data scarcity and heterogeneity. However, existing solutions suffer from high computational complexity or ineffective knowledge aggregation. To address these problems, we propose FedSPA (Federated Adaptation via Semantic-Visual Prototype Alignment). On the client side, FedSPA restricts local optimization to visual prototypes, enabling lightweight personalization. On the server side, we introduce a semantic alignment module that leverages client-uploaded prototypes to minimize a contrastive objective, aligning global semantic prototypes with heterogeneous visual distributions and thereby shifting the paradigm from traditional "learning-to-describe" (optimizing static prompts) to "learning-to-align". Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedSPA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both personalized and global benchmarks, while substantially reducing computational overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/eejiarong/FedSPA-main.

paragraphs: FedSPA addresses how to adapt a pretrained vision-language model across clients whose data are scarce or differ substantially. The central challenge is to support useful local adaptation while combining knowledge across those different visual distributions. The paper identifies computational cost and ineffective aggregation as weaknesses of existing approaches and makes prototypes the main objects being optimized and shared.

On each client, training adjusts only visual prototypes, giving personalization a lightweight target. Clients upload these prototypes to the server. There, a semantic alignment module uses a contrastive objective to bring global semantic prototypes into alignment with the clients’ varied visual distributions. Local visual adaptation and global semantic coordination thus play distinct roles in the same framework.

This changes the adaptation objective from optimizing static descriptive prompts to aligning semantic and visual representations. The reported experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on both personalized and global benchmarks, together with substantially lower computational overhead. The findings suggest that prototype alignment can make shared knowledge useful across heterogeneous clients while retaining the benefits of local specialization.
summary.tldr: FedSPA adapts federated vision-language models through local visual prototypes and global semantic alignment, improving reported performance while reducing computation.

title: Beyond Description: Federated Adaptation via Semantic-Visual Prototype Alignment

abstract: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) enable flexible decoding orders, yet existing samplers remain largely greedy, selecting locally certain tokens without accounting for their downstream effects. We show that this myopia can increase cumulative uncertainty and lead to suboptimal generation. To address this, we propose the Info-Gain Sampler, a training-free decoding method that uses the bidirectional structure of MDMs to balance immediate uncertainty with the information gained over remaining masked positions. Across reasoning, coding, creative writing, and image generation tasks, Info-Gain Sampler consistently outperforms existing MDM samplers, improving average reasoning accuracy by 2.9–11.6 percentage points and achieving a 62.8% average win rate in creative writing. The code is available at https://github.com/yks23/Information-Gain-Sampler.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models can choose the order in which they fill missing positions. Existing samplers often favor tokens that already appear most certain. The paper shows that this local strategy can leave greater uncertainty across the remaining generation, because an easy immediate choice may do little to clarify what comes next.

The Info-Gain Sampler balances uncertainty at the position being filled with the information that choice provides about positions still masked. It uses the model’s bidirectional structure to account for these downstream effects. Because the method is training-free, its contribution lies in changing the decoding procedure rather than learning a new model.

Across reasoning, coding, creative writing, and image generation, the authors report consistent improvements over existing masked-diffusion samplers. Average reasoning accuracy increases by 2.9–11.6 percentage points, and creative-writing comparisons yield a 62.8% average win rate. These findings support treating decoding order as an information-management decision: useful choices can help organize the unresolved parts of an output as well as resolve the current position.
summary.tldr: The training-free Info-Gain Sampler improves masked-diffusion generation by considering how each decoding choice reduces uncertainty in remaining positions.

title: Improving Sampling for Masked Diffusion Models via Information Gain

abstract: Several machine learning models are defined for inputs of any size, such as graphs with different numbers of nodes and point clouds with varying numbers of points. The universality properties of such any-dimensional models remain poorly understood, as universality is traditionally studied for models accepting inputs of a fixed size, defined on a compact subset of their domain. In sharp contrast, any-dimensional models can be viewed as sequences of functions defined on growing-sized inputs, and it is not clear in which sense they can be universal. We develop a systematic approach to establish any-dimensional universality by identifying any-dimensional functions with a unique function that takes inputs in a suitable infinite-dimensional limit space containing inputs of all finite sizes, as well as their limits. Using the symmetries of these inputs and relations between inputs of different sizes, we show that this limit space admits a natural topology with rich families of compact sets on which any-dimensional universality can be established. We illustrate our approach by showing that several existing architectures fail to be universal, and we propose simple modifications that restore universality.

paragraphs: Models for graphs and point clouds often accept inputs of many different sizes. Traditional universality results, however, usually concern approximating functions on compact domains with a fixed input size. This paper asks how to formulate an analogous guarantee for a single model family operating across growing input sizes.

The authors connect a sequence of functions on finite inputs to one uniquely identified function on an infinite-dimensional limit space. That space contains inputs of every finite size together with their limits. Using input symmetries and relationships across sizes, they define a natural topology and identify rich families of compact sets on which universality can be established.

This construction makes expressive capacity across sizes a precise mathematical question. Applying it, the authors show that several existing architectures fail to be universal in this framework and propose simple modifications that restore universality. The contribution therefore combines a way to state the approximation problem with architectural consequences: supporting variable-sized inputs alone does not settle whether a model has the desired approximation power.
summary.tldr: A limit-space framework defines universality across input sizes and exposes architectural gaps that simple modifications can repair.

title: Any-dimensional invariant universality

abstract: Large language models have recently enabled text-to-CAD systems that synthesize parametric CAD programs (e.g., CadQuery) from natural-language prompts. In practice, however, geometric descriptions can be under-specified or internally inconsistent: critical dimensions may be missing and constraints may conflict. However, existing fine-tuned models tend to reactively follow the user’s instructions and hallucinate dimensions when the text is ambiguous. To address this, we propose a proactive agentic framework for text-to-CadQuery generation, named as ProCAD, that resolves specification issues before code synthesis. Our framework pairs a proactive clarifying agent, which audits the prompt and asks targeted clarification questions only when necessary to produce a self-consistent specification, with a CAD coding agent that translates the specification into an executable CadQuery program. We fine-tune the coding agent based on a curated high-quality text-to-CadQuery dataset and train the clarifying agent via agentic SFT on clarification trajectories. Experiments show that proactive clarification significantly improves robustness to ambiguous prompts while keeping interaction overhead low. ProCAD outperforms frontier closed-source models, including Claude Sonnet 4.5, reducing the mean Chamfer distance by 79.9% and lowering the invalidity ratio from 4.8% to 0.9%. Our code and datasets are made publicly available on https://github.com/BoYuanVisionary/Pro-CAD.

paragraphs: Generating a CAD program from a written description becomes difficult when dimensions are missing or geometric constraints contradict one another. A model that immediately writes code may silently invent measurements. ProCAD addresses this problem before code generation by checking whether the requested object has a sufficiently consistent specification.

The system separates clarification from implementation. A clarifying agent audits the description and asks focused questions only when they are needed to resolve specification problems. A coding agent then converts the resulting specification into an executable CadQuery program. summary.tldr: ProCAD asks targeted clarification questions before generating CAD code, improving geometric accuracy and validity on ambiguous requests.

title: Clarify Before You Draw: Proactive Agents for Robust Text-to-CAD Generation

abstract: Deep learning for human sensing on edge systems presents significant potential for smart applications. However, its training and development are hindered by the limited availability of sensor data and resource constraints of edge systems. While transferring pre-trained models to different sensing applications is promising, existing methods often require extensive sensor data and computational resources, resulting in high costs and limited transferability. In this paper, we propose XTransfer, a first-of-its-kind method enabling modality-agnostic, few-shot model transfer with resource-efficient design. XTransfer flexibly uses pre-trained models and transfers knowledge across different modalities by (i) model repairing that safely mitigates modality shift by adapting pre-trained layers with only few sensor data, and (ii) layer recombining that efficiently searches and recombines layers of interest from source models in a layer-wise manner to restructure models. We benchmark various baselines across diverse human sensing datasets spanning different modalities. The results show that XTransfer achieves state-of-the-art performance while significantly reducing the costs of sensor data collection, model training, and edge deployment.

However, its training and development are hindered by the limited availability of sensor data and resource constraints of edge systems. While transferring pre-trained models to different sensing applications is promising, existing methods often require extensive sensor data and computational resources, resulting in high costs and limited transferability. In this paper, we propose XTransfer, a first-of-its-kind method enabling modality-agnostic, few-shot model transfer with resource-efficient design. XTransfer flexibly uses pre-trained models and transfers knowledge across different modalities by (i) model repairing that safely mitigates modality shift by adapting pre-trained layers with only few sensor data, and (ii) layer recombining that efficiently searches and recombines layers of interest from source models in a layer-wise manner to restructure models. We benchmark various baselines across diverse human sensing datasets spanning different modalities. The results show that XTransfer achieves state-of-the-art performance while significantly reducing the costs of sensor data collection, model training, and edge deployment.

paragraphs: Human-sensing applications on edge devices face two linked constraints: collecting sensor data is difficult, and the devices have limited resources. Reusing pretrained models can help, but transfer methods may still demand substantial data and computation. XTransfer is designed to transfer knowledge across sensing modalities using few examples while keeping training and deployment costs low.

The method combines model repairing with layer recombining. Repairing adapts pretrained layers using a small amount of sensor data to mitigate the shift between modalities. Recombining searches for useful layers in source models and assembles them layer by layer into a restructured model. Together, these steps adapt existing knowledge and select how it is organized for the target sensing application.

The authors compare XTransfer with several baselines across human-sensing datasets covering different modalities. They report state-of-the-art performance alongside significant reductions in data-collection, training, and edge-deployment costs. The findings support combining selective adaptation with model restructuring when transfer must work across sensor types under tight resource constraints.
summary.tldr: XTransfer repairs and recombines pretrained layers to transfer human-sensing models across modalities with few examples and lower resource costs.

abstract: Markov logic networks (MLNs) are a statistical relational model that consists of weighted firstorder clauses and generalizes first-order logic and Markov networks. The current state-of-theart algorithm for learning MLN structure follows a top-down paradigm where many potential candidate structures are systematically generated without considering the data and then evaluated using a statistical measure of their fit to the data. Even though this existing algorithm outperforms an impressive array of benchmarks, its greedy search is susceptible to local maxima or plateaus. We present a novel algorithm for learning MLN structure that follows a more bottom-up approach to address this problem. Our algorithm uses a “propositional” Markov network learning method to construct “template” networks that guide the construction of candidate clauses. Our algorithm significantly improves accuracy and learning time over the existing topdown approach in three real-world domains.

paragraphs: Markov logic networks combine weighted logical clauses with probabilistic modeling. Learning their structure means deciding which clauses should be included. The paper examines a weakness of an existing top-down method: it systematically generates many candidate structures before considering the data, then greedily searches according to how well those candidates fit.

Such a search can get stuck at local maxima or plateaus. The proposed bottom-up approach instead uses a propositional Markov network learning method to construct template networks. Those templates guide the creation of candidate clauses, allowing information learned from the data to influence which logical structures are considered.

The authors report significantly improved accuracy and learning time over the existing top-down approach in three real-world domains. These results support changing the way candidates are constructed, as well as evaluating their statistical fit. The contribution is a data-guided route into the structure search, with empirical evidence that this route can produce better models more quickly in the studied domains.
summary.tldr: Data-derived template networks guide bottom-up Markov logic structure learning, improving accuracy and learning time in three real-world domains.

title: Bottom-up learning of Markov logic network structure

abstract: We describe a causal learning method, which employs measuring the strength of statistical dependences in terms of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of kernel-based cross-covariance operators. Following the line of the common faithfulness assumption of constraint-based causal learning, our approach assumes that a variable Z is likely to be a common effect of X and Y , if conditioning on Z increases the dependence between X and Y . Based on this assumption, we collect “votes” for hypothetical causal directions and orient the edges by the majority principle. In most experiments with known causal structures, our method provided plausible results and outperformed the conventional constraint-based PC algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a method for learning causal directions by measuring how strongly variables depend on one another. Its dependence measure uses kernel-based cross-covariance operators and their Hilbert-Schmidt norm. In plain language, the method turns statistical relationships into numerical strengths that can be compared when assessing possible causal explanations.

The central assumption concerns what happens after conditioning on another variable. If conditioning on Z increases the dependence between X and Y, the method treats this as evidence that Z is likely to be a common effect of X and Y. The abstract relates this assumption to the faithfulness perspective used in constraint-based causal learning. It is an assumption guiding causal interpretation, rather than an unconditional rule that dependence changes establish causation.

The algorithm gathers votes for candidate causal directions from these comparisons and orients edges according to the majority. In most experiments with known causal structures, it produced plausible results and outperformed the conventional PC algorithm. Those findings support the usefulness of aggregating dependence-strength evidence in the tested settings while preserving the method's reliance on its stated causal assumption.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based causal learner uses changes in dependence to vote on causal directions under an explicit common-effect assumption.

title: A kernel-based causal learning algorithm

abstract: Nowadays, for many tasks such as object recognition or language modeling, data is plentiful. As such, an important challenge has become to find learning algorithms which can make use of all the available data. In this setting, called ``large-scale learning'' by Bottou and Bousquet (2008), learning and optimization become different and powerful optimization algorithms are suboptimal learning algorithms. While most efforts are focused on adapting optimization algorithms for learning by efficiently using the information contained in the Hessian, Le Roux et al. (2008) exploited the special structure of the learning problem to achieve faster convergence. In this paper, we investigate a natural way of combining these two directions to yield fast and robust learning algorithms.

(2008) exploited the special structure of the learning problem to achieve faster convergence. In this paper, we investigate a natural way of combining these two directions to yield fast and robust learning algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning when data is plentiful, as in object recognition and language modeling. In this setting, the challenge is to design algorithms that can make effective use of the available examples. The authors emphasize that learning and optimization become different tasks: a powerful method for optimizing an objective can still be a suboptimal learning algorithm.

They bring together two research directions. One adapts optimization methods to learning by efficiently using the Hessian, which describes how an objective’s curvature changes across parameter directions. The other exploits the special structure of the learning problem, an approach that earlier work used to obtain faster convergence. These directions suggest complementary ways to guide learning updates.

The paper investigates a natural combination of these ideas aimed at producing fast, robust learning algorithms. Its central contribution, as described in the abstract, is this combined direction. The stated motivation is that algorithm design should account for both optimization information and the structure of learning when abundant data makes their distinction consequential.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates combining Hessian information with the special structure of learning problems to develop fast, robust algorithms for settings with abundant data.

title: A fast natural Newton method

abstract: Minimization of the rank loss or, equivalently, maximization of the AUC in bipartite ranking calls for minimizing the number of disagreements between pairs of instances. Since the complexity of this problem is inherently quadratic in the number of training examples, it is tempting to ask how much is actually lost by minimizing a simple univariate loss function, as done by standard classification methods, as a surrogate. In this paper, we first note that minimization of 0/1 loss is not an option, as it may yield an arbitrarily high rank loss. We show, however, that better results can be achieved by means of a weighted (cost-sensitive) version of 0/1 loss. Yet, the real gain is obtained through margin-based loss functions, for which we are able to derive proper bounds, not only for rank risk but, more importantly, also for rank regret. The paper is completed with an experimental study in which we address specific questions raised by our theoretical analysis.

We show, however, that better results can be achieved by means of a weighted (cost-sensitive) version of 0/1 loss. paragraphs: Bipartite ranking seeks an ordering that minimizes disagreements between pairs of examples, equivalently maximizing AUC. Working directly with those pairs creates a problem whose complexity is inherently quadratic in the number of training examples. The paper asks how much ranking quality might be sacrificed by using a loss evaluated on individual examples instead.

The answer depends on the surrogate loss. Ordinary classification error, measured by zero-one loss, can produce arbitrarily high ranking loss, so optimizing it does not provide an adequate general solution. A cost-sensitive, weighted version yields better results. The strongest developments concern margin-based losses, for which the authors derive bounds connecting individual-example optimization to ranking performance.

Those bounds cover both rank risk and rank regret, with the latter addressing the gap from the best achievable ranking risk. An experimental study investigates questions motivated by the theory. The contribution is a principled account of when simpler classification-style objectives can support ranking, together with a clear warning that ordinary classification accuracy alone is insufficient.
summary.tldr: Margin-based losses on individual examples yield ranking guarantees, while minimizing ordinary classification error can give arbitrarily high ranking loss.

title: Bipartite Ranking through Minimization of Univariate Loss

abstract: A Bayes Point machine is a binary classifier that approximates the Bayes-optimal classifier by estimating the mean of the posterior distribution of classifier parameters. Past Bayes Point machines have overcome the intractability of this goal by using message passing techniques that approximate the posterior of the classifier parameters as a Gaussian distribution. In this paper, we investigate alternative message passing approaches that do not rely on Gaussian approximation. To make this possible, we introduce a new computational shortcut based on linear multiple-choice knapsack problems that reduces the complexity of computing Bayes Point belief propagation messages from exponential to linear in the number of data features. Empirical tests of our approach show significant improvement in linear classification over both soft-margin SVMs and Expectation Propagation Bayes Point machines for several real-world UCI datasets.

Past Bayes Point machines have overcome the intractability of this goal by using message passing techniques that approximate the posterior of the classifier parameters as a Gaussian distribution. In this paper, we investigate alternative message passing approaches that do not rely on Gaussian approximation. To make this possible, we introduce a new computational shortcut based on linear multiple-choice knapsack problems that reduces the complexity of computing Bayes Point belief propagation messages from exponential to linear in the number of data features. Empirical tests of our approach show significant improvement in linear classification over both soft-margin SVMs and Expectation Propagation Bayes Point machines for several real-world UCI datasets.

paragraphs: A Bayes Point machine performs binary classification by estimating the posterior mean of classifier parameters as an approximation to the Bayes-optimal classifier. Computing that mean is intractable in the setting considered. Earlier methods address the difficulty through message passing that approximates the parameter posterior with a Gaussian distribution.

This paper investigates message-passing alternatives that avoid that Gaussian approximation. Its enabling contribution is a computational shortcut based on linear multiple-choice knapsack problems. The shortcut reduces the cost of computing Bayes Point belief-propagation messages from exponential to linear in the number of data features, making the alternative inference approach substantially more manageable.

Experiments on several real-world UCI datasets show significant improvements in linear classification over both soft-margin support vector machines and Expectation Propagation Bayes Point machines. These results provide empirical support for the alternative message calculations. The contribution combines a different treatment of the posterior with a specific complexity reduction, rather than relying on the Gaussian approximation used by previous Bayes Point approaches.
summary.tldr: A knapsack-based shortcut makes non-Gaussian Bayes Point message passing efficient and improves linear classification on several UCI datasets.

title: Estimating the Bayes Point Using Linear Knapsack Problems

abstract: Hierarchical decomposition promises to help scale reinforcement learning algorithms naturally to real-world problems by exploiting their underlying structure. Model-based algorithms, which provided the first finite-time convergence guarantees for reinforcement learning, may also play an important role in coping with the relative scarcity of data in large environments. In this paper, we introduce an algorithm that fully integrates modern hierarchical and model-learning methods in the standard reinforcement learning setting. Our algorithm, R-maxq, inherits the efficient model-based exploration of the R-max algorithm and the opportunities for abstraction provided by the MAXQ framework. We analyze the sample complexity of our algorithm, and our experiments in a standard simulation environment illustrate the advantages of combining hierarchies and models.
originalAbstract: Hierarchical decomposition promises to help scale reinforcement learning algorithms naturally to real-world problems by exploiting their underlying structure. Model-based algorithms, which provided the first finite-time convergence guarantees for reinforcement learning, may also play an important role in coping with the relative scarcity of data in large environments. In this paper, we introduce an algorithm that fully integrates modern hierarchical and model-learning methods in the standard reinforcement learning setting. Our algorithm, R-maxq, inherits the efficient model-based exploration of the R-max algorithm and the opportunities for abstraction provided by the MAXQ framework. We analyze the sample complexity of our algorithm, and our experiments in a standard simulation environment illustrate the advantages of combining hierarchies and models.

paragraphs: The paper brings together two approaches intended to help reinforcement learning handle large problems: breaking a task into a hierarchy and learning a model of the environment. Hierarchical decomposition offers a way to exploit the structure of a problem. Model-based learning addresses a complementary concern, the relative scarcity of experience available in large environments.

The proposed algorithm, R-maxq, integrates the exploration approach of R-max with the abstraction opportunities of MAXQ. The contribution is their combination within the standard reinforcement learning setting. Rather than treating hierarchy and model learning as separate options, the algorithm is designed to use both as parts of the same learning procedure.

The authors analyze sample complexity, connecting the method to questions about how much experience learning requires. Experiments in a standard simulation environment illustrate advantages of combining hierarchies with models. These findings support the proposed integration in that setting, while the abstract’s discussion of real-world scalability remains a motivation rather than a reported deployment result.
summary.tldr: R-maxq combines R-max’s model-based exploration with MAXQ’s hierarchical abstraction, supported by sample-complexity analysis and simulation experiments.

title: Hierarchical Model-Based Reinforcement Learning: R-max + MAXQ
